25, or that their members came from different directories, which is the half a
person would need to act. That is O89.

### Twelve volumes that cannot be opened

Twelve files named `.cbz` are RAR archives. `taiyaku_read::sniff` gets this
right from the first 512 bytes and records `scan_entry.format = 'rar'` — the
half of `docs/sidecar.md`'s "a zip named `.cbr` and a RAR named `.cbz` are both
routine" that works. `derive::is_readable` then admits only `Dir` and `Zip`, so
all twelve are counted in `DeriveReport::unreadable` and never become members.
One series, invisible. That is O90. *(O90 closed on 2026-09-17 — see "O90"
below. The twelve were repacked to zip, and the counter now says why each
entry was skipped. The series was not wholly invisible: the twelve were
volumes 3–12, 19 and 20, and its other 25 volumes read throughout.)*

The thirteenth `unreadable` is the counter's other site: a member whose bytes
could not be hashed, not a format that cannot be read. One field, two causes.
*(Both halves wrong, found while closing O90 and left as written.
The thirteenth was `Bisque Doll de Chu ♡.cbz`, a zip that opens cleanly and
holds 185 JPEG XL pages, so the walk could not count its pages; `classify`
counts that before it hashes anything. And the field had four causes, not two,
as `DeriveReport`'s own doc already said.)*

### What a derive costs when there is nothing left to hash

**8.4 seconds**, wall clock, for 1858 works and 1883 members over 130 series —
walk, derive, proposals and `hand::reconcile` together, on local NVMe.

That closes the question §6 of the reconciliation design left open. The
concern was that `reconcile` is paid unconditionally on every derive where the
read-back beside it is gated on `!absorbed`. At real scale the whole derive is
8.4 s and `reconcile` is not visible in it. The synthetic figure taken on
2026-08-31 — 105 ms at 2000 works and 4 roots, in-memory SQLite on tmpfs — was
the right order and pessimistic about the surrounding cost, not optimistic.

Two measurement hazards found on the way, both worth not repeating:

- **The debug binary hashes about fourteen times slower.** 0.21 archives/sec
  against 2.9 in release, measured on the same files: 141 archives in eleven
  minutes, then 130 in forty-five seconds after `cargo build --release`.
  sha256 is what derivation spends its time on, and it is exactly the code an
  unoptimised build ruins. Any timing this project has taken with
  `target/debug/taiyaku` is an order of magnitude pessimistic on hashing.
- **An interrupted derive resumes.** The first run was killed mid-hash; the
  141 digests it had written to `scan_entry` were still there and the restart
  picked up from 141 rather than from zero. That is `derive` opening no file
  except to hash a member nothing has hashed yet, working as designed — and it
  means a first scan of a large library is safely interruptible, which nothing
  had checked.

### The walk over NFS, which is why the library was copied

Scanning the share in place, `--no-derive`, no hashing at all: **2 hours 50
minutes** for 6003 entries, at **0% CPU**. About 1.7 seconds per entry, all of
it round-trip latency. The same walk over the local copy is seconds, and
`rsync` pulled the 490 GB off the same mount at ~105 MB/s — so the link is
fine and it is per-file metadata that is not.

Not tracked as an item: the deployment target is a server with the library
local to it, so this measures the mount rather than the product. Recorded
because the number is surprising and somebody will otherwise re-derive it.

### One thing that worked, and one that will not on a read-only share

`proposals::raise` offered **29** suggestions on first contact, and the
scoring separated them correctly: `Full Color Edition`, `The Perfect Edition`
and `Digital Colored Comics` scored 2.0 against the edition vocabulary, while
`Gaiden`, `Side Story` and `Anthology Comic` scored 0.0 — the second group
being different works rather than editions, which is the judgement the score
exists to make.

The share itself is mounted `rw` but its directories are `root:root 755`
against uid 1000, so `watch::probe` was refused, named the refusal, and fell
back from 24-hour to 15-minute polling rather than failing the scan —
`watch.rs`'s "a write that fails is not an error return" under a condition no
test stages. On a library mounted that way `<root>/.taiyaku/` can never be
created and every correction answers `persisted: false`, which is O82's
read-only case as the ordinary case rather than the corner one. Not tracked
here either: the server that will run this owns its storage.

## What a *save* costs on a real library — 2026-09-05

The section below priced the preview and nothing priced the save, because
until C4 PR B there was no save: every rules route wrote the `rule` table and
returned. `preview::apply` is that missing half — the same derivation, without
the rollback and under `Documents::Reconcile` rather than `Skip`.

Measured through `apply_cost_on_a_real_library`, an `#[ignore]`d test beside
the preview's own and pointed at the same `TAIYAKU_PREVIEW_DB`, on a `--release`
build against a **copy** of the same library the section below used — 130
series, 1858 works, 2044 scan entries, 4 rules, and a root with
`keeps_documents` **off**.

| | run 1 | run 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `preview`, unchanged list | 287.1 ms | 308.4 ms |
| `apply`, unchanged list | 280.7 ms | 330.6 ms |
| `apply` again, unchanged list | 277.2 ms | 303.3 ms |

**A save costs what a preview costs.** The two straddle each other across the
runs, which is the finding: committing instead of rolling back is not where
the time goes, and neither is the reconcile pass. The derivation is the whole
cost, exactly as the preview's own measurement concluded — so the screen's
Save button needs no different treatment from its preview, and the ~281 ms the
editor was designed around is the right figure for both.

**Single-shot per run, not a median of ten** like the preview measurement
beside it, and the second run sat under a concurrently building workspace.
That is why two runs are tabled rather than one number: the honest claim is
"the same, within noise", not a figure to three digits.

**Two things this library could not measure.** It holds **0 accepted
proposals** (29 open), so the reopen path — the property
`a_save_of_the_unchanged_list_reopens_nothing` exists for, and the one an
import breaks — is asserted here against a library that cannot exercise it;
the fixtures are what cover it. And its root has `keeps_documents` off, so the
`Documents::Reconcile` pass had no document to write: what a save costs on a
root that *keeps* documents is unmeasured, and it is the only case where a
save should cost more than a preview.

**The impact agreed exactly**, both runs, and both saves reopened nothing:
`Impact { series_before: 129, series_after: 129, series_merged: 0,
works_rehomed: 0, works_orphaned: 0, proposals_reopened: 0,
proposals_raised: 0 }`. That the preview and the save agree is pinned on
fixtures by `a_preview_and_a_real_save_produce_the_same_structure`, where a
fixture has three works; this is the same claim where 1858 works give a
disagreement somewhere to hide.

*(129 series against the 130 the table above counts: `Impact` counts distinct
series **names** reached by a member, and one series in this library holds no
member the grouping query returns.)*

## What a rule preview costs on a real library — 2026-09-03

Spec C4 §11 marks its mockup's "34 ms" as **an illustration and not a
measurement**, and says so honestly: when that spec was written there was no
store, no scanner and no library to re-derive. This is the measurement it
asked for, and it changes one thing about the screen.

Measured on the local copy of the real library — **130 series, 1858 works,
1858 editions, 1883 members, 2044 scan entries, 4 rules** — with a `--release`
build, ten runs each, through `preview::preview`. The harness is
`preview_cost_on_a_real_library`, an `#[ignore]`d test pointed at a database
by `TAIYAKU_PREVIEW_DB`, the same shape the corpus tests use for
`TAIYAKU_CORPUS`. It was run against a **copy**: the preview writes nothing,
but that is not a reason to point a new code path at the only real library on
this machine.

| what | median | best | worst |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| preview of the library's own unchanged rule list | **281 ms** | 279 ms | 286 ms |
| preview of that list with one rule appended | **495 ms** | 489 ms | 510 ms |
| `grouping` alone, 1883 members | **1.3 ms** | — | — |

**The diff is free and the derivation is the whole cost.** `grouping` is 1.3
ms of the 281, so the remaining ~280 ms is `replace_all`, `derive_with` and
the rollback — that is, re-deriving 1858 works. Nothing here is worth
optimising by making the diff cheaper.

**So the preview is not affordable on every keystroke, and C4 §6's
"debounced" is not enough.** §6 says the route "writes nothing and is safe to
call on every keystroke, debounced". Safe, yes. Affordable, no: at 281 ms a
keystroke-driven preview is one derivation per typed character on a 130-series
library, and this library is *small* against the 156 series C4 §1's mockup
assumed and far smaller than the thousands §11 names as the unknown case.

**The screen previews on demand.** C4 §11 predicted this exact outcome and
pre-approved the remedy — *"if it is not, the fix is to debounce harder or
preview on demand, and neither changes this design"* — so this is a settled
question rather than a new one. The rule editor gets an explicit control
rather than a keystroke hook. Reordering by drag stays a preview trigger,
since a drag is one gesture rather than a stream of them.

**The second row is also the first evidence the mechanism works on real
data.** The appended rule is a bare `(?<series>.+)` capture over the whole
path, which is the degenerate case: it gives all but one work its own series,
and the preview reports `series_after: 1881, works_rehomed: 1880,
proposals_raised: 343` — 343 new proposals a person would face after saving.
That is the Impact tab earning its place. A screen that let someone save that
rule and *then* discover 343 proposals is the screen this one replaces.

**The write lock is held for the duration.** `preview` opens `BEGIN
IMMEDIATE` and holds it across the derivation, so a preview blocks any writer
for 0.3–0.5 s on this library — including a scan on the second connection
`Library::working` hands out. Not a defect and not tracked as an item: the
alternative is deriving outside a transaction, which is the thing the whole
design exists to avoid. Recorded because a person previewing rules while a
scan runs is an ordinary thing to do, and this is the number that says what
happens.

**Not measured:** a library of thousands of series, which §11 names and
nothing here answers; and the cost with override detection running alongside,
which is quadratic in rules and was measured on four. *(It was called conflict
detection until O95 closed on 2026-09-05; nothing about the cost changed.)*

## What a `VACUUM INTO` of the real library costs — 2026-09-04

The C4 PR 2 build design §4 left this unmeasured and said so, and §10 named it
as the one figure that PR could produce and had not. It decides whether
`POST /api/library/backups` can stay synchronous. It can, by two orders of
magnitude.

Measured on a **copy** of the real library — **130 series, 1858 works, 1883
members, 2044 scan entries**, 3,534,848 bytes — through the shipped command,
`taiyaku library backup --db <copy>`, `--release` build, seven runs:

```
run 1: 7 ms      run 5: 6 ms
run 2: 6 ms      run 6: 6 ms
run 3: 6 ms      run 7: 6 ms
run 4: 6 ms
```

**Median 6 ms**, and that figure is an **upper bound on the `VACUUM INTO`
itself**: it is whole-process wall clock, so it includes `exec`, opening the
database, the migration check `Library::open` runs, and the `strftime` that
mints the name. The statement is some fraction of six milliseconds and this
measurement cannot say which fraction — it does not need to, because the
question it was taken to answer is whether a route can afford to answer when
the copy is done, and at 6 ms the answer is not close.

For scale, the same library's **rule preview costs a median of 281 ms**
(2026-09-03, above). A backup is roughly **one fiftieth** of a preview the
screen already runs on demand.

**The backup is smaller than the database**: 3,338,240 bytes against
3,534,848, because `VACUUM INTO` writes a defragmented copy. That is a
property of the statement rather than a loss — the copy restores whole:
`sqlite3 <backup> "select count(*) from work, series, member"` answers
**1858 / 130 / 1883**, the same as the source.

**Isolation, proven rather than asserted** — the discipline the preview
measurement above records for the same reason. The command was pointed at a
copy in the scratch directory, and afterwards `cmp` reported the copy
**byte-identical to the source**, so nothing was written to either. The source
directory listing is unchanged. `VACUUM INTO` is a read of the source and a
write of a new file, and this is the evidence for that rather than the
assumption.

**Not measured:** what this costs on a library of thousands of series, which
is the same gap the preview measurement leaves; and whether a second
connection's `VACUUM INTO` is as invisible to the server's readers as WAL
promises, which the build design §10 names and which wants the process under
load rather than a command run seven times. Both are still open.

## What the roots screen's own scan costs, driven end to end — 2026-09-04

Spec C4's roots screen (PR A) is the first thing that can start a scan from a
browser, and the build design's §10 named the cost of one as a gap both spec B
and C4's server half carry. This is the first figure.

**Setup.** A copy of the real library's `library.db` (1858 works, 130 series,
one root at `/home/davey/temp/manga-test/Volumes`, 490 GB, never scanned by any
serving process — `last_scan_at` and `last_scan_status` both `NULL`), served by
a debug build on `127.0.0.1:8137`. The scanned root is **not** that one: it is a
scratch root of three four-page CBZs written into the session scratchpad, so the
walk is trivial and what the number measures is the derivation behind it. The
real tree was read and never written, and the proof is below.

**The figure: `elapsed_secs` 1.028**, from `POST /api/library/roots/2/scan` to
the poll that first read `running: false`. Wall clock across the screen's own
1 s polling loop was 1.05 s, so the poll interval is the resolution here rather
than the measurement. The walk itself is 2 directories and 3 files; the other
second is `derive::derive`, which is library-wide rather than per-root and so
re-derived all 1861 works. **That is the shape worth carrying: a scan's cost is
its root's walk plus a whole-library derivation, so scanning the smallest root
in a large library is not cheap.** A 1 s poll is therefore not obviously wrong,
and is still a guess: nothing has scanned the 490 GB root.

**What the report actually carried.** 8 fields from `ScanReport` and 29 from
`DeriveReport` — **37**, which is the number `ScanReport.test.tsx` asserts, now
confirmed against the wire rather than against arithmetic over the two structs.
Non-zero among the fields the screen draws *first*, the ones naming what the
scan did not do: `unreadable: 13`, `unattached_chapter_dirs: 1`,
`series_holding_no_work: 1`. The 13 are the real library's — O90's RAR-named
`.cbz` volumes and one member whose bytes could not be hashed — so the
confession-first ordering had something real to confess on its first run.
*(The thirteenth was not a member that could not be hashed. It was an archive
of JPEG XL pages whose pages the walk could not count — found while closing O90,
see "O90".)*

`last_scan_at` and `last_scan_status` were written for the first time by a
serving process: `2026-09-04 20:38:42` / `ok`.

**The three validations, each refusing with its own sentence:**

```
POST /roots {"path":"…/Volumes/Akame ga KILL!"}
  400  is inside existing root /home/davey/temp/manga-test/Volumes (id 1)
POST /roots {"path":"/home/davey/temp"}
  400  contains existing root /home/davey/temp/manga-test/Volumes (id 1)
POST /roots {"path":"/nope/not/here"}
  400  No such file or directory (os error 2)
POST /roots {"path":"…/scratch-root"}
  200  watching: true, watch_reason: null, interval_secs: 86400
```

Both nesting directions, and the probe answered on the *success* — which is the
only one of the three that produces anything when nothing is wrong, and is what
lets the screen state the regime before the first scan.

**The regime line for the real, never-scanned root** renders as
`watch state unknown — probed when a root is added · no scan interval set ·
never scanned` — no `null`, no `undefined`, which is the case the row that had
never been scanned would otherwise have shown three of.

**Single-flight held.** A second `POST` while the first was running answered
**409**, naming the root and its path, rather than queuing a second walk.

**`?dryrun=true` is still refused.** 400, `unknown field 'dryrun', expected
'dry_run'` — the `deny_unknown_fields` fix from PR 1's whole-branch review,
re-confirmed from the client side, since a client that misspells that key runs a
committed removal. `config.ts`'s own test pins the exact string for this reason.

**Removal quoted the same counts it then charged.** Dry run
`{works: 1, positions: 0, notes: 0}` with the work count unchanged at 1859
afterwards; the real `DELETE` reported the identical three and left 1858 — the
library's original count exactly.

**Proof the real tree was never written.** `find … -printf '%p %s\n' | sort |
sha256sum` over `/home/davey/temp/manga-test`, before and after the whole
session: `75c20e25f913ec55ecde79173dbb6f8e5a89a6baf1fc5258337e23563430fb13`
both times, and `find … -name .taiyaku` finds none. The root's
`keeps_documents` is `0`, so nothing should have been written under it, and
this is the measurement rather than the assumption.

## The users and backup screens against a real library — 2026-09-06

C4 PR C, driven end to end against a **copy** of the real library at
`/home/davey/temp/manga-test/library.db` — 3,534,848 bytes, the same 130-series
library every figure since 2026-09-03 is measured on. The copy is the whole
isolation: the server was started with `--db` pointing at it, and the original's
sha256 is `d1111d80beebab85479b8266dc00814b7a5bbca207bd4aae9ad4dcbc19fa0dce`
**before and after the session**, unchanged. Two accounts on the copy —
`local` (admin, the account the library already had) and `alice` (reader, added
for this) — with a session each and one API key.

**`GET /api/library/users` costs 0.3–0.7 ms** over the loopback, five
consecutive requests: 0.674, 0.479, 0.376, 0.328, 0.291 ms. The route assembles
three queries per account — sessions, keys, grants — so the figure is *two
accounts' worth*, and what is **not** measured here is a library with fifty of
them. That is the honest limit of this number: it says the shape is cheap, not
that it scales, and nothing on this branch depends on the latter.

**The flag this branch added is true end to end.** With Chrome signed in and a
`curl` session open on the same account, the list marked exactly one session
`current: true` — the browser's — and `false` for the other and for `alice`'s.
Read off the rendered card as well as the JSON: the Chrome row draws **this
browser** and the `curl` row (`user_agent: the admin browser`) does not. Before
this branch the field was `false` for every row, on the screen where revoking
the wrong one signs the administrator out.

**`POST /api/library/backups` costs 7.2 ms and 6.3 ms** through the route,
against the 6 ms median the CLI measured on 2026-09-04 — the same `VACUUM INTO`
plus HTTP, a session lookup and `spawn_blocking`. Output 3,338,240 bytes from a
3,534,848-byte database, which is the vacuum reclaiming free pages rather than
anything the route does.

**The same-second collision reproduces.** Two `POST`s issued concurrently after
a backup had already been taken that second both answered **409** with the
store's own sentence — *"a backup named library-20260907T034309Z.db is already
there; the name carries a whole-second timestamp, so a second backup inside the
same second has nowhere to go"*. The screen renders that sentence rather than
classifying by status, which is deliberate: the in-memory-library refusal is
also a 409, and a screen reading the number would have to guess which it had.

**The download hands over the file, exactly.** `GET
/api/library/backups/library-20260907T034309Z.db` answered 200,
`content-type: application/vnd.sqlite3`,
`content-disposition: attachment; filename="…"`, `content-length: 3338240`, and
the bytes' sha256 is identical to the file on disk
(`6496937690c1e7eda2f52862514ef44a17f77eb715a888c888a43cfaa6cc7c83`). Measured
with `curl` rather than through the browser deliberately: a browser download is
the one thing the request log reports as **0 bytes**, so the browser cannot be
the witness here.

**What the pixels found that the tests did not.** One defect, in copy: the add
form's paragraph carried a markdown backtick pair around `004_auth.sql` and
drew them as themselves. It is `<code>` now. Everything else the screens claim
was confirmed as drawn — the sole administrator's role control and Remove both
dead with one reason beside them, `local — this is you`, the removal dialog
reading *"Removing alice takes 0 in-progress positions, 0 notes, 1 open
session, 1 API key and 0 root grants"* with correct singulars, and the backup
list newest-first at `3.2 MiB` each.

**Re-driven after the review round**, on the same copy: the backticks are two
elements now, ticking a root on `alice` sent `roots: [1]`, the store answered
with the grant, and the card came back live with the box ticked — which is the
*hold* working, since the controls are dead from the click until the list read
that follows it lands. The real library's sha256 was unchanged again
afterwards.

**Counts after this branch:** 2028 Rust tests (from 2027 — Task 1's one server
test), and 2,006 in `web/` (1,146 `node`, 860 `jsdom`), from 1,933. The 73 new
web tests are 19 in the two clients and 54 across the three screens. **Fifteen
of those fifty-four were written after the screens were finished**, counted per
commit rather than estimated: 39 stood before any review, 2 came from a
self-review round, and the four whole-branch passes' fix rounds added 3, 3, 4
and 3.

**Four passes, fifteen findings, and they did not converge: 5, then 3, then 4,
then 3.** Every finding of passes 2, 3 and 4 lived inside a fix an earlier pass
had produced — the same shape #108 recorded over four passes and #110 over
three. What *did* fall is severity rather than rate: pass 1 found a control
that silently revoked a grant, pass 4 found three narrow races (a tombstone
outliving its account through a reused React key, a revocation writing back a
click-time snapshot, and two dry runs answering out of order). **A fifth pass
was not commissioned**, on spec A2's own precedent: the rate is a fact about
the process rather than about the code, and what measures whether a test can
see a defect is hand-applying it — which every fix on this branch has had, and
every one of the nineteen review-written tests fails against the defect it
names.

## O99: the document stamp, reproduced rather than waited for — 2026-09-06

**The failure came from CI run 437's push job on `main`**, not from a branch,
and not from anything this session ran. Read back off the forge rather than
quoted from a report: job `test` (id 7165) failed at
`preview/tests.rs:292:5`, 1109 passed and 1 failed of the 2027 that run held,
and the two trees differed in one file and one field —
`"updated": "2026-09-06T21:28:50Z"` against `"…49Z"` inside
`<root>/.taiyaku/<content_key>.library.json`, every other byte equal, the
archive beside it identical.

*(The local reproduction below produced its own pair, `05:28:20Z` against
`05:28:19Z` on 2026-09-07. Same defect, different clock; the CI pair above is
the one that is evidence of anything.)*

**Reproduced deterministically before anything was edited**, by copying the
test and sleeping 1.1 s between the settled snapshot and `preview::apply` — the
one variable, and the only change. It fails every run, and the instrumented
diff names exactly one path and one field. The stamp comes from
`librarydoc::of`, which fills `updated` from
`SELECT strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', 'now')` at projection time; no column
holds it, so two projections of an unchanged work differ whenever a wall-clock
second falls between them. `hand::reconcile` already normalises that field
before deciding whether a document is stale, and says why in its own comment:
comparing it would report every reachable document stale, including one written
a moment ago.

**Why the fix is a second helper rather than a change to `tree_snapshot`.**
Four call sites, and only one of them spans a write. The other three —
`a_preview_leaves_the_library_tree_byte_identical`,
`skipping_documents_leaves_the_library_tree_byte_identical` and
`removal_cost_touches_no_file_on_disk` — each assert that an operation wrote
*nothing*, so for them a rewrite that moved only the stamp is exactly the
defect the comparison exists to catch. Normalising inside the shared helper
would have blinded three tests to close one flake.

**Three checks on the fix, run in this order.**

1. The fixed test, with the 1.1 s sleep still in it: **passes**. The same sleep
   that made it fail deterministically no longer does.
2. The same sleep, plus `Documents::Reconcile` hand-swapped for `Skip` at
   `preview.rs:651`: **fails**, on its own assertion — *"a save derives under
   Documents::Reconcile, so it repairs the gap it found"*. The normalisation
   cost the test nothing of what it is for.
3. `NORMALISED_STAMP.clone_into(&mut doc.updated)` removed from the helper:
   `normalising_the_stamp_hides_a_second_and_hides_nothing_else` **fails**.

**The third test exists because the flake cannot be proved from the test that
carried it.** What differs is two projections a second apart, and a unit test's
two writes land inside the same second almost every time — which is why this
survived from #109 until a CI run happened to straddle a boundary. So the
normalisation is proved directly, on the two stamps that run produced, rather
than by leaving a 1.1 s sleep in the suite. Its last two assertions are what
keep it honest: a helper that returned an empty map, or dropped documents,
would satisfy the equality and fail the inequality after it, and one that tried
to parse every file under the root would panic on the archive beside it.

**The mutation sweep examined nothing, and that is the correct result rather
than a clean bill.** `scripts/mutants.sh --since main` answers *"No mutants to
filter"*: every line this branch changes is test code — a `pub(crate)` helper
under `#[cfg(test)]`, a test, and one call site — and `cargo-mutants` does not
mutate test code. Read as coverage it would say the branch is fully caught;
what it actually says is that it had nothing to look at. The three hand-applied
defects above are the whole of the evidence here. It is O87's point arriving
from a third direction — after a mutant caught only across a crate boundary,
and an `unviable` hiding a live hole — in its cheapest form: a sweep reporting
zero is a fact about the sweep until you check what it ran on. `--since main`
also reported no survivor outside the baseline, which is true and equally
uninformative about this branch.

**Counts after this branch:** 2029 Rust tests, from 2028 — the one new test
above. `web/` unchanged at 2,006.

## What a ComicInfo plan and a stamp cost on real archives — 2026-09-07

Spec C3 §6's build design asked for two figures in its §11 and said neither
had been taken. Both are now taken on the workstation, by
`stamp::tests::report` — `--ignored`, on the pattern `credential::tests::report`
set for argon2, because a figure that depends on the machine is a measurement
to record here rather than a threshold to fail a build on:

```
TAIYAKU_CORPUS=/home/davey/projects/taiyaku/corpus cargo test --release \
  -p taiyaku-library stamp::tests::report -- --ignored --nocapture
```

**`TAIYAKU_CORPUS` must be absolute.** `cargo test` runs a package's tests with
the working directory set to that package's own directory, so a relative
`corpus` resolves to `crates/taiyaku-library/corpus` and finds nothing — the
same trap `check-all.sh` resolves at the top of the file and documents there.
The first run of this measurement hit it.

Over `corpus/gotoubun-v01` — 3 works, 4 members, 615.6 MB of stampable
archive:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| scan and derive | 361 ms |
| **plan over every work** | **2.43 ms** |
| plain `fs::copy` of the largest archive (319.2 MB) | 58.5 ms |
| **`rewrite_one` of that archive** | **299 ms** |

**The plan is cheap, and cheap for the reason the design predicted.** 2.43 ms
across four archives is a central-directory read plus one small entry each; it
is not a page decode and it does not touch the 615 MB. So the confirmation can
stay synchronous, which was the open question §11 raised against it. The
caveat this figure does *not* answer: on the NAS over a spinning disk this is
four seeks rather than four warm reads, and nothing here has measured that.
The number above is a workstation figure with the files in page cache.

**A rewrite is about five times a plain copy** — 299 ms against 58.5 ms for
the same 319 MB, or roughly 1.07 GB/s. The difference is the zip parse, the
central directory rebuilt, and a sha256 over the output, which the stamp needs
anyway because the member row is about to record it. §6's *"not a cheap
click"* holds: at this rate the 4.1 GB the design uses as its example is
around four seconds of rewriting, before any of it is paid over a network.

**The measurement writes nothing to the corpus, and proves it rather than
claiming it.** `plan` only reads, so its half runs against the corpus in
place; the rewrite half copies one archive into a temp directory first, and
the test re-hashes the corpus original at the end and asserts it is unchanged.
An isolation that is only asserted in a comment is the kind that stops being
true later.

**Still not measured**, and both stay in the build design's §11: anything on
the NAS, and whether `raw_copy_file` preserves a data descriptor on an entry
written with one. The corpus's archives come from many tools and at least some
streaming writers emit them; nothing in `corpus/gotoubun-v01` exercised that
path, so the byte-identity test has not yet seen one.

## O97: how wide the import window actually is — 2026-09-08

The build design's §0.2 owed this figure and refused to guess it. O96 could
name its window — a save costs a median **280.7 ms** on the real library (the
`apply`-unchanged-list row above) — and the claim that an import "should be
cheaper, because `rules/import` writes the rule table and derives nothing" was
marked as the guess it was.

**Measured 2026-09-08, against an isolated copy of the real library**
(`/home/davey/temp/manga-test/library.db`, 3.5 MB, the four seeded rules),
copied into a scratch directory first. Ten runs of `taiyaku library rules
--import`, which reaches the same `rules::replace_all` the HTTP route does:

| | median | mean | min / max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| rule import, whole process | **2.3 ms** | 2.6 ms | 2.1 / 5.1 ms |

**What this figure is, precisely.** It is the whole CLI process — launch of a
17 MB binary, opening SQLite, the import, exit — so the store operation is
*at most* 2.3 ms and the real number is smaller. It is **not** the HTTP route:
it omits `Authorization`, the JSON parse, and the network. It is measured on
this workstation, not on the NAS.

**The result is two orders of magnitude, and it does not change the design.**
An import window is ~2 ms of store work against a save's 280.7 ms of
derivation. What keeps the window real is everything the measurement excludes
— a LAN round trip is 1–5 ms on its own, and the NAS is slower — so the
window is narrow rather than absent. §0.2 said the design is the same at 5 ms
as at 500 ms because a window that must not admit a second writer is not a
question of width, and the measurement is what makes that a statement rather
than an assumption. It also says why O97 survived from #109 to now with nobody
tripping over it: the window is short enough that hitting it takes either bad
luck or a slow link.

**Isolation proven afterwards rather than assumed**: the real `library.db`'s
mtime was identical before and after (`2026-09-02 05:51:48.853004102`), `find
-newer` against the start stamp returned nothing under the real tree, and
`git status` was clean.

**Still owed, and carried into O97's own entry rather than lost here**: the
same figure over HTTP, and the same figure on the NAS. Neither changes what
shipped; both would sharpen the sentence above about what keeps the window
real.

*Both were measured on 2026-09-08 and both are below, together with the drive
this section did not do. **The 2.3 ms above is a tmpfs figure** — the same
command against the same database on ext4 costs 15.2 ms, and the difference is
one `fsync`. The paragraph above is left as written; read the next section
before quoting the number.*

## O97: the same figure over HTTP and on the NAS, and the drive — 2026-09-08

The section above owed three things and did one of them. This is the other two
— the import window measured over HTTP and with the database on the NAS — and
the drive the build design's §5 Step 4 asked for and the branch shipped
without: a real library in a browser with the import held open at the
transport.

### Everything measured on the same day, same library, same binary

A copy of the real library (`/home/davey/temp/manga-test/library.db`, 3.5 MB,
130 series, 1858 works, 2044 scan entries, the four seeded rules), with its
root repointed to an empty scratch directory first. The HTTP figures are
`POST /api/library/rules/import` through `taiyaku serve --release`, timed by
`curl`'s own `time_total`, **interleaved** local-then-NAS on each of 20 rounds
so a background spike lands on both.

| what | median | mean | min / max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST …/rules/import`, database on local ext4 NVMe | **6.0 ms** | 5.9 ms | 5.1 / 10.7 ms |
| `POST …/rules/import`, database on the NAS over NFSv4 | **1.7 ms** | 1.7 ms | 1.4 / 2.3 ms |
| `GET …/rules` (connect + auth + read four rules), local¹ | 0.7 ms | 1.2 ms | 0.4 / 6.3 ms |
| `GET …/rules`, NAS¹ | 0.4 ms | 0.5 ms | 0.4 / 0.7 ms |
| `library rules --import`, whole process, tmpfs | 2.3 ms | 2.3 ms | 2.1 / 2.5 ms |
| `library rules --import`, whole process, ext4 NVMe | 15.2 ms | 15.3 ms | 14.1 / 18.0 ms |
| `library rules --import`, whole process, NAS | 6.8 ms | 6.9 ms | 6.3 / 7.7 ms |

The three CLI rows are ten runs each, repeated three times for the first two;
the medians moved by 0.1 ms across repetitions, so they are stable rather than
lucky. ¹ The two `GET` rows are ten runs each, taken separately rather than
interleaved — they are the baseline the two `POST` figures are read against,
not figures being compared with one another.

### The recorded 2.3 ms was a tmpfs figure, and that is the whole story

The section above says "copied into a scratch directory first" and does not
say which filesystem. It was tmpfs: the same command against the same database
reproduces **2.3 ms** on `/tmp` and costs **15.2 ms** on ext4, across three
repetitions each. So the figure that has been standing as "what an import
costs" excluded the only expensive thing a durable write does.

| `fsync` of a 4 KiB rewrite, 30 samples | median | min / max |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ext4 on this NVMe | **4.885 ms** | 4.417 / 5.554 ms |
| NFSv4 to the NAS | **0.144 ms** | 0.128 / 0.245 ms |
| tmpfs | **0.000 ms** | — |

That single measurement explains every row in the first table. `synchronous`
is left at SQLite's default (`Library::configure` sets `foreign_keys`,
`busy_timeout`, WAL and `recursive_triggers`, and no more), so in WAL mode a
commit is `FULL` and fsyncs. On tmpfs that is free; on this NVMe it is ~5 ms,
which is essentially the whole of the 6.0 ms HTTP figure; and to the NAS it is
0.14 ms.

### The NAS is *faster*, which inverts this file's own sentence

The section above said the window stays real because of "everything the
measurement excludes — a LAN round trip is 1–5 ms on its own, and the NAS is
slower". Both halves are wrong on this hardware. The round trip to this NAS is ~0.14 ms, not
1–5 ms; and an import with the database on the NAS costs **1.7 ms** against
**6.0 ms** with it on the local disk — three and a half times *cheaper*.

The reason is not that the NAS is fast, it is that the two fsyncs mean
different things. The local one waits for a flush the drive actually honours.
The NFSv4 `COMMIT` is answered by the server, and this one answers it from its
own cache — so the NAS number is a measurement of a weaker durability promise,
not of a faster disk. Worth knowing before anyone reads it as an argument for
putting a library database on a share; the honest reading is that the local
figure is the durable one.

**None of this changes what shipped.** §0.2's own argument was that the design
is the same at 5 ms as at 500 ms, because a window that must not admit a
second writer is not a question of width. That still holds — the correction is
to the sentence about *why* the window is real, not to the gate.

### The drive: a real library, in a browser, with the import held open

`taiyaku serve` on 8180 against the copy, a 40-line Node proxy on 8181 that
forwards every request verbatim and holds `POST /api/library/rules/import` for
a configurable number of milliseconds before forwarding it upstream, and vite
on 5199 with `TAIYAKU_SERVE` pointed at the proxy. **The hold is before the
forward, not after**, so during the window the store has genuinely not been
written: the client is waiting on the network rather than on a patched
`fetch`, and the server sees the request only when the hold ends. The proxy's
own log is the evidence:

```
20:58:36.635 HOLD  25000ms  POST /api/library/rules/import
20:59:01.641 SEND  POST /api/library/rules/import
20:59:01.647 BACK  200 /api/library/rules/import
21:00:20.490 HOLD  90000ms  POST /api/library/rules/import
21:01:50.491 SEND  POST /api/library/rules/import
21:01:50.495 BACK  200 /api/library/rules/import
```

Six and four milliseconds upstream, held for twenty-five and ninety seconds.

**All five of Step 4's assertions hold**, read out of the DOM rather than off a
screenshot:

- Save is `disabled` and reads its ordinary label — `Save — apply to 0 works`,
  never `Saving…`. The two are separate states and this is the one that proves
  it.
- Import reads `Importing…` and is `disabled`.
- Every rule row carries `draggable="false"` and all three controls on each row
  — the enable checkbox, the pattern button, the delete — report
  `disabled: true`, as does `+ Add`.
- The Overrides tab's two options (`Move rule 4 above rule 1`, `Edit rule 4`)
  are `disabled` during the window and enabled again after it. That row exists
  here because this library really does have the seeded-defaults conflict —
  *rule 4 overrides rule 1 on 178 files*, `Death Note (Colored Council)` — so
  the freeze was checked against a real override rather than a fixture's.
- The form stays live: all nine inputs and selects report `disabled: false`
  during the window. Typing `EDITED-DURING-IMPORT` into rule 4's pattern and
  pressing Tab drew the `refused` notice — *"An import was running, so your
  edit to rule 4 was not applied…"* — while `Importing…` still stood, and the
  list's own row 4 still showed the old pattern.
- When the import landed, the imported rules were on screen (three rules, the
  document's, replacing four) **with the `refused` notice still standing beside
  the import's own**. That is the whole reason the fourth slot exists, and it
  is now proven on real material rather than in a fixture.

### Three findings, none of them the gate — O100 and O101

**1. The refusal for a second import is written to the slot the first import
overwrites.** `doImport`'s guard puts both of its refusals in `importNotice`.
For a save in flight that survives, because a save's landing does not touch
that state. For an *import* in flight it does not: the running import's success
path calls `setImportNotice('The imported rules are stored…')`, so the sentence
that said *"An import was already running, so this one was not applied"* is
replaced by one saying an import worked. Driven and watched: the refusal stood
on screen at 21:02:44 while `Importing…` was up, and at 21:03:21 — after the
first import landed — only the success sentence remained, with the store
holding the *first* document and the second silently discarded.

This is the exact failure the build design's §5 names as its reason for
creating the `refused` slot ("**Not `importNotice`.** … its success path
overwrites it … leaving the person told the import worked and never told their
Save did nothing"), reached in the function that reasoning was written for.

**No test can see it.** No test delivers a second file during a held import;
`heldImport` picks one file and the case that follows asserts only that the
button is `disabled` and says `Importing…`, under the title *"so a second pick
cannot race the first"*. The button is the *first* guard. The second guard —
`doImport`'s own `writer.current !== undefined` check, the one for a picker
opened before the write started — has no test on its import-during-import
branch, and its message has no test at all.

**2. Both `refused` sentences assert a state that has not happened yet.** They
end *"The imported rules are on screen now"* and *"The imported rules are on
screen now; press Save to apply them"*, and both are set while the import is
still in flight — so for the width of the window the sentence is false, and
the second one points at a button that is `disabled` for exactly as long as it
is on screen. At 2 ms nobody sees it; held for ninety seconds it is the only
thing on screen. The tests match on `'was not sent'`, `'not applied'` and
`'rule 2'` — never on the clause that is wrong, which is the shape this
repository keeps finding: an assertion whose substring excludes the defect.

**3. The gate is taken after `file.text()` resolves, so the disabled button
does not cover the file-read window.** `onChange` does `file.text().then(doImport)`,
and `writer.current` is set inside `doImport` — so between picking a file and
its text arriving, Import is still enabled and the gate is still free. That is
the route by which finding 1 is reachable without a synthetic event: pick a
large file, click Import again while its text is still being read, pick a small
one, and the small one's import is running when the large one's `doImport`
finally fires. Not driven; derived from the code while writing finding 1 up.

None of the three touches the gate itself, which held under every condition
driven above. **A fourth turned up in the fix round for the second**, and is
recorded here because the shape recurs: the first rewording of the discard
notice ended *"Its rules replace the list when it lands"* — true when it does,
and a promise the screen breaks when the document is refused, which is the
commonest ending this route has. Trading one false sentence for another is
what happens when a wording fix is checked against the happy path only; the
test now drives the discard and then *fails* the import. It also surfaced a
decision nobody had made: a form commit discarded by an import stays discarded
even when the import fails and the list is therefore unchanged, where O96's
failed **save** keeps the held edit for exactly that reason. The first two are **O100**, the third **O101**, both opened and
closed the day of the drive.

*The decision was filed as O109 on 2026-09-13, with no code change.*

**Fixing the third closed a window that was not its own, and cost a test its
scenario.** With the gate taken inside the discrete `change` event — which
React flushes synchronously — `frozen` and `writer.current` change together,
where before there was a microtask in which the ref was taken and Save was
still drawn enabled. That microtask is what made `save`'s second guard
*reachable*, and O97's test for it can no longer stage its own case: React
skips a click handler whose props say `disabled`, so no click reaches `save`
during an import at all. The test is restaged as the assertion that now
protects the case — the button is disabled in the same tick the gate is taken,
with no `await` to hide behind — which makes it O101's regression guard. The
guard itself is kept and its message with it, unreachable, because the
invariant is what it states; O101's row carries that as what remains.

### Isolation, and one thing the ritual's own check gets wrong

The real `library.db`'s mtime was identical before and after
(`2026-09-02 05:51:48.853004102`), no `.taiyaku` was written anywhere under the
real tree, `Volumes/` was untouched (mtime still `2026-09-02 05:51:40`), and
`git status` was clean. The NAS probe directory was removed afterwards.

`find -newermt` against the start stamp did **not** come back empty: the
container directory `/home/davey/temp/manga-test` had a newer mtime, and
nothing had been written to it. **A read-only `SELECT` against a WAL database
moves its directory's mtime** — SQLite creates `-wal` and `-shm` beside the
file and removes them on close — while leaving the database file's own mtime
untouched. Reproduced deliberately on a copy: directory mtime `14:14:06` before
one `select count(*)`, `14:14:07` after, database mtime unchanged either side.
So the second half of the isolation ritual fires on a plain read, and the
mtime of the database file is the half that actually means something.

## O92's readable half, against the real library — 2026-09-08

The roots screen's *Exclude globs* box was write-only: `GET /api/library/roots`
did not send the column, so it started empty whatever the row held. `scan::Root`
carries it now, `scan::roots` selects it, `root_json` sends it and
`TextField.from` reads it. Driven against a copy of the real library — 1,858
works, 2,044 scan entries, the one `local` admin — served on `127.0.0.1:8123`
with `pnpm dev`'s proxy pointed at it through `TAIYAKU_SERVE`.

| What was driven | Result |
| ---- | ---- |
| `GET /api/library/roots`, unpatched root | `"exclude_globs": null` — the key present, not absent |
| `PATCH {"exclude_globs":"**/extras/**"}` then `GET` | `'**/extras/**'` comes back |
| The screen, loaded fresh | the box reads `**/extras/**`; before this it read empty |
| Emptying the box | column really goes to `NULL`, verified in SQLite |
| Typing the value away and back in one focus | no `PATCH` — the equality guard |
| A bare focus-and-leave on a box holding a pattern | no `PATCH` — the `edited` guard |

**Emptying the box is the interaction three passes of C4 PR A's review were
trying to make reachable**, and it works here for the first time with the box
also showing what is stored — the two were previously in tension precisely
because the row could not report the column.

**Isolation proven afterwards rather than assumed.** The writes went to a copy
under the session scratchpad; `/home/davey/temp/manga-test/library.db` still
carries its 2026-09-02 05:51:48.853004102 mtime and its 3,534,848 bytes, and
`find -newer` over the tree lists nothing. No scan or derive was triggered.

**What the mutation sweep could not say.** `scripts/mutants.sh --since main`
found 4 mutants — 2 caught, 2 unviable, 0 survivors — and none of the four
touches the column read itself: cargo-mutants does not mutate the SELECT's
string literal or a struct field initialiser. The two unviable are
`Ok(Default::default())` and `Ok(vec![Default::default()])` failing to compile
because `scan::Root` derives no `Default`, which is the known cause, not an
untested function. The evidence that the read is pinned is hand-applied:
`exclude_globs: r.get(5)?` → `None` fails two Rust tests, deleting the
`"exclude_globs"` key from `root_json` fails one, `from: () => ''` fails three
jsdom tests, and each of the two blur guards fails its own test and only its
own.

## O92's scanner half, against the real library — 2026-09-09

The walk applying `root.exclude_globs`, measured on a copy of the real library
at `/home/davey/temp/manga-test` — 490 GB, 129 directories under the root,
2,044 scan entries, 1,858 works. Release profile, this machine. Every write
went to a database under the session scratchpad; the isolation proof is at the
end.

**The library's shape matters to what follows**: this root is flat. 129 series
directories directly under `Volumes`, each holding archive files, and nothing
nested deeper. There is no `extras/` subtree anywhere in it.

### What the exclusion saved, once the page cache was controlled for

The pattern was `One Piece*`, which matched **five** directories, not the two
a look at the largest series suggested — `One Piece`, `- Digital Colored
Comics`, `- Definitive Edition (Colored)`, `- Cover Stories - Digital Colored
Comics` and `- Special One-Shot!`. The scan report named all five, which is
the confession working; a count alone would have hidden that the pattern was
broader than intended.

| walk | entries | wall |
|---|---|---|
| incremental, nothing moved, no patterns | 2,044 | 0.35 s |
| **cold, first walk of 490 GB**, no patterns | 2,044 | **30.06 s** |
| cold, `One Piece*` excluded | 1,778 | 1.28 s |
| warm, no patterns | 2,044 | 1.45 s / 1.46 s |
| warm, `One Piece*` excluded | 1,778 | 1.27 s / 1.28 s |

**The 30.06 s → 1.28 s reading is not a 23× speedup and must not be quoted as
one.** The 30 s run was the first walk over 490 GB and it filled the page
cache; the excluded run that followed inherited a warm one. Re-run with both
arms warm and twice each, the honest figure is **1.46 s → 1.28 s, a 12.3%
saving for 13.0% of entries skipped** (266 of 2,044). The saving is
*proportional to what is skipped*, and on this library that is all it is.

**Why proportional rather than multiplicative, which is the finding worth
keeping.** Skipping at descent avoids `read_dir`, `stat`, `sniff` and
`member_pages` for a whole subtree, and that is real — but a flat root has no
subtree to avoid descending into. Each excluded directory here costs one
`read_dir` and its files' opens, so excluding *n* entries saves about *n*
entries' worth of work. A library with deep junk subtrees would see more than
this; this one cannot. **The feature's value is a property of the tree's
shape, not of the feature.** Nothing in the design said otherwise, and nothing
in it said this either.

### §0.1's correction, tested rather than asserted

The design's §0.1 corrected O92's own entry: an exclusion was thought to make
`forget_unseen` drop `scan_entry` rows, derive produce fewer works, and
progress and notes go with them. Three links of that chain do not exist. Run
against 1,858 real works:

| | entries | works | editions | members |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 2,044 | 1,858 | 1,858 | 1,883 |
| after `One Piece*` + derive | **1,778** | **1,858** | **1,858** | **1,883** |
| after clearing the column + derive | 2,044 | 1,858 | 1,858 | 1,883 |

**266 entries forgotten, and not one work, edition or member destroyed.** The
scan reported `0 gone; 266 entries forgotten because a pattern now covers
them` — the two facts stayed apart, which is what that counter exists for. The
same derive that ran afterwards reported *"derived 124 series, 1616 works"*:
that is what the pass **produced**, while the library went on holding 1,858.
The 242 works under those five directories are standing and stale, exactly as
§0.1 predicted, and clearing the column brought all 266 entries back.

**What this run could not test.** This copy holds **no `progress` rows and no
`note` rows**, so the half of §0.1's claim about reading positions and notes
surviving is argued from the schema (`ON DELETE CASCADE` hangs them off
`work`, and no `work` row was deleted) rather than observed. A copy carrying
reading history would close that.

### Isolation, proven afterwards

`/home/davey/temp/manga-test/library.db` still carries its 2026-09-02
05:51:48.853004102 mtime and its 3,534,848 bytes. Every write went to
`o92.db`, `cold-base.db`, `cold-excl.db` and `tmp.db` under the session
scratchpad.

**One directory mtime did move, and it is the documented exception.**
`find -newermt 2026-09-09` over the tree returns exactly one path: the root
`Volumes` directory itself. `--add` runs `watch::probe`, which creates and
removes a probe file — the one file the scanner ever writes to a library tree
(`scan.rs`'s module doc says so). Confirmed it left nothing: the root holds 0
non-directory entries and 0 dotfiles.

**A first attempt at that proof reported success while erroring.**
`find … -newermt '-2 hours'` is rejected by this machine's `find` (it is
`bfs`, which wants ISO timestamps); the error went to stderr, the count came
back `0`, and it read exactly like proof of no writes. Re-run with
`-newermt 2026-09-09` it returns the one real hit above. Same shape as the
gate whose exit status a trailing `echo` masked earlier the same day.

### A correction to what this run assumed about the pattern, 2026-09-09

The whole-branch review asked which of the pattern shapes the design measured
its own leading example falls into, and the answer changes what the earlier
`**/extras/**` runs mean.

| pattern | `Naruto/extras` as a directory | `Naruto/extras/art.jpg` |
|---|---|---|
| `**/extras/**` | **not excluded** | excluded |
| `extras/` | excluded | never reached — no descent |
| `extras` | excluded | never reached — no descent |

**`**/extras/**` — the value this project set on the real library on
2026-09-08, and the design's own first example — excludes a directory's
contents and not the directory.** The walk still descends into it, still
records it as a `scan_entry` row, excludes its files one at a time, and
reports `excluded_dirs: 0`. None of the descent saving happens.

The `One Piece*` measurement above is unaffected: a bare name with a trailing
`*` matches the directory itself, so those five directories genuinely were
skipped at descent and the 12.3% figure stands. But it means **the saving
measured there is the best case for this pattern language, not the typical
one** — a `/**`-suffixed pattern saves strictly less, and reports nothing in
the field C4 §3 asks for.

Faithful gitignore, and not the matcher's fault. Recorded because the run
above would otherwise read as evidence about a pattern shape it never tested.

**The middle row is O98.** At 59 it printed `coverage-floor: 94 files (floor
