## O103: the branches margin, and what was actually under it — 2026-09-12

The web `branches` aggregate sat **0.80** points over its threshold of 92, down
from the 2.38 it was set with on 2026-08-09 and the 1.99 recorded on
2026-08-14. O98 measured **92.80** and deliberately left it: whether 92 still
holds is a judgement, not a transcription. This is that judgement, measured
first.

### The slide is dilution, not regression

Re-measured on `main` at `b6a1a0a`: 97.42 / **92.80** / 99.16 / 99.22 over 108
files, branches **2619/2822**. Splitting that report against `git log` — the 42
web source files added since 2026-08-15, none deleted and none renamed in the
window, so the two sets are exactly the old tree and C4's three UI PRs:

| set | files | branches | covered | uncovered |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| in the tree on 2026-08-14 | 66 | 1755 | 1649 | 106 |
| added since | 42 | 1067 | 970 | 97 |
| **total** | **108** | **2822** | **2619** | **203** |

93.96% against **90.91%**. The old tree measured 93.99% on 2026-08-14 and
measures 93.96% now — it did not move. Had the 42 new files landed at the tree's
own rate, the total would read 93.96% and the margin 1.96, which is the two
points the rule asks for. **The entire 1.19-point slide is new code arriving
three points below the tree**, and the gate was green at every commit on the way
down because an aggregate cannot see a marginal rate.

### What the 203 uncovered branches actually were

Classified by the source line each uncovered arm sits on:

| shape | count |
|---|---:|
| `err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)` | **30** |
| defensive early return (`if (!current) return`) | 38 |
| `??` fallback | 35 |
| race guard (`cancelled`, `seq !== latest.current`) | 26 |
| everything else | 74 |

The first is one idiom at **40 sites across 21 files**, 80 branch arms of which
30 were uncovered — and four of those files had already grown a private one-line
helper for it (`Labeller.tsx`, `RuleEditor.tsx`, `notesWrite.ts`,
`truthWrite.ts`), three under the name `messageOf` and one under `message`. That
is `bytes.ts`'s own argument arriving: a second formatter is one that drifts, and
here there were forty.

### Removing branches, then buying nine

Collapsing the forty sites into `web/src/message.ts` removes 78 branch locations
and 30 uncovered ones. Predicted before the edit and measured after:

| | branches | pct | margin |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `main` at `b6a1a0a` | 2619/2822 | 92.80 | 0.80 |
| after `messageOf` | 2571/2744 | 93.69 | 1.69 |
| after nine guard tests | 2580/2744 | 94.02 | 2.02 |
| after the `Tab` test | 2581/2744 | **94.05** | **2.05** |

94.00 is the figure at which the two-point rule re-derives the 92 that is
already set, which is why it was the target rather than a number chosen to feel
safe.

**Which nine, and why not the other seventeen.** The `??` fallbacks and the
`if (!current) return` guards are states the code refuses; a test for one asserts
that an impossible thing is handled. The race guards are the opposite — each is
reachable the moment two reads are in flight, and removing one changes what a
person sees. Nine of those were pinned, each by holding the *first* call open
with a deferred promise and settling it last (two `mockResolvedValueOnce`s
resolve in call order, so the guard is never true and the branch is never taken):

| file | branches | what a stale answer would do |
|---|---:|---|
| `Users.tsx` | 2 | the list as it was before the account was added |
| `Library.tsx` | 2 | another root's grid under this root's heading |
| `Series.tsx` | 2 | the series the reader just left, redrawn over the one they asked for |
| `RuleEditor.tsx` | 2 | a Save button counting works for a rule list nobody is looking at |
| `Search.tsx` | 1 | a red banner naming a query the box no longer holds |

Every one hand-mutated and watched: the guard deleted, the suite run, exactly
one test red, the file restored. The `RuleEditor` success guard had been
*evaluated* 116 times and taken none.

**The `cancelled`-on-unmount guards were left alone deliberately.** React 19
warns on nothing when state is set after unmount, so a test for one of those
passes with the guard removed — a test that passes against its own defect, which
is the thing this repository keeps finding by hand-applying the defect. They stay
uncovered and that is the honest reading.

### Two things found while re-deriving, both worse than the item

**The per-file branches floor was tighter than the aggregate and nothing said
so.** `Users.tsx` measured **78.78%** against `coverage-floor.mjs`'s floor of 78
— margin **0.78**, and at 26/33 branches a single uncovered one takes it to
75.76% and fails CI. It had overtaken the statements margin that the script's own
comment names as the one to watch. Found by re-deriving the table in
`docs/ci.md`, not by a run: every run was green.

**`docs/status.md`'s jsdom test count was two short before this branch.** It read
934 against an actual 936 on `main` — the ungated half of the figure, exactly as
the ritual predicts. Corrected to the measured **947** here rather than by adding
a delta to a wrong number.

### The one behaviour change, and the review pass that found it unpinned

`Account.tsx`'s two Revoke handlers read
`why instanceof Error ? \`That key was not revoked: ${why.message}\` : String(why)`
— the clause naming the gesture was on the `Error` arm alone, so a rejection that
was not an `Error` printed the bare reason under a row still sitting on screen.
That is the same indistinguishability the case above it in `Account.test.tsx`
exists to prevent (*"a revocation that did not happen must not look like one that
did"*, found by the third whole-branch review), reached by the other arm.
Collapsing the ternary made the prefix unconditional.

**It shipped unpinned and a pass over the branch's own diff is what caught it.**
The suite's existing non-`Error` case stubs `fetch` for POST and PUT only, and
both revocations are DELETE — so nothing in the file reached the arm that
changed. The test added for it asserts the whole sentence with `toBe` rather
than matching on the reason, because a match on the reason alone passes against
the defect. Hand-applied: restoring the pre-collapse ternary gives
`Received: "the network went away"` against
`Expected: "That key was not revoked: the network went away"`.

### The eight margins, before and after

| gate | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| aggregate statements | 1.42 | 1.72 |
| aggregate **branches** | **0.80** | **2.05** |
| aggregate functions | 2.16 | 2.16 |
| aggregate lines | 2.22 | 2.31 |
| per-file statements | 0.85 (`Labeller.tsx`) | 1.85 (`Shell.tsx`) |
| per-file **branches** | **0.78** (`Users.tsx`) | **3.25** (`Shell.tsx`) |
| per-file functions | 2.33 | 2.33 |
| per-file lines | 3.00 | 3.00 |

The tightest gate in the web half is now aggregate statements at 1.72, which is
the one to watch next. **`Shell.tsx` is the lowest file on two metrics because
of this branch, not despite it**: its `messageOf` ternary had *both* arms covered,
so collapsing it took 2 covered branches out of 15/18 and left 13/16 — the
refactor lowers a per-file figure wherever the idiom was fully tested, and raises
the aggregate because the block as a whole was 62.5% covered against a tree at
92.8%.

One test was needed beyond the nine: `Labeller.tsx` lost a covered statement with
its private helper, taking the per-file statements margin from 0.85 to 0.78. The
fix is the one `coverage-floor.mjs`'s comment prescribed — *"a test for
`Labeller.tsx` rather than an 89 here"* — and it turned out to be the one
documented key nothing had ever pressed: **`Tab`**, handled ahead of every other
binding and returning before them, with three statements behind it that had never
run. It cycles the boxes under the *cursor* rather than through the list, which
is how two stacked balloons are reached without clicking through the top one.

## O104: nothing synced before a rename, measured where it would bite — 2026-09-12

Found while sizing the write-back design's §11 against the host that will run
it, and the measurement is recorded here because it is both how the defect was
found and how large it is.

### The defect, from the code

`stamp::rewrite_one` stages a whole archive beside the original and
`std::fs::rename`s it over the top; `taiyaku_read::atomic::write` does the same
for sidecars, hand documents, exports and covers. **Neither synced anything
first, and `rg -n 'sync_all|sync_data' crates/` returned nothing** outside
tests. Both doc comments promised crash atomicity — "a crash leaves either the
old archive or the new one, never a half-written file" and "write a file so a
crash cannot publish half of one". A rename is atomic for bytes already on
disk; without a sync the rename can reach the journal before the data does,
and a crash in between leaves the path naming data that was never written,
with the old file already unlinked. ext4 carries a heuristic
(`auto_da_alloc`) for exactly this replace-by-rename pattern; the NAS's array
disks are XFS, which does not.

### The host, measured

taiyaku will run in a Docker container on the Unraid NAS, bind-mounting
`/mnt/user` — the Manga share spans `disk1` and `disk4` with no cache pool, so
no single-disk mount sees the whole library and `shfs` is in the path. For a
bind mount the container layer adds nothing to I/O, so these were taken on the
host. Load average 4.2–5.8 throughout.

*Wrong in one respect, found the next day: the NAS has a cache pool —
`/mnt/nvme_cache`, which a check for `/mnt/cache*` and `/mnt/*pool*` missed —
and the library share stages new files on it. The figures in this section are
the parity array's; see "The library share writes to NVMe first" below.*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| array filesystem (`disk1`, `disk4`) | xfs |
| RAM / page cache | 62 GB / 46 GB |
| `dirty_ratio` / `dirty_background_ratio` | 5 / 3 |
| `dirty_expire_centisecs` | 1000 (10 s) |

`dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=2048 conv=fdatasync`, into a scratch directory
inside an existing share on a named disk, deleted after:

| target | throughput |
| --- | --- |
| `disk1` (93% full) | **41.2 MB/s** |
| `disk4` (88% full) | 56.8 MB/s |
| `/mnt/user` (shfs) | 58.9 MB/s |

`shfs` costs nothing measurable for a sequential write.

**A stamp's own I/O pattern, on the largest archive in the library**: a
same-disk copy of `Monster - The Perfect Edition - v09.cbz` (2,394,270,047
bytes, on `disk1`), its page cache dropped first with `dd iflag=nocache
count=0`, written with `conv=fdatasync` — **55.3 s, 43.3 MB/s**. The prediction
that reading the original would stack on the write, since both land on one
spindle, was wrong: parity bounds the copy, so the write-only figure was
accurate rather than optimistic. The source's coldness was advised, not
verified with `fincore`; a warm read would only make a true cold stamp slower.

**So the exposure**: a stamp of that archive left about a minute in which a
crash would destroy a reader's only copy of a volume, and a median archive
(218 MB) about fifteen seconds. `atomic::write`'s files are small and their
window is the 10 s writeback delay, but one of them is a sidecar, which its own
doc calls the alignment of every edition in the work. *That is the exposure
on the parity array; the library share as configured writes a stamp's staged
copy to NVMe instead — see below.*

**Directory sync through `shfs`**, checked before making it strict, since a
directory `fsync` that errors on FUSE would fail every stamp in production:
`perl`'s `IO::Handle::sync` on an `O_DIRECTORY` handle succeeded on
`/mnt/user/miscellaneous`, `/mnt/user/media 1/Manga` and
`/mnt/disk1/miscellaneous`.

**Isolation, proven afterwards**: no `taiyaku-measure-*` directory left under
any disk or `/mnt/user`, free space identical before and after (1.4T / 2.3T /
23T), share count unchanged at 14, and the source archive's size and mtime
identical before and after the copy.

### The fix, and the tests that fail without it

Both functions now sync the staged file before the rename and the directory
after it, through one `atomic::sync_directory_of`. Nothing a test can read
tells a synced file from an unsynced one, so each test re-runs itself as a
child under `strace -f -qq -y` — `-y` prints the path behind each descriptor,
so a sync names its file without tracking `openat` — and asserts on the order
of the calls. The harness is `taiyaku_read::test_support`, reached from
`taiyaku-library` through a dev-dependency feature.

Every defect the tests name was hand-applied, run, and the file restored
byte-identical:

| applied to both `atomic::write` and `rewrite_one` | fails at |
| --- | --- |
| no file sync | "renamed … without being synced after its last write" |
| no directory sync | "not synced after the rename" |
| directory synced *before* the rename | "not synced after the rename" |
| file synced *after* the rename, through the destination | "renamed … without being synced after its last write" |
| file synced *before* its bytes are written — `atomic`'s empty temporary; `stamp`'s archive through a clone, before `finish` writes the central directory | "renamed … without being synced after its last write" |
| `atomic` only: the same bytes written again to the destination after the rename | "written to after the rename" |
| the child's `--exact` name no longer matching | "the traced child must actually have rewritten" |
| `strace` absent from `PATH` | the `expect` naming strace, exit 101 |
| `atomic` only: no fallback for a bare filename's empty parent | the child's own write fails |
| `atomic` only: a fallback to the wrong directory | "not synced after a rename onto a bare filename" |

The fourth matters because libtest exits 0 when `--exact` matches nothing, so
strace reports success and the only thing standing between that and a pass is
the assertion that the child wrote.

**The last two rows came from the coverage report, not from the plan.** The
first gate run listed `atomic.rs` among the files under the aggregate, and one
of its uncovered lines was `sync_directory_of`'s fallback: `Path::new("out.json")
.parent()` is `Some("")`, and opening `""` fails, so without it `taiyaku align
--write out.json` writes the sidecar and then reports that it failed. The
line was written before any test reached it, so the test was written after and
proven the other way round — both defects applied by hand and watched red.
What stays uncovered is the directory-sync error arm in both functions, which
no unprivileged test can reach: making a directory unopenable after a rename
into it needs a permission the CI container, running as root, ignores.

**What the fix costs**: the sync is now most of a stamp. Before it the request
returned once the new archive was in page cache — `dirty_ratio` is 5% of
dirtyable memory, roughly 2.4–3.1 GB on this host, which every archive fits
except perhaps the 2.39 GB largest — and flushed afterwards. Now the
largest archive holds the request for about 55 s *on the array*. taiyaku sets no timeout of
its own (no `TimeoutLayer`, no `AbortSignal` in `performStamp`, and the screen
shows a `writing` state), so this is only a failure if something in front of
the container cuts a request sooner. If one does, the stamp still completes —
`spawn_blocking` is not cancelled by a dropped connection — and the screen
reports an error for a stamp that succeeded. No Dockerfile or proxy
configuration exists in this repository to say which.

### The whole-branch review, and what it found in the tests

**The first version of these tests passed against the defect they exist for.**
They asserted that *some* sync of the staged path came before the rename, and
never that nothing was written to it after that sync. Syncing `atomic`'s empty
temporary and then writing the bytes left all six `atomic` tests green; syncing
a clone of a stamp's staged archive before `writer.finish()` — so the central
directory and end-of-central-directory record land after the sync — left all 24
`stamp` tests green. After a crash on XFS that archive has no central directory,
which is O104 exactly. Found by the review, and reproduced here before anything
was changed: both mutations applied, the three O104 tests run, all three
`PASS`.

**The fix traces every syscall that can put bytes into a file** — `write`,
`writev`, `pwrite64`, `pwritev`, `pwritev2`, `copy_file_range`, `sendfile`,
`splice`, `ftruncate`, `fallocate` — and `assert_replaced_durably` requires, in
order: at least one write to the staged file (or the ordering would be vacuous
for a write syscall nobody listed), a sync after the last of them, the rename,
no write to the destination afterwards, and a sync of the directory. Two parser
details it needed. A data string can hold `<` and `>` of its own — a ComicInfo
document is XML — so only the destination descriptor's `-y` decoration is read,
except for the three calls whose arguments are all descriptors. And tracing
writes makes strace's `<unfinished ...>`/`<... resumed>` split likelier, so the
two halves are rejoined per pid before parsing.

**The mutation table above was then re-run in full, and the first run of it was
itself a test that could not fail.** The script read nextest's stdout, where
nextest writes nothing; with no `PASS` line to see, every mutation classified
as red. Caught by running the untouched tree through the same classifier as a
control, which it would also have called red. Rewritten to read both streams
and to require a `FAIL` line for red. **One row then failed for the wrong
reason**: appending to the destination after the rename tripped the
content assertion before the new one, so the check that it existed for was
never reached — rewritten to write the identical bytes, and it fails at
"written to after the rename". Every row now fails at the assertion it names.

**Checked and left, with the reasons.** A directory-sync failure after a
successful rename is a hard error; the review measured `EINVAL` from directory
`fsync` only on `/proc`, `/sys` and cgroup2, and ext4, XFS, tmpfs, vfat and FUSE
return 0, so no filesystem a library lives on reaches it. In that unreachable
case `export::work` would skip `record_absorbed` for a file it did write — read,
not triggered. `hand::rename_for_rekey`'s bare rename is not synced; a lost one
leaves the document at its old key, which `reconcile` reports as an orphan,
with the hand fields still in the database. And the `perl` check through `shfs`
proves a directory `fsync` does not error there, not that FUSE forwards it —
the file sync is the half that protects data, and `dd`'s 58.9 MB/s through
`/mnt/user` with `conv=fdatasync` says those reach the disk.

**Not settled here, and not a defect: whether cache writes should pay the
sync.** `atomic::write` also writes the cover, page and filmstrip cache, where
two `fsync`s now stand before every first view, and `hand::save` calls it while
holding the library connection's mutex, twice per sibling on a series edit. The
review measured the same syscall sequence on this workstation's NVMe at a
median 10.0–10.2 ms against 0.04 ms without the syncs; on the NAS it is
unmeasured. *Measured the next day, below: about 1.1 ms.*

### The library share writes to NVMe first — 2026-09-13

Measuring what the sync costs a cache write turned up what the section above
got wrong. **The shares' own configuration decides which disk a write reaches**,
read from `/boot/config/shares/*.cfg`:

| share | `shareUseCache` | pool | include |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `media 1` (the library) | **yes** | `nvme_cache` | `disk1` |
| `appdata` | prefer | `nvme_cache` | `disk1` |
| `miscellaneous` | no | — | `disk1,disk4,disk10` |

`/mnt/nvme_cache` is btrfs on a non-rotational NVMe device, 1.9T. So a file
created through `/mnt/user/media 1/…` — a stamp's staged archive, a hand
document's temporary — lands on NVMe, and the mover takes it to `disk1` later;
and `appdata`, where a container's `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` conventionally maps, stays
on NVMe.

**What a rename does across the two**, probed in `mirrors`, whose configuration
matches `media 1`'s (`cache=yes` on `nvme_cache`, include `disk1`), so the
library was not written to. An original `a.dat` created directly on
`/mnt/disk1/mirrors/…`; `a.dat.tmp` created and synced through `/mnt/user`,
which placed it on NVMe; `rename` through `/mnt/user` onto `a.dat`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| the temporary landed on | NVMe only |
| `rename` | succeeded |
| `a.dat` through `/mnt/user` afterwards | the new content |
| `a.dat` on NVMe | the new content |
| `a.dat` on `disk1` | **gone** |

So `shfs` carries out a rename onto a file held by another branch as a rename on
one filesystem and an unlink on the other — two operations, not one, and what a
crash between them leaves was not measured. **This does not change O104's fix**:
a share's cache setting is not something taiyaku can rely on, `miscellaneous`
has none, and the mover puts every archive back on the array. **It does change
the exposure and latency figures above**, which are the array's: a stamp on the
library as configured writes its staged copy to NVMe, where the flush is cheap,
and is more likely bounded by reading the original off `disk1` — unmeasured.

**What the sync costs on this path**, `write`, `fsync`, `rename` and a
directory `fsync` in `perl` through `/mnt/user/mirrors`, against the same
sequence without the two syncs. Three interleaved rounds of 30 for new files,
two of 20 for replacing an original on `disk1`; load average 13.5–17.2
throughout, which can only inflate these:

| case | without syncs, median | with syncs, median |
| --- | --- | --- |
| new, 4 KB | 0.50–0.61 ms | 1.54–1.72 ms |
| new, 165 KB | 1.28–1.57 ms | 2.53–2.62 ms |
| replacing a `disk1` original, 4 KB | 0.54–0.72 ms | 1.69–1.71 ms |

**About 1.1 ms a write**, against 96–221 ms to decode a cover and roughly ten
times less than the review's figure for this workstation's ext4. Every scratch
directory was removed from both branches and `ls -d /mnt/*/mirrors/taiyaku-measure-*`
returned nothing.

## O105: the cover cache served whatever file it found — 2026-09-13

Found by the whole-branch review of O104. The reviewer's throwaway test put an
empty file at a reading page's cache path and got back `Some` of zero bytes.

### The defect, from the code

`cover::at_path` serves every cover and filmstrip tile, and
`cover::cached_or_generated_page` serves reading-sized pages. Both began with
an `if let Ok(found) = std::fs::read(…)` that returned `found`. #124's "What
remains" named only the second. The series cover redirects to a tile, so every
surface that serves a generated image went through one of those two lines. The
path is keyed on the member's `sha256` and the generation parameters. Neither
changes, so a broken file at that path was served on every request and never
replaced.

### What the real caches hold

No taiyaku container runs on the NAS: `docker ps -a` there lists none, and
`/mnt/user/appdata` has no `covers` or `thumbs` directory. This workstation has
three caches the server wrote before this work began (the drives and reviews
below used scratch caches of their own). Every file in them was read and checked for a
JPEG start marker (`FF D8 FF`) at the beginning and an end marker (`FF D9`) at
the end:

| cache | covers | tiles | reading pages | made | whole |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `~/.cache/taiyaku` | 7 | 336 | 74 (`v2`) | 2026-08-11 to 2026-09-09 | 417 of 417 |
| `web/.taiyaku-cache` | — | — | 312 (`v1`) | 2026-08-09 | 312 of 312 |
| `.superpowers/sdd/scratch/cache` | — | 422 | 5 (`v2`) | 2026-08-13 | 427 of 427 |

None of the 1,156 is empty. So the marker check the fix applies rejects
nothing this server has written, under either page format version. Nothing
ever replaced a broken file before O105, so a broken file served to a client
would still be on disk unless someone deleted the cache by hand. None is, which
means no client has been served one from these caches. That matters for the `ETag` finding below.

**The first count said one cache and 417 files, and it was wrong.** The search
for cache directories used `fd`, which skips anything `.gitignore` names, and
both other caches sit under ignored paths in the repository. The whole-branch
review found them. `fd --no-ignore` finds all three. `web/.taiyaku-cache` is
what the relative default left before `cache_root` existed.

### The drive, before and after

The drive used a copy of the real library's `library.db` in scratch, a key
minted against the copy, and `serve --cache` pointed at a scratch directory.
Three requests for `akame-ga-kill----v01--2015--cbz`, edition `raw`: the OPDS
cover, the tile for page 5, and page 5 at `?w=300`.

| | cover | tile | page `?w=300` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cold, pre-fix binary | 200, 36843 B | 200, 7678 B | 200, 22091 B |
| all three files emptied, pre-fix binary | **200, 0 B** | **200, 0 B** | **200, 0 B** |
| the same empty files, fixed binary | 200, 36843 B | 200, 7678 B | 200, 22091 B |
| cut in half / zero-filled / one byte short, fixed binary | 200, 36843 B | 200, 7678 B | 200, 22091 B |

Every body the fixed binary served was a whole JPEG, and each file on disk was
back at its original size. A third round of requests left every file's
nanosecond mtime unchanged, so those requests were served from the cache and
not regenerated. Isolation checks afterwards: the real `library.db` kept its
mtime (2026-09-02 05:51:48), and `find -newermt` from the drive's start time
returned nothing under the real library or `~/.cache/taiyaku`.

### The permit tests, and the deadlock their first version had

The whole-branch review found that moving the cache hit inside
`GENERATION_LIMIT`, in either `at_path` or `cached_or_generated_page`, left
every test green. The fix added two tests that hold every permit and require a
warm hit within five seconds. **The review of that fix round found they could
hang each other.** `.cargo/mutants.toml` runs sweeps with plain `cargo test`,
where tests are threads in one process sharing the static semaphore. The
helper takes the two permits one at a time, so the two tests could each take
one and wait forever for the second, with every other test that needs a permit
queued behind them. The reviewer attached gdb to a hung run and found both
helpers inside `Semaphore::acquire` on their second acquisition.

| run under plain `cargo test` | hung (timeout) |
| --- | --- |
| `cover::tests`, before the fix, 60 s limit | **5 of 6** |
| `cover::tests`, a lock held for the whole helper, 60 s limit | 0 of 30 |
| the whole `taiyaku-serve` lib, the same lock, 180 s limit | 0 of 10 |

With the lock, a hit moved inside the permit still fails its test in about
five seconds: 5.1 s under nextest for `at_path`, and 5.8 s under plain
`cargo test` for the page site.

**The same review found the permit's other half untested.** Deleting
`let _permit = GENERATION_LIMIT.acquire();` in `at_path` or in
`cached_or_generated_page` left every test green, and cargo-mutants never
generates that mutant because it does not delete statements. Two tests now
hold every permit, through the same lock, and require a cold generation not
to have fetched its page after 300 ms and to have fetched it once the permits
are released. *(Since O111, on 2026-09-17, a reading page fetches outside the
permit, so the page test watches its resize finish instead — see "O111".)* Hand-applied: deleting the permit in `at_path` fails the cover
test, deleting it in `cached_or_generated_page` fails the page test, and
building `GENERATION_LIMIT` with `MAX_CONCURRENT_GENERATIONS + 1` fails both.
Setting `MAX_CONCURRENT_GENERATIONS` to 64 passes, deliberately: the tests
hold however many permits it names, and its value is a tuning choice
justified in its own doc comment. After adding them, under plain
`cargo test`: 0 of 20 runs of `cover::tests` and 0 of 5 of the whole crate failed or hung.

### What the fix does not reach

A reading page's `ETag` is `"<sha256>-p<offset>-r<edge>"`, which is the cache
key and not a digest of the bytes. After the fix, a request for the page above
that sent back the tag its empty response had carried got **304**. So a
browser that had already cached an empty page would keep showing it after the
server was fixed. Covers and tiles are sent with `private, no-cache` and no
`ETag`, so a browser re-fetches them in full and recovers. Given the cache
check above, no browser can hold an empty page today.

*O106 has since added the format version to every resized tag, which changes
each one once and so replaces such a page. See the O106 entry below.*

## O106: a resized page's tag left out the format version — 2026-09-13

Found by reviewing what O105's fix left behind: O105 found that a browser
holding an empty page would get `304` for it, and the cause was in the tag.

### The defect, from the code and its history

`cover::page_cache_path` named a cached page
`<sha256>-p<offset>-r<edge>v<PAGE_FORMAT_VERSION>.jpg`. `routes::page_etag`
built the tag for the same rendering separately, as
`"<sha256>-p<offset>-r<edge>"`, without the version.

**It was reached once, on the branch that introduced it.** The first version
of this entry said it had never been reached, on the strength of `git log -S`
on `main`: the resized tag and `PAGE_FORMAT_VERSION = 2` arrive in the same
commit, `f81913d` (#35), and there is no `= 1` on `main` at all. But `main`
holds only #35's squash. The whole-branch review read the PR's own commits,
which `refs/pull/35/head` keeps:

| commit | time, 2026-08-09 | cached page | tag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `69eb898` "Serve pages at reading size" | 00:49 | `…-r<edge>v1.jpg` (`FORMAT_VERSION`, shared with covers) | `"<sha256>-p<offset>-r<edge>"` |
| `08daa05` "reading pages get a real resize filter" | 01:48 | `…-r<edge>v2.jpg` (the new `PAGE_FORMAT_VERSION`) | unchanged |

`web/.taiyaku-cache/thumbs` still holds 312 version-1 reading pages from that
night, all whole JPEGs, so resized pages were served at version 1. After the
bump, a browser holding one would have revalidated with the unchanged tag,
been answered `304`, and kept the old filter's rendering. That is the same
lesson as `refs/pull/*` keeping every commit of every PR, from the other side:
a search of `main` sees the squash and not the hour the branch spent at
version 1.

### The drive, before and after

The drive used the same copy of the real library and the same scratch cache
as O105's, with page 5 of `akame-ga-kill----v01--2015--cbz` (edition `raw`)
and the member's hash written as `<sha>`:

| | O105's binary | O106's binary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tag for `?w=300` | `"<sha>-p5-r300"` | `"<sha>-p5-r300v2"` |
| tag for the full-size page | `"<sha>-p5"` | `"<sha>-p5"` |
| `?w=300` with `If-None-Match: "<sha>-p5-r300"` | **304, 0 B** | 200, 22091 B |
| `?w=300` with `If-None-Match: "<sha>-p5-r300v2"` | 200, 22091 B | 304, 0 B |
| full size with `If-None-Match: "<sha>-p5"` | 304, 0 B | 304, 0 B |

The page file O105's binary had cached,
`<sha>-p5-r300v2.jpg`, kept its nanosecond mtime across every request to
O106's binary, so the file name did not change and nothing was regenerated.
Isolation checks afterwards: the real `library.db` kept its mtime, and
`find -newermt` from this drive's start time found nothing under the real
library or `~/.cache/taiyaku`.

**What it costs.** Every resized tag changes once. Each browser re-fetches
each resized page it holds one time, from the server's cache, which is still
warm because no file name changed. The only server so far is this
workstation, so the cost falls on the browsers that have read from it, the
test devices included.

### The review of the fix round

**The first corrections made the wording worse in two places.** This entry and
the O106 row said a browser "was answered `304`". That was never observed. At
`08daa05` pages were sent with `private, max-age=86400`, so a browser holding
a version-1 page would not have asked at all for a day, and would then have
been answered `304`. The row now says so. The key test's doc and the row said
a key without the offset would serve "page 0's picture". It would serve
whichever page of the member was cached first.

**The same hole was one function over.** `thumb_cache_path` built a tile's
name as `<sha256>-p<offset>-<THUMB_LONG_EDGE>v<FORMAT_VERSION>.jpg`, and only
its offset was ever varied on its own (`each_page_of_a_member_gets_its_own_tile`).
Dropping the hash, the long edge or the version from that format string passed
all 559 `taiyaku-serve` tests. Without the hash, page N of every member shares
one tile file. It now goes through `thumb_keyed_path`, which takes the
parameters as arguments, and
`changing_any_tile_parameter_changes_the_tile_path` changes each one alone
and pins the name every cached tile already has: all 758 tiles in the three
caches above have the shape `<sha256>-p<offset>-160v1.jpg`.

**Routes could use a page's index where its offset belongs.** Hand-applied at
the tip of this branch, each of these left every test green:

| site | change |
| --- | --- |
| `get_page`, the `ETag` | `offset` → `index` |
| `get_page`, the reading-page cache key | `offset` → `index` |
| `get_thumb`, the tile key | `offset` → `index` |
| `opds::stream_page`, the `ETag` | `offset` → `index` |
| `get_page`, the resize and its cache key | the clamped width → the raw `?w=` |

Every route fixture asks for pages whose index equals their offset, and its
16×16 page never resizes where the raw and clamped widths differ. The shipped
code is right at all five. Opened as O108, because closing it needs a
multi-member fixture and a route test that reads the cache, which is a branch
of its own.

*O108 has since closed — see "O108: route tests that can tell a page's index
from its offset" below. The first clause of the paragraph above is wrong: route
tests did ask for pages whose index and offset differ, and that section says
what was missing instead.*

## O108: route tests that can tell a page's index from its offset — 2026-09-13

Opened by the review of O105's and O106's fix rounds, above, which found five
changes to the routes that left every test green. The shipped code was right at
all five, so this closed with tests and a fixture and no production change.

### The fixture

`test_support::state_with_a_shared_member` builds work `m` from two archives:

| edition | members | page 2 is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ab` | `a.cbz` (2 pages), `b.cbz` (3) | `b.cbz`'s first page, red |
| `b` | `b.cbz` (3) | `b.cbz`'s third page, blue |

Page 2 of `ab` and page 0 of `b` are one page, and page 2 of `b` is a different
page at the same index. A route that keys by index gives page 2 of `ab` what
belongs to page 2 of `b`: its tag and its cached renderings. The pages are solid
colours because a resize and a JPEG encoding keep a colour where they would blur
a pattern, and `test_support::colour_of` reads the colour back from the centre
pixel. `a.cbz`'s second page is `MAX_FIT_LONG_EDGE + 4` pixels wide, so a
request for `MAX_FIT_LONG_EDGE + 8` resizes it only if the width is clamped.

### Every break, watched

Each change below was applied by hand to the tree with the new tests, run with
`cargo nextest run -p taiyaku-serve --all-features --no-fail-fast` over all 567
tests, and the file restored byte for byte afterwards. A control run of the
unchanged tree passed 567 of 567, once before the breaks and again after
`rustfmt` reformatted the new tests.

| applied | red | failing assertion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `get_page`'s `ETag` from `index` | the tag test | `304` for page 2 of `b`'s tag |
| `get_page`'s cache key from `index` | the resized-page cache test; the tag test | `"blue"` served where `"red"` belongs, in both |
| `get_thumb`'s tile key from `index` | the tile cache test | `"blue"` served where `"red"` belongs |
| `opds::stream_page`'s `ETag` from `index` | the PSE tag test | `304` for page 2 of `b`'s tag |
| `get_page`'s resize given `?w=` unclamped, its `> 1` filter kept | the ceiling test | `image/png`: the page served whole |
| `get_page` caching in `cache_dir` rather than `thumbs` | the resized-page cache test; the ceiling test | the cache file is missing |
| `get_thumb` caching in `cache_dir` rather than `thumbs` | the tile cache test; `tests::serve_caches_covers_and_tiles_under_the_resolved_root` | the cache file is missing |
| `get_page`'s tag from `?w=` unclamped, its `> 1` filter kept | the ceiling test; `a_width_above_the_ceiling_carries_the_ceilings_tag` | the tag names `r4104` and the cache file `r4096` |

No test from before this branch went red under any of the first five rows, which
reproduces the review's finding on this tree. The tag test goes red under the
cache-key break because its resized request is served the wrong picture too.

**The first try at the width break was wider than the defect.** It handed the
resize `query.w` as sent, which also dropped the filter that treats `?w=0` and
`?w=1` as absent, so `a_width_of_one_is_absent_rather_than_a_one_pixel_page`
went red beside the new test. The table's row is the rerun with only the clamp
removed.

**The two cache-directory rows are not among O108's five, and they are why the
cache tests read the files.** Under an index break, both cache tests fail first on the colour
they were served, so the index rows cannot show that reading the cache adds
anything. Pointing a route's cache at the covers directory serves the right
picture from a cache in the wrong place. For tiles, an earlier test already
pinned the directory. For reading pages, nothing did until these tests read the
file.

**The last row checks the ceiling test's own last assertion.** Its clamp break
fails first on the content type, so nothing above reaches the assertion that the
tag is the cache file's name. Building the tag from the unclamped width does,
with every earlier assertion in that test still passing. The O106 test that pins
the ceiling's tag catches the same break.

### The review of this branch

A whole-branch review reproduced every row of the table above and every count
in `docs/status.md`, and found three more mutants that left all 567 tests green.
Each was rerun here with the same result:

| mutant | site |
| --- | --- |
| a page that already fits is read by `offset` | `get_page`, the arm that serves the original bytes |
| a tile's hash is taken from the edition's last member | `get_thumb` |
| a cover's hash is taken from the edition's last member | the OPDS cover route, which predates this branch |

The first is the same mix-up of index and offset, one line from the sites O108
named. Every resized request in the new tests was smaller than its page, so none
reached the arm that serves a page that already fits. The second was hidden by
the tile test asking only for pages of `b.cbz`, the last member of both
editions. The third route's only test has one member with pages, and it is the
last.

**It also found the O108 entry's reason wrong, and this branch had repeated it**
in the status row and the fixture's doc. Route tests did ask for pages whose
index and offset differ: `test_support::work`'s `raw` edition is two members of
two pages each, and `the_reader_can_list_a_work_read_its_sidecar_and_fetch_a_page`
and `a_stale_validator_gets_the_page_rather_than_a_304` ask for its page 2. What
no fixture did was put one member at two positions. A name built from the index
is still unique within one edition, `state_with_two_editions` gives both its
editions the same members in the same order, and `work`'s pages cannot be
decoded, so none of its requests reached a resize or a tile.

`cargo mutants --list --in-diff` over this branch's diff says "No mutants to
filter", where O106's diff lists mutants in `cover.rs` and `routes.rs`. So the
reasoning above about `mutants.sh` holds, now measured.

**After the fix round each of the three fails a test.** Run against 569 tests,
after a control that passed 569 of 569:

| mutant | red | failing assertion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a page that already fits is read by `offset` | `a_page_that_already_fits_the_width_is_read_by_its_index` | `"grey"` served where `"red"` belongs |
| a tile's hash is taken from the last member | the tile cache test | page 0 of `ab` served `"red"` where `"grey"` belongs |
| a cover's hash is taken from the last member | `each_edition_s_cover_is_cached_under_the_member_its_first_page_is_in` | the cover cache file under `a.cbz`'s hash is missing |

No other test went red under any of the three. `colour_of` now names grey, so
the assertions about `a.cbz`'s first page state the colour rather than the

`tests::serve_caches_covers_and_tiles_under_the_resolved_root`.

## O107: a page that already fits is read once — 2026-09-13

Opened by the whole-branch review of O105, which counted archive opens under
`strace` and found a `?w=` request for a page that already fits read out of its
archive twice. `cover::cached_or_generated_page` fetched the page inside a
generation permit to learn that it fit, and dropped the bytes when `fit_at`
answered `None`. `routes::get_page` then read the page again to serve it. The
row deferred the fix until a page turn had been timed on the editions it names.

**Substrate.** Everything below ran on the development workstation: 32 cores,
the corpus on local NVMe with a warm page cache, a release build of `4ff7c6a`
serving a scratch copy of `gotoubun-v01`'s sidecar with every member path made
absolute, and a scratch database and cache. It is **not** the production host,
which is a container on the Unraid NAS. The 1-minute load average is given
beside each timing. Another session's gate finished before any timing began.

### Which requests reach the arm that serves a page that fits

Every page header in three editions, read out of the archives:

| edition | pages | shapes | fit at 768 | 1024 | 1536 | 2048 | 3072 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `raw-mono` | 195 | all baseline JPEG, 685×1024 | 0 | 195 | 195 | 195 | 195 |
| `en-fan` | 235 | c001, c003, c004: JPEG 950×1364; c000, c002, c005, c005.5: mostly PNG 1070×1600 or 1114×1600; a few spreads and credits | 4 | 5 | 112 | 234 | 234 |
| `en-mono` | 187 | progressive JPEG 2146 or 2147×3056, one PNG, seven 4294×3056 spreads | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 180 |

`pageSize.ts` asks for the smallest rung at or above the box's long edge
times `devicePixelRatio`. In `two` mode the box is the larger of half the
window's width and its height. In `single` mode it is the larger of the width
and the height. So at `devicePixelRatio` 1, any window taller than 768 CSS
pixels asks for at least 1024 in either mode, and every `raw-mono` page fits.
In `single` mode, a window whose larger dimension is over 1536 asks for 2048,
and nearly every `en-fan` page fits. `raw-mono` is missed only by a window no
taller than 768 and no wider than 768 in `single` mode, or 1536 in `two`. At
`devicePixelRatio` 3, a phone asks for 3072, and 180 of `en-mono`'s pages fit
too. The browser confirmed two points of this: 1440×900 in `two` mode asked
for `?w=1024`, and 1600×900 in `single` mode asked for `?w=2048`.

### The reads, counted

`strace -f -e trace=openat` on the pre-fix server, counting opens of the member
archive for each request:

| request | archive opens | served |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `raw-mono` page 10, full size | 1 | `image/jpeg`, 197077 B |
| the same at `?w=1024` (fits) | 2 | the same bytes |
| the same at `?w=1024` again | 2 | the same bytes |
| the same at `?w=2048` (fits) | 2 | the same bytes |
| the same at `?w=768` (resize) | 1 | `image/jpeg`, 83482 B |
| the same at `?w=768` again (cache hit) | 0 | the same |
| `en-fan` page 49 (c001), full size / `?w=1536` fits / `?w=1024` resize / hit | 1 / 2 / 1 / 0 | JPEG 639744 B / same / 166292 B / same |
| `en-fan` page 10 (c000), full size / `?w=2048` fits / `?w=1536` resize / hit | 1 / 2 / 1 / 0 | **PNG** 462228 B / **PNG**, same / JPEG 410656 B / same |

The row's counts hold, and one thing the row did not say: nothing is cached
for a page that fits, so the double read is paid **on every request** for it,
not once.

### What the second read costs the server

Keep-alive requests from Python, 20 pages × 20 rounds, with full size and
`?w=` interleaved and each page requested at both URLs once before timing.
Milliseconds, n = 400 each:

| pages | rung | full size TTFB median / p90 | fits TTFB median / p90 | difference in medians | load |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `raw-mono` JPEG 685×1024 | 1024 | 1.349 / 1.621 | 2.545 / 2.909 | 1.196 | 6.60–7.11 |
| `raw-mono` JPEG 685×1024 | 2048 | 1.357 / 1.573 | 2.574 / 2.957 | 1.217 | 7.11 |
| `en-fan` c001 JPEG 950×1364 | 1536 | 1.606 / 1.895 | 3.005 / 3.449 | 1.399 | 7.11 |
| `en-fan` c000 PNG 1114×1600 | 2048 | 0.438 / 0.606 | 0.711 / 1.065 | 0.273 | 7.11 |

The difference is the second read, plus the header parse and the cache lookup
that misses. The fix removes only the second read, so the table after the fix,
below, is what separates them. Why the PNG member reads three times faster than
the JPEG ones was not looked into.

### What a page turn costs, in the browser

Playwright's Chromium against vite, proxying to the pre-fix server. Keypress to
the first animation frame after every cell holds the new `src` and has finished
loading. Synthetic `keydown` on `window`, 700 ms between turns, a
`PerformanceObserver` on resource entries and a `MutationObserver` on `src`.

| run | window, mode, rung | turns | median | p90 | worst | load |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `raw-mono` p17 → p56, first visit | 1440×900, `two`, 1024 | 20 | 52.5 ms | 55.2 ms | 85.9 ms | 1.63 |
| `en-fan` c001 p71 → p90, browser cache cleared | 1600×900, `single`, 2048 | 20 | 53.3 ms | 54.5 ms | 58.7 ms | 2.94 |
| `en-fan` c002 PNG p97 → p116, browser cache cleared | 1600×900, `single`, 2048 | 20 | 54.0 ms | 77.2 ms | 96.5 ms | 1.94 |

Most turns land near 36 or 53 ms, a frame apart, which is frame quantisation. **Every
one of the 60 turns requested its page's `?w=` URL after the keypress**, so the
double read landed on the turn itself, not on prefetch. The browser also gives
a comparison within the same turns. Prefetch requested the next pages at full
size within about a millisecond of the turn's `?w=` request. Both went through
the same proxy and both were cold:

| run | `?w=` TTFB median / p90 (two reads) | full-size prefetch TTFB median / p90 (one read) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `raw-mono` | 5.9 / 11.2 ms, n = 39 | 4.2 / 10.0 ms, n = 39 |
| `en-fan` c001 | 5.6 / 9.3 ms, n = 20 | 3.6 / 8.2 ms, n = 21 |
| `en-fan` c002 PNG | 7.6 / 10.7 ms, n = 20 | 8.5 / 10.6 ms, n = 20 |

So on this machine the second read is about a millisecond of a 50 ms turn,
smaller than the 17 ms frame the turn is counted in.

**Found on the way, and not fixed here: prefetch warms URLs the reader never
draws.** `App.tsx`'s prefetch effect builds `pageUrl(work, edition, page)`
with no long edge, while the cells ask for `pageUrl(…, pageLongEdge)`. Every
prefetch request in these runs was a full-size URL. So prefetch does not warm
the turn, the turn's `?w=` request is always cold on a first visit, and a page
is sent to the browser twice, once whole and once at reading size. It is a web
defect with its own measurement to make, and is reported rather than widened
into this branch.

*Filed as O110 on 2026-09-13, with no code change, and closed on 2026-09-14 —
see "O110" below.*

**One run measured nothing, and one measured something else.** `gotoubun-v01`
reads right to left, and `stepFor` maps ArrowRight to a step back, so twenty
ArrowRight presses from page 0 left the reader where it was. Each wait timed
out at ten seconds. Every result after that used ArrowLeft. The first `en-fan`
run then reached its start with a 42-page flick back through the pages it went
on to turn. That flick had already requested every `?w=` URL on the way: all
20 turns were `304`s, which `get_page` answers before reading anything (median
36.5 ms, p90 53.2 ms). It shows a repeat visit never reaches the double read,
because pages are sent `private, no-cache` with a tag. It does not time the
double read. The two cold `en-fan` runs cleared Chromium's cache over CDP first
and started without a flick.

### The permit wait

A cold filmstrip holds both generation permits, and a page that fits was fetched
inside one. Staged with Python: the tile cache wiped, all 187 `en-mono` tiles
requested over six connections, as a browser would. 300 ms in, a fitting
`raw-mono` page at `?w=1024`, the same page at full size, and a cache hit at
`?w=768` were requested in turn, every 50 ms for three seconds. Milliseconds:

| run | filmstrip | fits `?w=1024` median / p90 / max | full size median / p90 / max | cache hit median / p90 / max | n | load |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | no | 2.93 / 3.29 / 8.73 | 1.38 / 1.54 / 1.77 | 0.18 / 0.26 / 0.54 | 55 | 5.14 |
| 2 | yes, 7.1 s, tiles 225 ms median | **164.28 / 212.62 / 220.50** | 1.80 / 2.24 / 8.51 | 0.32 / 0.39 / 0.70 | 14 | 4.73 |
| 3 | no | 3.07 / 3.96 / 8.56 | 1.52 / 1.93 / 2.15 | 0.25 / 0.35 / 0.55 | 55 | 4.51 |
| 4 | yes, 7.0 s, tiles 220 ms | **166.49 / 201.92 / 250.24** | 1.61 / 1.84 / 8.82 | 0.28 / 0.46 / 0.52 | 14 | 4.31 |
| 5 | no | 3.04 / 3.47 / 8.24 | 1.51 / 1.74 / 6.98 | 0.25 / 0.34 / 16.16 | 55 | 4.28 |
| 6 | yes, 7.0 s, tiles 223 ms | **163.82 / 209.77 / 242.74** | 1.60 / 1.95 / 1.95 | 0.25 / 0.41 / 0.55 | 14 | 4.02 |

**The wait shows, and it is over a hundred times the second read.** While a
filmstrip generates, a request for a page that already fits queues for a
permit, and the full-size request and the cache hit beside it do not. The fix
below does not change that, because the fetch and the header parse still run
inside the permit. Moving them out is a separate change, and its memory
question is narrower than bounding how many pages are held. A full-size request
already fetches with no permit at all, and the permit's own doc comment
justifies it by decode memory (`MAX_DECODE_ALLOC`). What would change is that
a request needing a resize would hold its fetched page while it queues for the
decode.

*Filed as O111 on 2026-09-13, with no code change, and closed on 2026-09-17 —
see "O111" below.*

### The fix

`cached_or_generated_page` returns `cover::Fitted<P>`, where `P` is whatever
the caller's fetch returned. `Resized(Vec<u8>)` is a JPEG from the cache or
just made. `Original(P)` is the fetched page, handed back when it already fits.
`get_page` now passes `state.page(…)` whole and serves `Original(page)` as it
is, content type included. `ServedPage` implements `AsRef<[u8]>` so the header
parse can read its bytes. The fetch is still an `FnOnce`, so it happens once.
The permit is untouched.

`test_support::CountingSource` wraps `LocalLibrary` and records every read as
the member's path and the offset within it. The route test makes the four
requests `strace` counted above, against O108's shared-member fixture: full size,
a page that fits, a resize and a cache hit. They must read once, once, once and
not at all, and each read must be `b.cbz`'s first page. Before the fix it failed
on the second request with `[("b.cbz", 0), ("b.cbz", 0)]`. A cover test hands
back a page that is not a bare `Vec`, so "as it was fetched" covers the field
beside the bytes, and requires that nothing is cached for it.

### Every break, watched

Each change was applied by hand to the fixed tree and run against all 571
`taiyaku-serve` tests under nextest. The file was then restored and its
SHA-256 checked. A control run passed 571 of 571 before the six and again after.

| break | red | failing assertion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the second read put back in `get_page`'s arm for a page that fits | `a_page_that_already_fits_the_width_is_read_once` only | two reads of `("b.cbz", 0)` where one belongs |
| that arm serving `image/jpeg` over the original bytes | the new route test; `a_page_that_already_fits_the_width_is_read_by_its_index`; `a_width_larger_than_the_page_serves_the_original_bytes_untouched` | `image/jpeg` where `image/png` belongs |
| the second read put back, by offset | `…_read_by_its_index`; the new route test | `"grey"` where `"red"` belongs; the new test stops first at the bytes |
| the one fetch made by offset | `…_read_by_its_index`; the new route test; `a_resized_page_is_cached_under_its_offset_in_its_member_not_its_index` | `"grey"` where `"red"` belongs |
| a page that fits written to the cache | `a_page_that_already_fits_is_fetched_once_and_handed_back` only | "and nothing is cached for it" |
| a page that fits answered as `Resized` of its own bytes | the cover test; the new route test; `…_read_by_its_index`; `…_serves_the_original_bytes_untouched` | the cover test's `Original`; `image/jpeg` where `image/png` belongs |

The first row is O107's defect in the new shape, and no test from before this
branch goes red under it. That reproduces the review's finding that nothing
could see it. "Fetch twice" has no row at the cover level because `page` is
`FnOnce`: a second call does not compile. Under plain `cargo test`, which
mutation sweeps use, the crate passed 571 of 571 three times, in 15.4 to
15.7 s, with no hang.

### What the mutation sweep could and could not see

`scripts/mutants.sh --since main` found eight mutants: four caught, none
missed, and four unviable, with no survivor outside the baseline. **All four
unviable mutants are `cached_or_generated_page`'s**, and this branch is why.
It returns `Fitted<P>`, which has no constructor, `From`, `FromIterator` or
`Default`, so each whole-function replacement cargo-mutants tried fails to
compile. With the old `Option<Vec<u8>>` it would have built `Ok(None)` and
`Ok(Some(vec![]))`. The sweep therefore made no viable mutant of the one
function this item changed. It also made none of the match arms, the permit
or `get_page`'s arm for a page that fits, since it does not mutate statements.
The two whole-function replacements it could not build were applied by hand
instead. `Ok(Fitted::Resized(Vec::new()))` and `Ok(Fitted::Resized(vec![0]))`
each turned 11 of 571 tests red, three in `cover` and eight in `routes`, among
them both new tests.

### After the fix

The same `strace` requests against the release build of the fix:

| request | archive opens before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| full size, `raw-mono`, `en-fan` c001, `en-fan` c000 | 1 | 1 |
| a page that fits, each of the four | **2** | **1** |
| a resize | 1 | 1 |
| a cache hit | 0 | 0 |

Every response was byte for byte what it had been, and `en-fan` page 10 at
`?w=2048` is still served as `image/png`.

The server A/B again, on the fix and then on the pre-fix build straight after,
so a quieter machine cannot pass for the fix. TTFB medians in milliseconds,
n = 400 each, load 6.40 falling to 5.97:

| pages | rung | fix: full size / fits / difference | pre-fix again: full size / fits / difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `raw-mono` JPEG | 1024 | 1.222 / 1.260 / 0.038 | 1.223 / 2.311 / 1.088 |
| `raw-mono` JPEG | 2048 | 1.283 / 1.327 / 0.044 | 1.254 / 2.339 / 1.085 |
| `en-fan` c001 JPEG | 1536 | 1.480 / 1.512 / 0.032 | 1.500 / 2.809 / 1.309 |
| `en-fan` c000 PNG | 2048 | 0.437 / 0.431 / −0.006 | 0.430 / 0.718 / 0.288 |

The pre-fix repeat's difference is within 0.14 ms of the first pre-fix run's
in every case, and the difference that remains after the fix is about
0.04 ms. So the header parse and the missed cache lookup cost next to nothing,
and the millisecond was the second read.

The permit wait is unchanged, as expected. Two more pairs of runs against the
fix, with a filmstrip: a page that fits waited a median 170.13 and 169.72 ms
(p90 214.54 and 204.93), with full size at 1.65 and 1.68 ms and the cache hit
at 0.31 ms. Load was 5.24–5.38.

The page turns again, against the fix through the same vite, with the same
starting pages and the browser cache cleared before each run:

| run | before: median / p90 / worst | after: median / p90 / worst | load after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `raw-mono` from 17\|16, `two`, `?w=1024` | 52.5 / 55.2 / 85.9 ms | 41.3 / 52.9 / 53.7 ms | 2.19 |
| `en-fan` c001 p71 → p90, `single`, `?w=2048` | 53.3 / 54.5 / 58.7 ms | 54.6 / 60.0 / 72.5 ms | 1.61 |

**The turn did not measurably change, and was never going to at this size.**
Both `raw-mono` runs have nearly every turn on a frame boundary near 36 or 52 ms. The
median moved because more turns landed on the earlier frame, which a
millisecond of server time can tip but twenty turns cannot attribute. `en-fan`
moved the other way. What did change is visible one level down. In the same
turns, the proxy's time to first byte for a fitting `?w=` request now matches
the full-size prefetch beside it: 4.7 against 4.4 ms on `raw-mono` and 8.2
against 8.2 on `en-fan`, where before the fix it trailed by 1.7 and 2.0 ms.

### What remains

- **The permit wait**, measured above at a 164–170 ms median while a cold
  filmstrip generates, before the fix and after it. The fetch of a page that
  fits, and the header parse that decides it fits, still run inside
  `GENERATION_LIMIT`. Taking them out would let a page that fits skip the queue.
  A request that needs a resize would then hold its fetched page while it
  queues for the decode, which it does not today. That is narrower than it
  sounds: a full-size request already fetches with no permit at all, and the
  permit's own doc comment justifies it by decode memory. That trade is its
  own item. *Filed as O111 on 2026-09-13, and closed on 2026-09-17 — see
  "O111" below.*
- **Prefetch warms full-size URLs** the reader then never requests at that size
  when it draws a page fit-whole, above. On a first visit every turn fetches
  its page cold, and a page is sent twice. *Filed as O110 on 2026-09-13, and
  closed on 2026-09-14.*
- **The production host is unmeasured.** On the NAS a read is a disk seek
  behind a parity array, not a warm NVMe page cache, so the second read this
  removes was likely dearer there than the millisecond measured here. That is
  an expectation, not a measurement, and the permit wait was not measured
  there either.

### Isolation

The corpus was read and never written. Every server served a scratch copy of
the sidecar, with its database and its `--cache` in scratch, so progress
writes, tiles and reading pages landed there. `date -Iseconds` was stamped
before the first request, at 2026-09-13T21:39:53-07:00. After every server,
browser and permit run had finished,
`find corpus -newermt 2026-09-13T21:39:53-07:00` returned nothing.
The corpus volumes' own `.taiyaku-cache` directories kept their August
modification times. The standing corpus checks ran after that, 24 of 24
passing, and the same `find` at 22:26:17 still returned nothing, as did one
over the repository-root `.taiyaku-cache` those checks share with `align`.
Their only new file was the one they write by design,
`/tmp/taiyaku-corpus-star.json`.

## O110: prefetch warms the page a turn draws — 2026-09-14

Opened while timing O107, which saw every prefetch request in its browser runs
ask for a page at full size while each turn asked for its page at `?w=`.
`App.tsx`'s prefetch effect built `pageUrl(work, edition, page)` with no long
edge, and a cell builds it with `pageLongEdge`. The browser caches a page once
per URL, so prefetch warmed nothing a turn drew. The row asked for a page turn
on `en-mono`, where decode dominates, timed before the fix and after it.

**Substrate.** The development workstation: 32 cores, the corpus on local NVMe
with a warm page cache, and a release build of `3e06320`, which this branch
does not change. It served a scratch copy of `gotoubun-v01`'s sidecar with
every member path made absolute, a scratch database, and a new, empty
`--cache` for every run. It is **not** the production host. The reader was the
production bundle, built with `vite build` once from `3e06320` and once from
this branch, each served by `vite preview` through the same `/api` proxy. The
browser, driven by Playwright, reported itself as Chrome 153 on Linux. The
1-minute load average read 2.13, 2.43 and 2.74 before the first, second and
fourth runs.

### A page turn, before and after

Each run cleared the browser's cache over CDP, signed in, recorded `en-mono`
slot 20 as the position, set `two` mode, and opened the reader at 1440×900 and
a `devicePixelRatio` of 1, which asks for `?w=1024`. It waited for the pages to
load and two seconds more, then dispatched `ArrowLeft` twenty times on
`window`, waiting 700 ms after each turn had painted. `gotoubun-v01` reads
right to left, so that steps forward. A turn's time runs from the keypress to
the first animation frame in which the page images' `src`s have changed and
every one of them has loaded. A drawn page counts as requested after the
keypress when the first resource timing entry for its URL started after it.
The runs alternated: before, after, before, after.

| run | build | median | p90 | worst | drawn pages requested after the keypress | page requests, full size / `?w=1024` | transferred |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `3e06320` | 229.5 ms | 339.9 ms | 341.6 ms | 36 of 36 | 55 / 38 | 91.78 MB |
| 2 | this branch | 3.8 ms | 6.9 ms | 16.2 ms | 0 of 36 | 0 / 44 | 6.86 MB |
| 3 | `3e06320` | 210.6 ms | 325.7 ms | 381.0 ms | 36 of 36 | 55 / 38 | 91.78 MB |
| 4 | this branch | 3.1 ms | 7.4 ms | 7.5 ms | 0 of 36 | 0 / 42 | 6.86 MB |

Twenty turns drew 36 pages: sixteen landed on a pair and four on a page drawn
alone. The p90 is the second slowest of twenty. Requests and bytes cover the
whole visit, the first load included, read 2.2 s after the last turn, and the
bytes are resource timing's `transferSize` summed over page requests.

Before the fix, every page a turn drew was requested only after its keypress,
in both runs. After it, none was, and the median turn fell from 210–230 ms to
3–4 ms, in line with the 4 ms median `modules/prefetch.ts` records for its
default window.

### What the server saw

The request log (`--log-requests`) for the same four runs. Its `micros` runs
from a request's arrival to its response being recorded.

| run | full size, 200 / 304 | `?w=1024`, 200 / 304 | distinct pages | pages sent both whole and resized | `?w=1024` 200s, median / p90 / max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 42 / 13 | 38 / 0 | 42 | 38 | 122.2 / 156.1 / 261.6 ms |
| 2 | 0 / 0 | 42 / 2 | 42 | 0 | 125.7 / 243.5 / 369.2 ms |
| 3 | 42 / 13 | 38 / 0 | 42 | 38 | 123.6 / 145.1 / 254.8 ms |
| 4 | 0 / 0 | 42 / 0 | 42 | 0 | 125.4 / 242.7 / 381.6 ms |

Before the fix, all 38 pages the reader drew were sent twice, once whole to
prefetch and once resized for the cell that drew them. The other four were
prefetched whole and never drawn. A resize took a median of 122–124 ms of the
server's time, a little over half the median turn. After the fix, nothing was sent
whole. The 304s are requests for a URL the browser already held: thirteen
full-size ones a visit before the fix, and two `?w=` ones in run 2. `status.md`'s
O1 entry records one way the reader makes them, prefetch's throwaway `Image`
and then the swap's own decode asking for the same URL, but whether that
accounts for these was not checked.

**The resize now waits longer, but ahead of the reader rather than on a
turn.** The `?w=1024` p90 rose from 145–156 ms to 243 ms, and the worst from
255–262 ms to 369–382 ms. The likely reason, not isolated here: prefetch runs
up to three decodes at once (`maxConcurrent: 3`), each now a resize, and
`GENERATION_LIMIT` admits two, so the third queues. No turn waited on it: the
slowest turn after the fix took 16.2 ms.

### The fix

`pageLongEdge` moved up in `App.tsx` to sit ahead of the prefetch effect, and
so ahead of the component's `if (!session) return null`, where the effect can
read it. The effect builds each URL with it and lists it among its
dependencies, so a resize or a zoom that moves the rung warms the window again
at the new size. A turn carries the zoom, since `readerIntent` applies
`clampRect` rather than resetting the view, so the page a turn lands on is
drawn at the rung the reader is already at. Cells and prefetch now build their
URLs from one binding.

A borrowed page needs no rung of its own here. `prefetchTargets` answers
nothing unless the reader is `at` a page, and every target is a page of the
edition being viewed, which a cell draws with `pageLongEdge`.

### Every break, watched

Three tests in `App.test.tsx` stub `Image` to record every URL handed to an
off-screen image, turn a page, and require that the URL the turn draws was
recorded before the keypress. One turns from the page the reader opened on,
one resizes the window from 1024 to 2000 CSS pixels first, and one zooms a
step first. The last two also require that the rung moved, or the warm-up at
mount would satisfy them. The first requires that the drawn URL carries a
`?w=`, or a full-size prefetch would satisfy it.

All three failed before the fix, each on the assertion that its drawn URL,
`/raw/pages/3?w=1024`, `?w=2048` or `?w=1536`, had been recorded. Two breaks
were then applied to the fix by hand:

| break | tests red |
| --- | --- |
| the prefetch URL built without the long edge | all three |
| `pageLongEdge` left out of the effect's dependencies | the resize and zoom tests; the first still passes, since the rung at mount is right |

`App.tsx` was restored from a copy and compared byte for byte. The web suite
now counts 1,157 tests in `node` and 950 in `jsdom`, three more than before,
and `check-all.sh` ended `all green, except NOT MEASURED: standing corpus
checks (TAIYAKU_CORPUS unset)`. No Rust changed, so the mutation harness has
nothing to sweep.

### What remains

- **A new rung does not drop the old one's queued work.** `superseded` compares
  the position a job was queued for and not its size, so after a resize or a
  zoom the jobs already queued at the old rung still run. A wheel zoom through
  several rungs can warm the neighbours at every size it passes. Not measured.
- **Prefetch now spends generation permits.** Its full-size requests took no
  permit. Its `?w=` requests take `GENERATION_LIMIT` whenever the page is not
  already cached, so prefetch now queues for the same two permits as a cold
  filmstrip. O111's wait was measured before that. *Added to O111's entry.*
  *O111 closed on 2026-09-17: a page that already fits takes no permit now, so
  this holds only for a page that needs a resize — see "O111" below.*
- **The prefetch window was tuned against full-size decodes.** `ahead: 1`,
  `behind: 1` and `maxConcurrent: 3` were settled by #35's runs, when every
  page prefetch warmed decoded at 2147×3056, about 26 MB. Fetched at 1024 an
  `en-mono` page decodes to about 6 MB (`pageSize.ts`'s table), and the window
  has not been measured against that. *Noted in `modules/prefetch.ts`.*
- **The production host is unmeasured.** On the NAS a resize reads its page
  behind a parity array, so the turn this saves is expected to be longer
  there. That is an expectation, not a measurement.
- **Only one configuration was timed**: `en-mono`, `two` mode, 1440×900 at a
  `devicePixelRatio` of 1. `single` mode, a zoomed reader and the other
  editions were not.

### Isolation

The corpus was read and never written. Every server ran with `--db` and
`--cache` in scratch. `date -Iseconds` was stamped before the release build and
the first server, at 2026-09-14T00:23:48-07:00. After the last run, with every
server stopped, `find corpus -newermt 2026-09-14T00:23:48-07:00` returned
nothing, and the default library database kept its modification time of
2026-08-31.
