### O57: what a burst costs, measured three times

**The rig.** Release builds, each run a fresh process on a fresh copy of a
small scratch store. `o57-burst.py` opens N connections, releases N logins
together, each with a name nobody holds and a wrong password, all from one
address, and reads the server's resident memory from `/proc`: before, at its
peak (sampled every 2 ms, and the kernel's own high-water mark), and after.
This workstation: glibc 2.44, 32 threads, with other work running on it. The
figures move between runs: `main`'s peak for forty read 709.2 MiB in one run
and 626.9 MiB in another.

| build | allocator | burst | answered 401, 429 | resident before | peak | later |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `main` `451f6910` | default | 40 | 40, 0 | 13.0 MiB | 709.2 MiB | not read |
| `main` `451f6910` | default | 40 | 40, 0 | 11.0 MiB | 626.9 MiB | 33.2 MiB at 1 s |
| `main` `451f6910` | default | 200 | 155, 45 | 13.4 MiB | 1211.8 MiB | not read |
| `7f39f666`, the cap alone | default | 40 | 40, 0 | 11.1 MiB | 603.2 MiB | 603.6 MiB at 30 s |
| `7f39f666`, the cap alone | default | 200 | 52, 148 | 13.5 MiB | 629.6 MiB | not read |
| `7f39f666`, the cap alone | `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=1048576` | 40 | 40, 0 | 11.6 MiB | 90.3 MiB | 14.4 MiB at 1 s |
| `7f39f666`, the cap alone | `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=1048576` | 200 | 53, 147 | 11.4 MiB | 95.7 MiB | 19.8 MiB at 1 s |
| `7f39f666`, the cap alone | `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1` | 40 | 40, 0 | 11.1 MiB | 89.5 MiB | 13.7 MiB at 1 s |
| `da47d1f6`, the branch | default | 40 | 40, 0 | 13.4 MiB | 92.1 MiB | 92.2 MiB at 30 s |
| `da47d1f6`, the branch | default | 200 | 52, 148 | 12.3 MiB | 96.5 MiB | 95.9 MiB at 30 s |

(`o57-burst-main-451f6910-40.log` and `-200.log`, `o57-burst-probes.log`,
`o57-burst-branch-7f39f666-200.log`, `o57-burst-final-da47d1f6.log`.)

**The cap does what it says for the count, and at first did not for the
memory.** Of two hundred at once the capped server verified between 51 and
53 and answered the rest 429, where `main` verified 155: the lockout is read
again under a permit, so at most three requests are past that read when the
fiftieth failure lands. But with the cap alone the server held about
600 MiB after a burst of forty and still held it thirty seconds later,
where `main` with the same defaults, in the one run that read it again, was
at 33 MiB a second later.

**Why.** argon2 asks the allocator for its 19 MiB a run. On `main` the forty
requests of a burst ask together, glibc serves those that ask before the
first is freed with `mmap`, and a block served so is unmapped when it is
freed. Once a large block has been freed glibc raises
its `mmap` threshold to that size, and later requests of that size are
served from the calling thread's own arena, where a freed block stays. Under
the cap the verifies run four at a time on as many blocking-pool threads as
the burst is wide, so all but the first few are served that way, and the
arena that served one keeps it. The two settings in the table separate the two
things: with the threshold pinned, or with one arena, the same capped build
peaks near 90 MiB and a second later is under 20 MiB, which is four buffers
in use and none kept. `unsafe_code` is forbidden in this workspace, so
`mallopt` was not open, and a setting in the image would have left the
binary as it was. The image is `debian:bookworm-slim`, so the deployed
server is glibc as well.

**The fix** was to stop asking the allocator. `argon2`'s
`hash_password_into_with_memory` runs in memory the caller supplies. A
verify permit owns one such memory (`credential::WorkingMemory`), a server
makes a new one only when every one it has is in a permit holder's hands,
and a memory is wiped after every run. Hashing a password takes a memory
from a store the process keeps and puts it back. The last two rows are the
result: a peak of four memories over the starting size, kept.

**What it costs.** Those memories are the server's for the life of the
process: about 80 MiB over its starting size once four verifies have run at
once. With glibc's defaults `main` was at 33 MiB a second after its burst,
in the one such run that read it again.

**The verifier is now this project's own, held to argon2's.**
`credential::verify_password_in` is `password-hash`'s default verifier and
`argon2`'s `hash_password_customized` written against supplied memory: the
algorithm, version and parameters are the stored hash's, the salt is the
hash's salt decoded, and the comparison is `Output`'s own. `credential`
no longer exports `argon2`'s allocating verifier, which is the oracle in
`credential/tests.rs`. `the_two_verifiers_agree` puts a table of cases to
both, each case in a memory filled with other words first. Task B4's review
put 219 odd PHC strings by three passwords to both, in fresh, reused and
pre-filled memory, and 1,017 parameter cells in dirty memory to argon2's
hasher and the mirror's: no disagreement and no panic
(`b4-review/review_probe.rs`). The review of the fixes ran the same probe
again at `da47d1f6`, in a debug build and a release one, with the same
result (`delta-rust/review_probe.adapted-da47d1f6.rs`). It found one panic
that is `argon2`'s own, in both verifiers alike: `p` at or above 2^29
overflows a multiplication in `argon2`'s `params.rs`, which panics in a
debug build and answers `false` in a release build.

**The wipe, read in a release build.** `cargo build --release -p
taiyaku-cli` at `da47d1f6`, the image's build command but for its
`--locked`, with this machine's toolchain, disassembled by the review of the
fixes (`delta-rust/hash_in.release.asm`, `hash_password.release.asm`).
`credential::hash_in` is a function of its own in that build. Each way out
of it joins at one `memset` over the run's blocks, and the unwind's landing
pad makes the same call. By the review's reading of the binary, `hash_in` is
called from `hash_password` and `verify_password_in`, and the hash store's
lock is released before the call. That is one build read, and no test holds
it.

**What the wipe covers** is the working memory. `argon2` keeps the run's
initial hash and a copy of its last block on its own stack, and the output,
the decoded salt and the password are not wiped either. So the wipe takes
away the copy that would have stayed for the life of the process, and does
not stop somebody who can read the process's memory just after a verify.

**A flood, and the blocking pool (the whole-branch review's measurement).**
A request waiting for a permit parks a blocking-pool thread, and every
request needs one of those. Release builds; an open loop of `GET /api/works`
with a wrong Basic password, each request on its own connection and from its
own address, so nothing is ever locked out; a reader with an API key probing
every 100 ms; the server pinned with `taskset`; the store on tmpfs; machine
load about 13 (`wbr-rust/flood-*.log`, `flood.py`).

| CPUs | flood | build | reader median, 90th, slowest | most threads | most resident |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 200/s, 6 s | branch | 0.4, 0.6, 1.0 ms | 13 | 90 MiB |
| 8 | 200/s, 6 s | `main` | 0.8, 3.7, 6.2 ms | 24 | 300 MiB |
| 8 | 360/s, 20 s | branch | 0.4, 1.1, 3.3 ms | 242 | 107 MiB |
| 8 | 360/s, 20 s | `main` | 7166, 10923, 13315 ms | 521 | 13477 MiB |
| 8 | 500/s, 6 s | branch | 0.5, 1199, 1463 ms | 521 | 128 MiB |
| 8 | 500/s, 6 s | `main` | 5542, 7305, 10018 ms | 521 | 10895 MiB |
| 16 | 420/s, 18 s | branch | 4781, 7955, 8480 ms | 529 | 170 MiB |
| 16 | 420/s, 18 s | `main` | 0.5, 1625, 4343 ms | 529 | 11231 MiB |

The branch in that table is `6c771e25`, before the wipe and the hash store;
nothing since changes where a waiter waits. On eight cores, which is what
the NAS has, the branch was no worse than `main` at any rate tried and far
better past about 350 a second. On sixteen, at the one rate tried there,
`main` mostly coped and the branch's reader waited seconds: four permits
answer
about 350 verifies a second here whatever the core count, and `main`'s
ceiling rises with cores until its memory does. That is O214, and the
review's way to close it needs no bound: wait for the permit in the async
handler and not on a pool thread.

**Tests.** In `session/tests.rs`, for each of the three paths: a request
that waited for a permit reads the lockout again; a caller already locked
out is refused while the test holds every permit; a burst against a counter
one failure under its ceiling is verified at most four times; the failure is
recorded holding the permit, seen from a SQLite commit hook on the recording
thread; the lockout read fails closed. And: only a password verify waits for
a permit; a request waiting for one does not hold the library's connection;
the password change gives its permit back before it hashes; each of the five
verifies runs in its permit's memory; a server makes no more memories than
it has permits. In `credential/tests.rs`: the two verifiers agree over a
table of cases; a working memory grows to what a run needs and is not made
again, read from a count of its growths that only the test build has; it
holds nothing of a run that returned, was refused or unwound; hashes one
after another run in one kept memory, read from a count of the memories the
store has made; a hash does not wait for a run that is holding a memory; and
a lent memory goes back to its store zeroed when its run unwinds. None needs
a race to pass: where a test waits, it is the defect that needs the time.
The implementers' mutations are in `o57-task-B2-mutations.md`,
`o57-task-B3-mutations.md` and `o57-task-B4-mutations.md`, and the review of
the fixes' own in `delta-rust/logs/`.

**What no test holds** is O215's list in `docs/status.md`.

**SQLite 3.40.1.** The three crates' tests ran in `rust:1-bookworm` at
`4aa8cf21`, where `libsqlite3-0` is 3.40.1-2+deb12u2
(`bookworm-sqlite340-4aa8cf21.log`, whose first lines print the image and
that version). Two failed, the two that trace system calls: the container
has no `strace`.

**The standing corpus checks** passed at `4aa8cf21`, 24 of 24
(`corpus-4aa8cf21.log`). One of them compares against a Stump server and
does nothing where no address for one is set. Run again alone at `9a4f9e98`
it printed that it was skipping (`corpus-stump-skip-9a4f9e98.log`).

**What the plan got wrong about its own tests.** It said nothing in a test
could order a permit's release against the record of the failure. A commit
hook can, and two reviewers each showed it.

**Not measured.** The NAS, for any of it. A flood through the proxy in
front of the deployed server. What a wipe costs there.

## O216: the strip under a hand, its mark and its drag (2026-10-12)

*Its width rule, an eighth of the share on show and never under 32 px,
was replaced on 2026-11-14 by the owner (O286): the share, between 64 and
160 px.*

**The hand check.** `main` at `1eb5723e`, a release build and a production
build of the web app, served on this machine from a scratch copy of the test
library's database, in the user's Firefox (asked later that day which
browser it had been, the user said Firefox). A notch of the wheel over the
strip moved it "just over 1 page", and "it feels fine". Those are the two
readings O216 asked for. The user then said "there's no indication of how
far along in the strip we are (no scroll bar)", and that "it would be nice
if you could click+drag with a mouse to scroll the strip".

**What the user chose, by trying it.** Of three forms for the indication (a
thin thumb under the tiles, a mark on the progress line, the browser's own
thin scrollbar) the user chose the mark on the line, to see it. On a
prototype served the same way:

| round | what the user said | what changed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "it works, though the scroll bar is quite huge", and to let the progress bar show underneath, "some amount of opacity" | the mark half transparent, its outline dropped |
| 2 | "by size I meant that it was wide, not tall" | the mark no longer as wide as the share of the volume shown: 32 px, placed by how far the rail is scrolled |
| 3 | "32 is ok for a volume this size- it should potentially be scaled larger for a short volume" | an eighth of the share shown, never under 32 px |
| 4 | "ok the scroll bar width is great now" | nothing |

**The prototype's widths, measured** in headless Chromium 151.0.7922.34 on
that server, the mark's box read from the page:

| volume | pages | window 1,440 px | window 2,560 px |
|---|---|---|---|
| `akame-ga-kill----v01--2015--cbz` | 237 slots | 32 px | 32 px |
| `darling-in-the-franxx---v01--2022--cbz` | 71 | 32 px | 97.6 px |
| `hunter---hunter--official-colored----v35-cbz` | 48 | 45.3 px | 144.2 px |
| `yu-yu-hakusho-tales---two-shots-colored--colored-council--cbz` | 32 | 67.9 px | 216.2 px |

The 97.6 px was stale: the rail's numbers at that moment gave 91 px. The
prototype told the bar where the rail stood after a scroll and after a
render, and a thumbnail that loads late changes the rail's length with
neither.

The same check, on the 237-slot volume, which is read right to left: a
600 px drag moved the rail's `scrollLeft` from 0 to −600 and the mark with
it, the page stayed where it was, and a press that moved 2 px turned the
page (`prototype/selfcheck-widths-and-drag.log`). Of the copy's 1,896
volumes, 1,723 are between 120 and 259 pages and 15 are under 120; those
counts, the four volumes' pages and the browser's version are in
`volume-lengths-and-browser.log`.

Every log named here is in
`.superpowers/sdd/strip-position-and-drag-evidence/`, which is not
committed.

**What building it found wrong in the prototype.** Four things, each now a
rule in the spec's §7 and held by a test.

- The mark went through React state, so a scroll rendered the bars and the
  strip on each frame it moved the mark. It is written on its element now.
  The whole-branch review, at `987c6492`, with a real mouse over a 1,300 px
  drag in both directions: the press committed twice, through the strip's
  own `focusin` listener, and the moves and the release committed nothing.
  That was before a drag handed focus back. Since the glide's change, focus
  the rail hands back leaves the strip's window where it is (`leaves the
  strip's window where it is when it hands focus back to a tile`).
- A movement under a two-thousandth of the rail's length was not told. On
  21 pages at a 2,400 px window, where the rail's travel is 67 px of its
  2,467, the task's review found the mark 31 px short of the line's end
  with the rail at its end. `follows a rail that barely overflows to its
  end a pixel at a time` is that case.
- A press let go where the rail could not hear it was left standing. Task
  2's implementer read it with a real mouse: press a tile, leave the strip
  with under 5 px of travel along it, let go outside, come back with no
  button down, and the rail followed the mouse, 122 px in Chromium and
  121.25 and 122.5 px in Playwright's Firefox (`task-2/`).
- A drag left focus on the tile it began on. The whole-branch review, in
  the whole reader with a real mouse and key: page 30 current, a drag begun
  on tile 33, Space, and tile 33 was current.

**Where the click after a drag lands.** On the rail, since the pointer is
captured, in Chromium and in Playwright's Firefox, in both reading
directions, let go on the strip or 200 px below it. It arrives before a
0 ms timer set as the release began. Chromium is held by the suite; the
Firefox reading is a probe of Task 2's implementer, its source kept in
`task-2/`.

**The built app, with a real mouse.** The branch at `b882763a`, before the
glide was built, built and served as the prototype was, in headless Chromium with Playwright's
mouse, on the 237-slot volume, which is read right to left
(`built-app-gestures-b882763a.log`). A press on a tile carried 300 px moved
the rail's `scrollLeft` from 0 to −300 with the cursor `grabbing`, left the
page where it was, and left focus on the `Library` button, which had it
before the press. A press 2 px above a tile's lower edge, carried 3 px out
of the rail and back, then 42 px along, dragged the rail 42 px and turned
no page. A press let go above the strip with 2 px of travel, then another
press out there carried in over the strip, moved the rail 0 px. A click
turned to its tile.

**The glide.** Asked of the built drag, the user said: "strip dragging
works, but there's no momentum. is it possible to add this? and make sure it
doesn't conflict with any mobile native scrolling for this". A prototype was
served the same way, and of it the user said "yeah it feels good". Its
numbers are the ones built: the speed over 100 ms, a travel of that speed
times 325 ms, no glide after a rest of 60 ms or under 0.1 px a millisecond.
On the prototype's build in headless Chromium (`momentum-prototype/glide.log`):
a release while moving carried the rail on 536 px in the 800 ms after it; a release after a rest, 0; a glide into the start of the volume, 0; and
a press during a glide stopped it and turned no page.

A finger's press begins neither a drag nor a glide: both begin from a
mouse's press alone. What a finger's press on the rail does is stop a glide
that is under way. The glide's review sent a touch through the browser's
own input protocol: a tap in mid-glide stopped it and turned the page, and
a finger's pan was
given a `pointercancel` and moved the rail by itself.

**What building the glide found wrong in its prototype**, each fixed and
held by a case:

- A press that stopped a glide could leave part of the strip with no tiles.
  Focus handed back to a tile moved the strip's window to it, which the
  glide had carried the rail on from, and with the glide stopped no scroll
  followed to move it again. Task 3's implementer measured 213 px bare read
  left to right and 280 px right to left, still there a second later. Focus
  the rail hands back moves no window now.
- A click on a strip that looked at rest did nothing for about two seconds
  after a flick, since every press during a glide was taken for one that
  stopped it, to the glide's last half pixel. A press is taken so only while
  the glide still carries the rail at 0.1 px a millisecond or more: from a
  release at 1 px a millisecond that is the first 748 ms of a glide that
  runs 2,105 ms (325 × ln 10; held in `tiles.test.ts` at 748 and 749 ms).
- A press that had only just become a drag read its speed from too little.
  The glide's review: 6 px crept in 202 ms, the last two moves 2 ms apart,
  was carried 155 px on. The speed is read from the press on now, and the
  same creep is carried nothing.
- A frame stamped before the release moved the rail back; a rest of exactly
  60 ms still carried; a change of reading direction did not stop a glide;
  and `Tab` onto the strip in mid-glide was overridden by it.

The glide's review, with a real mouse in both reading directions at
`612e2f95`: glides from 2, 4, 8 and 16 px a millisecond came to rest within
1 px of the speed times 325 ms with no part of the strip bare; a page turn
in mid-glide centred the new tile to 0.5 px; a wheel moved the rail exactly
100 px from where it stood; in the whole reader a flick carried 324 px with
animation on and 0 with the reader's motion setting off; and the mark was
0 px off the rail's numbers in 40 frames of a glide
(`review-of-the-glide/`). The branch at `e1c918cb`, the last commit to
change its code, was built and driven as before
(`built-app-glide-and-gestures-e1c918cb.log`): a release while moving
carried the rail on 539 px in the 800 ms after it; a release after a rest,
0; a glide into the start of the volume, 0; a press during a glide stopped
it and turned no page. Of the drag's gestures, a 300 px drag left the page
and the focus where they were, the press that slips off the strip's edge
and back read 54 px of the rail moved and turned no page, the press carried
in from outside read 1 px, and a click turned to its tile.

**A real flick in a test.** Chromium stamps a mouse event with the time it
is sent with, so `web/tests/support/mouse.ts` can clock a flick: its moves are
15 px each and stamped 15 ms apart whatever the machine does, the speed the
page reads is 1 px a millisecond, and the cases hold 325 px on to 2 px. The same review
put a 300 ms stall before the release and 80 ms between moves, and the
reading did not change.

**The built stylesheet.** `--reader-mark` ships as `#ece4d480`, and the mark
computes to `rgba(236, 228, 212, 0.5)` under a light and a dark colour
scheme alike (`final-review/`). The tokens around it do not, which is
O218 *(closed since, on the same day: see "O218" below)*. Read on the prototype's build in headless Chromium, inside `.reader`,
whose computed `color-scheme` was `dark` both times
(`prototype/built-css-token-readings.log`):

| colour scheme | the progress line | the bottom bar's text | the readout |
|---|---|---|---|
| light | `rgb(214, 204, 185)` | `rgb(35, 30, 23)` | `rgb(107, 97, 81)` |
| dark | `rgb(53, 49, 42)` | `rgb(236, 228, 212)` | `rgb(166, 155, 135)` |

The same log has what the build made of a token,
`--line:var(--lightningcss-light,#d6ccb9)var(--lightningcss-dark,#35312a)`,
and the rules it gave the two switch properties to.

**Not held, and not measured.**

- Three mutations the implementers and reviewers could not get any test to
  catch, with Task 2's implementer's argument for each. The rail's capture
  released without asking whether the rail holds it: the same thing for a
  pointer that is active, by the Pointer Events specification as read, not
  measured. The cleanup leaving the `pointerdown` listener behind once the
  others are gone: it then sets a variable nothing reads. The rail keeping
  listeners of its own for a release beside the window's: the window's
  hears the release first and ends the press, so the rail's finds none.
- One more, in the glide: the loop that trims the pointer's trail to the
  last 100 ms may be taken out and nothing fails, since `releaseSpeed`
  applies that window itself. It bounds how many moves a long drag keeps.
- A release the window does not hear, outside the browser's window or over
  another document, was not read. Such a press would stand until the rail
  next hears a move, which ends it if the button is up.
- Focus handed back after a drag is not drawn. The review of the fix read
  `:focus-visible` true with a 2 px outline on `Library` after `Tab`, and
  false with none after a drag had handed focus back to it. Recorded on
  O168's row.
- A rail pulled past its start reads as scrolled into the volume, since its
  standing is read through `Math.abs`. By arithmetic only.
- The whole-branch review saw that `d`, pressed while the mouse is down,
  leaves the press holding the other direction's `scrollLeft`, and that
  `main`'s strip mounted alone also puts its rail at the volume's start on
  a flip. Not looked into further.
- While correcting, a glide carries tiles under a still pointer, and each
  one the pointer comes over is a request for its page: the glide's review
  saw one flick tell the preview of 22 pages. Whether the preview should
  wait for a glide to stop is not decided.
- On a device with a mouse and a touch screen, a finger's tap that stops a
  mouse's glide is a tap on the tile under it, and turns the page.
- Firefox and Safari by any test; a physical finger or pen; the cursor a
  browser draws while the pointer is captured over a tile; the cost on a
  phone.

## O218: the built stylesheet's tokens (2026-10-12)

**The cause.** Vite 8.2.1 minifies the build's stylesheet with Lightning CSS
1.33.0 and hands it `build.cssTarget` as the browsers to write for. Unset,
that option takes `build.target`'s value, and `main`'s resolved config printed
`chrome111`, `edge111`, `firefox114`, `safari16.4` and `ios16.4` for both
(`resolved-config.log`). Lightning CSS compiles `light-dark()` for a target
that lacks it. Read by transforming `:root{--x:light-dark(red,blue)}` for one
browser at a time (`lightningcss-thresholds.log`):

| browser | compiled at | left as written at |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome | 122 | 123 |
| Edge | 122 | 123 |
| Firefox | 119 | 120 |
| Safari | 17.4 | 17.5 |
| Safari on iOS | 17.4 | 17.5 |

**The change.** `web/vite.config.ts` sets `build.cssTarget` to the five
versions in the right-hand column. `build.target` is not set, and the
resolved config prints the same five for it as before. The first edit put the
option in a `build` key of its own above `test`; the config already had a
`build` key further down, which replaced it, and the new test stayed red until
the option moved there.

**The built stylesheet**, from `vite build` on `main` at 55eaac53 and on the
branch:

| | bytes | `--lightningcss-` | `light-dark(` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main` | 603,334 | 36 | 0 |
| the branch | 602,543 | 0 | 13 |

`main`'s file with each compiled pair turned back into a `light-dark()`, and
the switch properties and the one rule the compile added removed, is the
branch's file byte for byte (`uncompile.sh`, which ends in `cmp`). The rules
that differ are `:root`'s token rule, the two `data-theme` rules, `.reader`,
and that added `@media (prefers-color-scheme:dark)` rule
(`built-css-main-vs-fix.diff`).

**A page of the bottom bar's markup, loading each build's stylesheet**
(`probe.cjs`), in headless Chromium 151 and Firefox 153, under a light and a
dark colour scheme with `data-theme` absent, `paper` and `ink`. `.reader`'s
computed `color-scheme` was `dark` in all twenty-four readings, and the two
browsers read the same colours. Inside `.reader`:

| build | the progress line | the bottom bar's text | the readout |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main`, the page's scheme light | `rgb(214, 204, 185)` | `rgb(35, 30, 23)` | `rgb(107, 97, 81)` |
| `main`, the page's scheme dark | `rgb(53, 49, 42)` | `rgb(236, 228, 212)` | `rgb(166, 155, 135)` |
| the branch, all six | `rgb(53, 49, 42)` | `rgb(236, 228, 212)` | `rgb(166, 155, 135)` |

The page's scheme is light in three of the six: a light colour scheme with no
`data-theme`, and `paper` under either colour scheme. A paragraph outside
`.reader` followed the page's scheme in both builds.

**The app.** The branch's build served by `taiyaku serve`, `main`'s release
binary, from a copy of the test library's database, with the reader open on a
volume and its bars shown (`app-probe.cjs`, `app-fix/`). In the same six
combinations and the same two browsers the progress line read
`rgb(53, 49, 42)`, its fill `rgb(232, 113, 90)`, the mark
`rgba(236, 228, 212, 0.5)`, the readout `rgb(166, 155, 135)`, and the bottom
bar's text, the top bar's and the title's `rgb(236, 228, 212)`. The theme was
set by writing `data-theme` on `<html>`, not through the app's own control. A
screenshot of each was kept; the Chromium one with `paper` under a light
colour scheme was looked at, and shows dark bars with light text.

**The test.** `web/tests/builtStylesheet.test.ts` builds `src/index.css` alone
with the project's config and reads the one stylesheet that comes out: each of
the thirteen tokens `tokens.css` writes as a pair is declared once, as a
`light-dark()`, and the file names neither switch property. A plugin logging
what that build loaded saw one module, `src/index.css`
(`test-build-modules.log`), and its stylesheet carried the app build's content
hash, `u1V7LL1n`. Hand mutations of the config, the test run after each
(`mutations.log`): each of the five versions lowered by one, and the
`cssTarget` line deleted, failed fourteen of the fifteen cases. Before the
change fourteen failed too, the fifteenth being the one that counts the pairs
in the source (`test-before-fix-55eaac53.log`). The `node` project went from
1,510 tests to 1,525.

**Not measured.**

- Safari, on either build.
- A browser older than the five versions. The build now gives it
  `light-dark()` as written, where it gave it `var()` fallbacks before; "Safari
  below 17.5" in the style pass's notes above says what such a browser draws
  from the source. The user's iPhone reported Safari 26.6.1 in the device
  passes recorded above.
- The reader's panels and its note editor, which were not opened.

The evidence is in `.superpowers/sdd/o218-evidence/`.

## Libraries, F3 (2026-10-17)

The branch `libraries-browse` builds F3, browsing by library
(`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-17-libraries-f3-browse.md`): the sidebar
lists the libraries an account may read, each library has a page of its own,
search narrows to one, and OPDS lists them. This section records what was
decided, what was built and what was measured. The logs it cites are in
`.superpowers/sdd/libraries-browse-evidence/`, which is not committed.

**Decided by the user, 2026-10-17**, on three of the plan's four spec
corrections:

- **OPDS narrows by folders by default, and a second view lists each library
  by `work.library_id`** ("can we do by folder by default but also export an
  opds thing that shows by work.library_id separately?"). The spec had the
  library feed read `work.library_id`; the grid, search and home narrow by
  folders, and the two disagree for a work that keeps an edition under
  another library's folder (O191's shape).
- **A status entry carries `scanned`, per library**, where the spec had a
  folder count, and the top-level `scanned` goes: it was true when anything
  at all had been scanned, so for a restricted account it reported on
  libraries the account cannot see.
- **Search has a "Search in" select**, drawn where the account can see two
  or more libraries, kept in the URL as `?library=`.

The third, that the library feeds are navigation feeds, as
`/opds/v1.2/works` is, and that a library outside the grant answers 404 as
one that does not exist does, was not put to the user separately; both views
behave so.

**What a narrowing is.** `browse::library_scope` answers the folders of a
library that the caller's grant allows, with the library's name, or `None`
where there are none: the library is outside the grant, holds no folder, or
does not exist. A listing narrowed to a library (`series`, `unfiled`,
`search`, `home`, each taking `library: Option<i64>`) reads those folders in
place of the grant, so the narrowing is the grant's own SQL pointed at fewer
folders, and a library's page lists what an account granted only that
library sees. `None` is answered as nothing found, and never handed on as an
empty list, which every function in `browse` reads as no restriction at all.
The single-folder `?root=` narrowing it replaces (`only_clause`, and `only`
through `pair_clause`) is deleted, so no parameter group interleaves with
the folder list any more. Before the plan was written, a throwaway test built
two libraries and called the old `series`, `home` and `search` with each
library's folder ids as the grant: one library answered its one series with
both its folders' editions, the other its two series, and the same title
made a series in each (`plan-probe-15e03a9d.log`).

**The routes.** `/api/library/series`, `/home` and `/search` take
`?library=`. `/api/library/series?root=` answers 400, naming `library`.
`/api/library/status` answers
`{"libraries":[{"id","name","scanned"}]}`, listed by name (`COLLATE NOCASE`).
OPDS adds `/opds/v1.2/libraries` and `/opds/v1.2/libraries/{library}/works`
(by folder), and `/opds/v1.2/libraries/by-work` and
`/opds/v1.2/libraries/{library}/works/by-work` (by `work.library_id`, with
every edition the grant allows); the flat `/opds/v1.2/works` is unchanged.

**The web app.** The sidebar lists the libraries for every account, each
linking to `/?library=N`, and marks the one on screen; the `showRoots`
preference is gone. A library's page narrows the grid and the continue
strip, is titled with the library's name, and says "Not read yet" for a
library none of whose folders has been walked and "No such library" for an
id the status does not list. The sidebar is read again when
Configuration → Libraries reads its list. Once the status has been read,
search narrows only to a library the "Search in" select can show.

**What the task reviews found.** A library id and a folder id are both
`i64`, and on a store whose libraries each got one folder in turn, as
migration 15 makes them, library N holds folder N: a test built that way
passes against a query that reads one as the other. Task 1's review found
two such tests; they, and Task 2's fixtures, number their libraries apart
from their folders. Search's
review found the screen naming one scope while searching another: a
`?library=` the status does not list narrowed the search while the select
read "Every library".

**What the whole-branch reviews found.** The Rust half's reviewer ran the
boundary from outside, sending unknown, ungranted, negative and zero
library ids, folder ids as library ids, and a library with no folder to the
browse routes and the OPDS views (not every value to every route): each
answered 404 or an empty list, and an id past `i64` answered 400
(`review-rust/probe1.log`). It
found one gap: no server test pinned `scanned: true`, so a handler that
always answered `false` passed every test; one does now. The web half's
reviewer found that switching library left the old library's grid and
continue strip on screen under the new library's name until the new load
landed, and for good if it failed: the page now draws only what was loaded
for the library it is asked for. `?library=` was read three ways (the
library page as a number, the sidebar as text, search against the status);
one parser now reads it for all three, and only a whole number with no
leading zero names a library. Two smaller ones: nothing held the order of
two status reads, and a failed read of Configuration → Libraries' list did
not re-read the status. **Left as they are:** the "Not read yet" words on the
page of every library, which speak of one library; the two `h2` headings
"Libraries" on Configuration → Libraries, one in the sidebar; a status that
goes stale outside Configuration → Libraries until the next read (a scan
that finishes while the person is elsewhere), and a failed read of it, which
stays on every screen until a read succeeds; and, for an account with no
grant limits, a library's by-folder feed counting a divided work's editions
under its folders while the work's own feed lists them all (O191's row).

**On real material** (`drive.log`), with the build of `513d0b09`, before
the whole-branch reviews' fixes: a copy of the test library's store,
migrated, with its one folder as the library `Volumes`, and two libraries
made on the copy from four volumes copied out of the real one: `Ecchi`, of
two folders, scanned, and `Chapters`, of one, not scanned. As the
administrator, the grid answered 134 series for `Volumes`, 2 for `Ecchi`
(its own `Asobi Asobase` and `Akane-banashi`, apart from `Volumes`' series
of those titles), none for `Chapters` or for a library that does not exist,
and 136 unnarrowed; `?root=1` answered 400. An account granted `Ecchi` alone
was shown `Ecchi` alone in the status, the grid, search and both OPDS views,
and `Volumes`' id answered 404 as a missing one does. The two OPDS views
listed the same works for each library (1896, 3 and 0, against 1899 in the
flat feed), since every work on the copy is filed where its folders are. In
a browser, removing `Chapters` took it out of the sidebar without a reload,
and its page then read "No such library".

**The user's try**, the same day, on that server: the sidebar, the empty
states, search, the restricted account, and a library made and removed
under the sidebar. They found Configuration → Libraries confusing,
cluttered and long (O219), and asked that a library an
account can see be removable even where it is the account's last (O220).

**Counts against `main`:** Rust 2704 → 2720 tests; `web/` 1,525 → 1,529 in
the `node` project, 1,679 → 1,713 in `jsdom`, and 327 → 331 in the browser
project. The mutation sweep over the Rust the branch changed, at
`38c7d2d9`, made 56 mutants: 40 caught, 16 unviable, none missed; `search`,
`home` and `status` in `browse` had no viable mutant, and their evidence is
the hand defects the tasks put back and watched fail.

**Not measured:** the NAS; an OPDS client showing the Libraries level, which
§13 of the spec names; a store whose `work.library_id` disagrees with its
folders on real material.

## Books: what the library's EPUBs hold (2026-09-30)

A read-only survey for the "Books" entry under `docs/status.md`'s "Later",
over `/mnt/user/media 1/Books/Literature` on the NAS, read through the NFS
mount. Fourteen EPUBs, chosen for their apparatus or because a second
edition of the same book sits beside them: Harry Potter 1 in English and in
Korean (Pottermore), Moby-Dick (Norton Critical), Beowulf (Norton, Heaney,
"Bilingual Edition"), Paradise Lost (Longman, Fowler), Hamlet (Arden Third
Series), The Landmark Herodotus, Inferno (Anchor, Hollander), Infinite Jest,
The Annotated Lolita, The New Annotated Sherlock Holmes vol. 1 (Klinger),
Crime and Punishment in Oliver Ready's and in Pevear and Volokhonsky's
translations, and Captain Blood (Standard Ebooks). A throwaway lxml script
walked each spine; nothing was written to the NAS. A paragraph below is a
non-empty `<p>`, and a chapter runs from one table-of-contents target to the
next.

**No file marks its notes semantically.** Ten are EPUB 2 and four EPUB 3.
None of the fourteen carries an `epub:type` of `noteref`, `footnote` or
`endnote`, or a `doc-noteref`, `doc-footnote` or `doc-endnote` role. Each
publisher names its own classes instead: `fn-ref` and `fn` (Moby-Dick),
`footnote`, `footnote1` and `footnote2` (Hamlet), `Annote` (Klinger), `note`
(Paradise Lost), `notes` (Inferno), `x13-End-Note-Number` (Ready), and no
class naming a note at all (Lolita, whose links are its only trace). Captain Blood, the one file with rich
semantics, has no notes. Only Pevear and Volokhonsky mark page breaks
semantically — 566 `pagebreak` elements behind a 566-entry page list; Ready
has a 558-entry page list over bare `<span id="pageMap_…"/>` anchors.

**Four shapes of apparatus.** *Linked notes*, a reference and a note that
link to each other: 1430 of Moby-Dick's 1496 references point into their
own file; Infinite Jest's endnotes carry sub-notes of their own (`fna`,
lettered `a.` to `l.`), so a note can open another note. *Commentary keyed
to line numbers, with no links*: in each of Paradise Lost's twelve books,
all the verse comes first and all the notes after it, in the same file,
each note a paragraph opening with a line number or range in italics —
"*547–65*." — and the verse carries its own line numbers every five lines
as text inside the line (`<p class="verse-lineno"><i>235</i> …`). *A tiered
apparatus*: Hamlet's play text links into commentary kept in separate files
at the back of the book (`part0034` to `part0038`), where
`footnote` is a note on a line, `footnote1` a further lemma on the same
line, and `footnote2` the textual variants in collation form (`90 return]
return'd F`). *A facing-page text, flattened*: Beowulf's "bilingual" EPUB
holds the whole Old English in three files, then the whole translation in
three more, so the facing pages are gone; Inferno keeps its Italian and
English in separate files.

**Some books carry their own alignment.** Beowulf numbers both texts every
ten lines, 10 to 3180, in a table cell beside the line — though the
translation's cell changes class partway through (`sgc3`, then `num` from
line 1600 on, in `part0012.html`), so a rule written for one class misses
half the poem. Inferno links each Italian tercet to its English one by id
(`c24-s01-i` to `c24-s01-e`), and carries the print page as an anchor
(`<a id="page436"/>`). The two Crime and Punishment page lists do not align
with each other — two translations paginate differently — but each is a
citation key for its own edition.

**Two translations in one language keep the original's paragraphing.**
Across the first eighteen chapters, Part One I to Part Three IV, Ready and
Pevear and Volokhonsky differ by at most three paragraphs a chapter (Part
Three IV: 132 against 129), with character counts within 0.97–1.02 of each
other. **Then they part, because Ready's table of contents has no Part Three
VI** — and its text has no heading there either: the chapter opens with
`<p class="Basic-Paragraph"><span id="pageMap_249"/><span
class="x15-All-Caps">VI</span></p>`. So
Ready's Part Three V holds 235 paragraphs against Pevear and Volokhonsky's
164 + 70 = 234 for V and VI, and every chapter after it is off by one. Read
one chapter along, the counts agree again: Part Four's six chapters are 128,
111, 63, 186, 95 and 106 against 128, 111, 64, 186, 95 and 104.

**A translation into another language does not.** Harry Potter 1 has
seventeen chapters in both editions' contents, but the Korean splits
paragraphs: 1.03 to 1.32 times as many a chapter, while its character count
stays between 0.62 and 0.75 of the English. The English also puts each
chapter's opening in a file of its own — 44 spine items against 28 — so the
spine is no unit to align on either.

**Every spine document parses as strict XML.** Adding Mandelbaum's Inferno
to the fourteen, 763 spine documents across fifteen books went through lxml's
strict parser with no failure, calibre's conversions included — so the
extractor does not need an HTML parser on this evidence. One thing a naive
reader of the package would get wrong: Captain Blood's manifest names a spine
document with a `../` in its path, which must be resolved against the
package document's directory before the archive is asked for it.

**Four of the critical editions are PDF only**: Emma (Belknap, annotated),
Ulysses (Cambridge Centenary), King Lear (Arden Third Series) and The
Comedies of Machiavelli (bilingual).

**Both Emmas are scans.** Cambridge's (677 pages, `pdfinfo` Creator
`DuXiu/SuperStar`) yields no text at all from `pdftotext` on pages 20, 100,
300 and 500; Belknap's (584 pages, Creator `Internet Archive`) carries an OCR
text layer, 1856 to 3402 non-space characters on the same four pages. So a
PDF edition enters taiyaku as page images, and aligning one against an EPUB
by its text needs that text from somewhere — its own OCR layer where there is
one, a recognition pass where there is not.

## O237: zip 9.1.3 against the test library (2026-11-02)

Two checks on real material behind O237's bullet, each taken under `main`'s
zip 7.2.0 and this branch's 9.1.3. Neither wrote to the test library at
`/home/davey/temp/manga-test`: the first only reads it, and the second stamped
copies, with the originals' sha256 the same before and after. The scripts and
their output are in `.superpowers/sdd/zip-9-evidence/`, which is not committed.

**Listing every archive changed one page name.** A throwaway Rust probe, built
once against each version (`realcheck/scripts/names-probe/`), opened every
`.cbz` in the test library and printed `ZipArchive::file_names` for each, and
the two listings were diffed. Every archive opened under both, and no entry
count moved. The one difference is in Death Note v05: a page whose name is
UTF-8 stored with the UTF-8 flag clear, "Ch 37 DEATH_NOTE_カラー版_5_…", and
its `__MACOSX/._` twin. 7.2.0 read both through codepage 437, and 9.1.3 reads
them as written.

**Stamping kept every page, and only 9.1.3 kept that name.** Two `taiyaku
serve` builds, `main` and this branch, each served its own copy of Death Note
v03 and v05 and Gabriel Dropout v12. `drive.py pages` fetched and hashed every
page of each work by index, `drive.py stamp` fetched each work's
`stamp-comicinfo` plan and posted it back, `drive.py pages` ran again, and
`zipraw.py compare` read each original and its stamped copy header by header
(all in `realcheck/scripts/`). In both builds every page came back at the same
index with the same bytes, and every entry's compressed data was unchanged.
7.2.0's stamp rewrote the v05 name and its twin as the UTF-8 of their codepage
437 reading, with the flag set; 9.1.3's kept the stored bytes and the clear
flag. Neither copies a header whole (`realcheck/out/compare.txt` lists every
field that moved), so O237's bullet claims the name and its flag and nothing
more.

**The Unicode Path exception is read from the source.** 9.1.3's
`apply_extra_fields` puts an Info-ZIP Unicode Path field's name in place of the
stored one when the field's CRC matches the stored name and its content is
UTF-8, and sets the flag, and `raw_copy_file` copies that name and flag. None of the three archives carries the field.
`realcheck/scripts/upath_scan.py`, reading every archive's central directory,
found it in volumes of several series in the test library, Hunter × Hunter
among them, most often naming something other than the stored bytes, so by
that reading a stamp of those volumes writes the field's name.

## Narrowing a merged edition on the test library (2026-11-04)

The second part of the overlapping-libraries PR 1 (spec §3.8, decisions 6–11)
narrows an edition that a library's directories hold some of and not all of,
for an account granted some of the libraries holding it and not all, and lists
each such edition on Configuration → Split editions. It was driven on the scratch
store of "Overlapping libraries PR 1 on the test library", under that drive's
isolation rules. The commands and their output are in
`.superpowers/sdd/overlap-evidence/pr1/drive/`, which is not committed.

**The case.** A release build of 80a82bb8 served a copy of that store, at
schema 18 and not migrated on open, which holds O239's case: Bocchi the Rock!
v06 has one `raw` edition of two members, an 8-page file under Kids'
directory first and a 130-page file under Manga's second (`T19-store.log`,
`T19-sql-case.log`).

**What administrators are shown.** `GET /api/library/split-editions` listed
that edition alone, with both files and their directories, Kids seeing one
file of 8 pages and Manga one of 130 (`T19-admin.log`). The tab drew the same
as "Kids sees 1 of 2 files, 8 of 138 pages", with Manga's line under it, and
each file's path above the directories holding it, each linking to its page,
and did not scroll sideways on a narrow screen (`T19-browser.log` and two screenshots).

**An account granted only Manga** was sent the edition as one file of 130
pages. Its pages 0 to 129 were byte for byte the administrator's pages 8 to
137, and its page 130 was refused
(`T19-manga-pages.log`, `T19-manga-pages-extra.log`); its thumbs and cover
were taken the same way (`T19-manga-thumbs.log`). A position and a note it
wrote on its page 20 read back on 20 and were stored on slot 28, the full
numbering, and one past its last page was refused
(`T19-manga-progress-notes.log`).

**An account granted only Kids** was sent the 8-page file as the whole
edition, the administrator's first 8 pages, and its page 137 was refused with
404 (`T19-reader.log`). For each account granted one library, the work
document, the library work route, the series page and the home card gave one
page count. The administrator's work document and library work route gave 138
pages, while its series page gave the share of the library it was opened from,
130 from Manga's and 8 from Kids' (`T19-libraries.log`). The user ruled on
2026-11-04 that a series page counts an edition by what the account opens,
whichever library it was opened from, and `browse::editions_by_work` now does,
so that page gives what the work document gives. Each library's works count
matched the works its account was served (`T19-libraries.log`). **Both of what "Overlapping libraries PR 1 on the test
library" found under O239 are closed:** a Kids-only account is no longer
served a page only the Manga file holds, and the reader and the library
routes no longer disagree on its page count. Neither limited account could
read the administrators' route (`T19-manga.log`, `T19-reader.log`), and
nothing under the test library was written (`T19-isolation-before.log`,
`T19-isolation-after.log`).

**Read, not driven (no stamp was run): a stamp hides the stamped edition from
every account with a limit until the registry reads the library again.** The
view reads which members an account
sees from the store (`browse::visible_members`) and hides an edition whose
flags are not of the sidecar's members, by `sha256` and path, in order
(`view::Seen::of`). `stamp::apply` rewrites an archive in place and updates
`member.sha256`, so from the stamp until the registry holds the new sidecar,
that check fails for the edition, whether the account sees it whole or
narrowed. A live registry reads the library again at its next poll, which
comes every `REFRESH_EVERY`, since the write moves the structure counter;
`serve` given sidecars on its command line builds `Works::fixed`,
which never reads it again, so there the edition stays hidden until a
restart. `Access::Every` reads no flags and is not affected. This fails
closed, as spec §3.8 asks of flags that do not number an edition's members.

## Books: Harry Potter 1, English against Korean, aligned by length (2026-11-14)

Phase 1 of the books work (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-30-book-alignment-measurement-design.md`)
on its first pair: the Pottermore EPUBs of Harry Potter 1 in English (3,248
blocks) and in Korean (3,629), read by `taiyaku_read::read_book`, aligned whole
by `taiyaku_core::align_blocks`, and scored by `book_experiment` against a key
for chapter 1. Run with `TAIYAKU_CORPUS="$PWD/corpus" cargo test --release -p
taiyaku-cli book_experiment -- --nocapture`. *The experiment has since grown
to every pair and more settings, so a run now prints the tables of "Books:
nine pairs, five keys, and what held out" below rather than this one's.*

**The key.** Chapter 1, 112 English blocks against 147 Korean, in 111 links:
84 are 1:1, 18 are 1:2, six 1:3, two 1:4 and one 2:1. No block of the chapter
is on one side only. It was drafted by reading the two texts side by side, with
no aligner run, and checked as §3 asks: twenty links drawn by
`random.Random(20261114).sample`, each read on both sides. The owner delegated
that check, so a separate reviewer that had not seen the drafting judged them,
and all twenty were right. Both books also end with the first chapter of
Chamber of Secrets as a preview, so neither has text the other lacks there.

**The controls held.** The key scored against itself is 100% on every metric,
and shifted by one Korean block it falls to 23.9% exact landing, 0% strict F1
and 23.4% lax F1. No key link ends outside the ±400 band: the experiment
counts them through `Band::holds`, and found none of 821 across the five keys
on 2026-11-15. The fitted ratio is 0.585 Korean characters to an English one.

**Length alone lands 99.6% of swaps exactly**, at groups of up to four and a
one-sided cost of 4.5 (Gale and Church's 1:0 prior) or 9. The other 0.4%, one
block of 259, lands one block off. Strict F1 is 98.2% and lax F1 100%. A
selection of the 36 runs:

| scorer | max group | skip | exact | ±1 | unpaired | strict F1 | lax F1 | seconds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| length | 2 | 4.5 | 89.6% | 7.3% | 2.3% | 83.3% | 92.1% | 0.41 |
| length | 3 | 4.5 | 98.8% | 1.2% | 0.0% | 96.4% | 100.0% | 0.75 |
| length | 4 | 2.25 | 98.8% | 0.4% | 0.8% | 95.5% | 99.1% | 1.28 |
| length | 4 | 4.5 | 99.6% | 0.4% | 0.0% | 98.2% | 100.0% | 1.27 |
| length + anchors | 4 | 4.5 | 99.6% | 0.4% | 0.0% | 98.2% | 100.0% | 1.52 |
| length + anchors | 4 | 2.25 | 93.8% | 2.7% | 3.5% | 92.6% | 93.4% | 1.52 |
| length, refitted (1.3) | 4 | 4.5 | 97.3% | 2.7% | 0.0% | 94.5% | 99.5% | 1.25 |

What the table says, for the spec's four questions:

1. **One reading-order program aligns this pair**, by length alone. The spec
   expected a cross-language pair to need embeddings; on this key it does not.
2. **Anchors add nothing at the best setting** and cost 2.25 runs 5 points
   lower, where they tip borderline pairings toward one-sided steps. Length is
   enough for this pair.
3. **The unit is the paragraph, with groups of up to four.** A program limited
   to pairs tops out near 90%, since the key's eight 1:3 and 1:4 links cannot be
   expressed; three reaches 98.8% and four 99.6%.
4. Not asked of this pair: it has no PDF.

**Refitting the variance makes it worse.** Re-estimated from the first pass's
1:1 links it comes out near 1.3, against Gale and Church's 6.8, and every
setting loses one to twenty points. A guess at why: the first pass keeps as 1:1
the pairings whose lengths already agree, so the refit measures the agreeable
ones and underestimates the spread. 6.8 stays.

**Cost.** 1.3 seconds a whole-book alignment at groups of four and the ±400
band, in release, on the workstation. The table it fills is 3,249 rows of 801
cells, a cost (8 bytes) and a step (2 bytes) each: about 26 MB, computed, not
measured.

**What it does not show.** One chapter is keyed, and every setting above was
chosen on that same chapter, which is a mild overfit, stated as one. A second
keyed chapter, held out, is what would check it. The fitted ratio also leans on
the two books holding the same text: a fixture with one extra block in seven
moved the ratio enough to merge where it should skip
(`book_align::tests::a_block_one_side_lacks_is_a_one_sided_link` is built of
twenty shared blocks for that reason), so a pair whose editions differ by more
than a preview chapter may need the ratio fitted some other way.

## Books: nine pairs, five keys, and what held out (2026-11-14)

The first pair's figures were chosen and scored on one chapter, so this tests
them across the corpus. Nine pairs under `corpus/books/`: Harry Potter 1 to 7 in
English against Korean (Pottermore), Crime and Punishment in Ready's and
Pevear and Volokhonsky's translations, and Anna Karenina in Bartlett's and
Schwartz's. `book_experiment` aligns each whole at every setting in its
`SETTINGS` and scores three ways: each hand key, chapter anchors, and how much
it left one-sided.

**Four more hand keys**, each drafted by one reader that had not seen an
aligner's output and checked by another that had not drafted it:

| key | links | shapes | check |
|---|---|---|---|
| HP1 chapter 9 | 212 | 1:1 ×184, 1:2 ×23, 1:3 ×4, 2:2 ×1 | 20 drawn, 20 right |
| HP1 chapter 16 | 319 | 1:1 ×305, 1:2 ×10, 1:3 ×1, 2:1 ×1, 2:2 ×2 | 20 drawn, 20 right |
| HP7 chapter 1 | 108 | 1:1 ×66, 1:2 ×14, 1:3 ×27, 2:3 ×1 | 20 drawn, 20 right |
| Crime and Punishment III.VI | 71 | 1:1 ×71 | all 71 read, all right |

The Crime and Punishment key was checked whole rather than drawn from, since an
all-diagonal key drafted quickly is what a lazy one looks like. It is not: the
two translations paragraph that chapter identically.

**Chapter anchors are a free key with two wrong drafts behind them.** A
chapter number appears more than once on a side, in a contents page before the
text or a preview of the next book after it (every Korean volume from 2 to 6
ends with the next book's first chapter, as the English does). Paired from the
last occurrence back, English chapter one went to a Korean contents entry;
paired by nearest place in the book, Ready's long introduction put its
contents entries for Part One I and II nearer Pevear and Volokhonsky's
chapters than its own. Both passed the order check, which is why it is not the
only check. What stands: a contents page is a run of markers each within three
blocks of the last and numbered after it, dropped first, and the rest paired
nearest first by place. Every pair then gives one anchor a chapter, none from a
contents page (204 for Harry Potter, 41 for Crime and Punishment).

**Held out, the baseline holds and anchors help.** Baseline is length at groups
of four, skip 4.5, variance 6.8, band 400, the setting chosen on HP1 chapter 1.

| pair, key | baseline | + anchors |
|---|---|---|
| HP1 ch1 | 99.6% | 99.6% |
| HP1 ch9 | 98.0% | 100.0% |
| HP1 ch16 | 99.5% | 100.0% |
| HP7 ch1 | 83.3% | 93.0% |
| Crime and Punishment III.VI | 100.0% | 100.0% |
| Crime and Punishment, 41 chapter anchors | 100.0% | 100.0% |

So the first pair's "anchors add nothing" was the one chapter it was read on:
on every held-out key they help or tie. Crime and Punishment finds Part Three
VI, which Ready's contents leave out, without being told it exists.

**The alternatives, each one change from the baseline:**

- Groups of three cost HP1 chapter 1 0.8 points; five gain nothing anywhere.
- Variance 3.4 costs a point or more; 13.6 helps HP7 (88.5%) and nothing else.
- Skip 9 helps HP7 (88.5%) and moves two Crime and Punishment chapter anchors
  by 51 blocks.
- A sentence-count term is worse on nearly every key (HP7 74.2%, Crime and
  Punishment 85.9%).
- Shared words, for the one same-language pair, ties length at 100% and costs
  45 times its time.
- A band of ±100 is four times faster and drops Crime and Punishment's chapter
  anchors to 68.3%, one 203 blocks off: whole books drift further than that.
- Anchors with skip 9 and variance 13.6 together: HP7 93.7%, the rest as
  anchors alone.
- One-sided runs (a skip of up to 32 blocks costing 4.5 then a per-block
  extension): at 0.5 a block they leave text out rather than pair it (HP7 61%
  one-sided, 23.7% exact); at 3 they change nothing; at 2 HP7 reaches 88.5%
  but some chapter headings go unpaired.

**Decided: length with anchors** at the baseline's other settings, the simplest
setting that is best or tied on every key.

**What remains wrong, and why:**

- *A chapter heading lands one block early.* "CHAPTER THIRTEEN" is sixteen
  characters, and length cannot tell which side of a break it belongs to, so it
  joins the last paragraph of the chapter before. The chapter's first
  paragraph lands right. This is why HP2 to HP6 read 37% to 64% on chapter
  anchors while HP1 reads 89%: those Korean volumes set the number and title in
  one block, which the English splits in two.
- *HP7 drifts at its start.* Its English has a sixteen-line epigraph the Korean
  lacks, which the aligner folds into merges rather than leaving out, and its
  first chapter's thirteen opening links are wrong because of it; anchors take
  the chapter to 93%.
- *Bartlett's Anna Karenina cannot be aligned at paragraph level.* Its
  conversion uses `<br>` both for a paragraph break and for a line break in the
  middle of a sentence, so its 2,221 blocks are not paragraphs. Every setting
  leaves 27% or more one-sided. It is the one pair here a reader should not be
  offered.
- *Extraction had a bug these found.* Text outside any `<p>`, which Bartlett
  has, was gathered out of order into one block; it is now split around the
  nested blocks as a browser lays it out.

## Books: a chapter number keeps its heading with its chapter (2026-11-14)

The section above left a chapter heading landing one block early: length
cannot tell which side of a break sixteen characters of `CHAPTER THIRTEEN`
belong on, and in the two ways to pair it the merge costs come to the same
4.6. What tells them apart is the number. The Korean title carries it as
digits (`13장 아주 비밀스러운 일기장`), and the English heading spells it in
capitals. So `Anchors::of` now counts an English number word set in capitals
as a number, read by `taiyaku_core::english_number` (`zero` to `ninety-nine`,
tens before ones), and the heading's number pulls it onto the Korean title.

A number word in running text is not counted. Measured both ways, at the
anchors setting:

| pair | chapters exact before | capitals only | every number word |
|---|---|---|---|
| HP1 | 88.9% | 100.0% | 100.0% |
| HP2 | 36.8% | 89.5% | 89.5% |
| HP3 | 34.8% | 91.3% | 91.3% |
| HP4 | 39.5% | 86.8% | 94.7% |
| HP5 | 61.5% | 92.3% | 92.3% |
| HP6 | 48.4% | 96.8% | 96.8% |
| HP7 | 94.4% | 97.2% | 94.4% |

Every key is unchanged by either: HP1 chapters 1, 9 and 16 at 99.6%, 100% and
100%, HP7 chapter 1 at 93.0%, Crime and Punishment at 100% on its key and its
41 chapter anchors. Counting every number word wins one pair and loses one,
and in running text a translation as often spells a number as a word (`두
남자` for "two men"), so capitals only stands.

## Books: Harry Potter read in the browser, end to end (2026-11-14)

A release build of 87daf97 served a fresh store holding one directory, the

  더즐리 씨는 서류가방을 집어 들고…") at the top, and Space again English 45.

## O282 and O284 on the test library (2026-11-14)

A copy of the test library's store (`/home/davey/temp/manga-test`) was
opened by a release build of `main` (`taiyaku library user password`), which
migrated it from schema 13 to 22. Three reading positions, three notes and
the hand title `Mine.cbz` on work 1271 were planted in it
(`task4-plant.sql`), and a release build of this branch then opened it the
same way: the open took the `-before-v23` backup and ran migration 23. Each
open's backup holds the schema it was taken at (`task5-setup.txt`). The
commands and their output are in `.superpowers/sdd/shorter-urls-evidence/`
(`check.txt`, `task4-http.txt`, `task5-lengths.txt`), which is not
committed.

**Slugs.** The 1,896 works hold 1,896 distinct slugs, and none kept its old
one. Each of the 1,880 with a volume is its series' name and its volume
(`berserk---v01--2003--cbz` became `berserk-v01`), and each of the 16
without one is the slug its title gives (`look-back-2022`); none needed a
`-2`. The average slug went from 41.68 characters to 27.28, and the longest
from 108 to 80. Sixteen slugs now hold a letter outside ASCII, which O262's
rule keeps and no old slug held (`kabushikigaisha-magi-lumière-v01` was
`kabushikigaisha-magi-lumi-re---v01--2024--cbz`).

**Titles.** Each of the 1,896 derived titles lost one archive extension and
nothing else, and none ends in one now. The title shown changed on 1,894
works. The other two hold a hand title: work 1271 still shows the planted
`Mine.cbz`, while the derived title under it became `One Piece - v085
(2018)`.

**Positions and notes.** The planted positions and notes read the same
before and after (the dumps' `diff` is empty), and the server gave each back
under its work's new slug. Against the `-before-v23` backup, no `work` row
changed outside the three columns the pass writes, and the only other tables
that changed were `meta` (the schema version), `user` (the opening command
set the password again) and `structure_version`, a counter a trigger moves
on every update of a `work` row, three times for each work here; the search
index's tables were not compared.

**Over HTTP**, with the branch's build serving the copy:
`/api/works/berserk-v01`, which the reader asks for to open
`/read/berserk-v01`, answered 200 with the title `Berserk - v01 (2003)`, and
its first page with a JPEG. The old slug `berserk---v01--2003--cbz` and
`no-such-work` answered alike, 404 with the same body but for the slug, on
the API and on OPDS. OPDS listed 1,896 entries with 1,896 distinct ids,
Berserk v01's being `taiyaku:work:berserk-v01`, and `-cbz` nowhere. No
browser was driven: the server ran without `--web`, so it served no app, and
`/read/berserk-v01` itself answered 404.

**Not exercised.** The test library has no `bridge:` row, so leaving one's
slug and title alone rests on `schema::remake`'s `a_bridge_row_keeps_its_slug`.
Nothing under `/home/davey/temp/manga-test` was written: `find -newer` a
marker touched before the copy printed nothing, and the sha256 and `stat` of
its `library.db`, `-wal` and `-shm` were the same before and after.

## O286: the strip's progress line as a scrollbar (2026-11-15)

The spec is `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-14-strip-scrollbar-design.md`
and the plan `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-14-strip-scrollbar.md`. The
files named below are in `.superpowers/sdd/strip-scrollbar-evidence/`,
which is not committed.

**The six rounds.** The owner settled the line over six rounds of a
prototype served from a scratch copy of the test library, and tried each in
Firefox; the prototype as they tried it is commit `6ebbebbc`. The spec's
Goals say what each round settled, in the owner's words: the drag and the
jump, and a mouse only, were the owner's picks (goals 1 and 2); round 3
gave the press band (goal 6); round 4 the mark's width and how thick the
awake line is (goals 3 and 5); round 5 the wake and its motion (goals 4
and 7); round 6 the fill's round end (goal 8). The rounds' own check
scripts and their logs are in `prototype-checks/`.

**The long drag** (`T4-long-drag.log`, `T4-report.md`). The spec asked for
this measured rather than assumed: a drag on the line moves the rail many
pixels for each pixel the pointer moves, so it meets the strip's window
rebuilds near a spacer more often than the rail's own drag does. A scratch
browser case, deleted before Task 4's commit, took a 400-page volume at
1440×900 and dragged the mark's centre along the whole line in 93 steps of
15 px, each step moving the rail about 503 px, with a Profiler around the
bars, reading eight frames after each step. It ran outside `act` and with
an `act` per frame, in both reading directions, and the four runs read the
same: 50 commits of the bars over the 93 steps, none or one a step, and no
spacer in view two or three frames after any step. The browser case
"drags a long volume's mark from end to end with tiles in view as each move
settles" (`Chrome.drag.browser.test.tsx`) holds the last: no step shows a
spacer three frames after its move.

**The 4.4 px sample** (gap 7; `T4-chase.txt`, `check5-rerun.mjs`,
`T4-chase-head-*.log`, `T4-chase-fix-*.log`, `T4-chase-browser*.log`). The
prototype's `check5` once read the mark 4.4 px off the pointer during a
long drag. The chase read every frame two ways: a `requestAnimationFrame`
loop asked for a frame ahead, which reads what the last frame painted and
any write since, and a `ResizeObserver` forced every frame, which reads
what that frame paints. On the built app (the 237-page volume at 1280×800,
`check5`'s drag and jump, 20 runs a direction at CPU throttling rates 1
and 4) the 4.4 px was a read taken between a write and the next frame,
never painted: a window rebuild changed the rail's length mid-drag, the
rebuild's render told the share from a passive effect, in a task between
frames, and wrote the mark about 4 px off, and the next frame's scroll put it
back before that frame painted. A jump, though, did paint the mark off the
pointer for one frame, 1.36 px, in every run: with the pointer held still
after the jump, the rail's length changed in a frame callback, `placeMark`
wrote the mark from the new share, and the rail's scroll event came only in
the next frame. In the browser project the same thing, thumbnails loading
late under a still hold, painted it 13.57 px off for a frame. `placeMark`
now writes the mark, while a hold is on, where the pointer puts it
(`alongAt`), in the same write that stands the rail there; after that no
sample in either place was over 1 px. The browser case "keeps a still-held
mark under the pointer in every frame as thumbnails load late" holds it.

**A reason the comments no longer give.** Task 1 cut the prototype's
comments in `Chrome.tsx` and `styles/reader.css` to within the comment
guard's eight lines (`T1-report.md`). One reason they gave is held nowhere
else: the line's thickness eases on the main thread, with the rest of the
mark's drawing, and not by a compositor's `scaleY`, which would stretch
the mark's round ends out of true (the comment keeps that) and would also
run apart from the mark whenever the page is busy. The other reasons cut
are in the spec's goals 4 to 7, in `reader.css`'s comment on the awake
line (the mark stays inside the band), or in `reader.css.test.ts` (quick
to wake and slower to sleep, as an overlay scrollbar is).

**What the band leaves, accepted and not fixed.** The band is drawn wherever
some pointer is fine, and its top 4 px lie over the rail's bottom padding,
below the tiles, though the band is not inside the rail.

- A wheel there lands on the band, not on the rail whose listener turns a
  wheel into a scroll of the strip, so it no longer scrolls the strip: a
  cost of the band against O138's "the wheel scrolls it" (`preflight.md`,
  M21; found by reading the code, then driven: see the drive, below).
- A pen's press there no longer reaches the rail either, so it no longer
  stops a glide the rail is running, which O216 had any press on the rail
  do (`preflight.md`, M22; found by reading, not driven). A pen's press is
  not moved as a finger's is, below: under Task 3's mutation that let
  `onLineDown` take a pen, a pen's press on the line's row took the line
  and moved the rail (`T3-report.md`, mutation 05).
- A finger's press there is another matter in Chromium, whose touch
  adjustment moves it: on every row of the band that Task 3's probe tried,
  a finger's `pointerdown` went to a tile inside the rail
  (`T3-mut-04-probe3-browser.log`; `T3-report.md`, "Where the cases
  differ from the brief, and why", 1). So in Chromium it still reaches the
  rail's press listener, `Filmstrip.tsx`'s `onDown`, which ends a glide at
  any pointer's press: read from the code, not driven. The tap then lands
  on that tile, the edge the last bullet records.
- `onLineMouseDown` prevents every primary `mousedown` on the band, a pen's
  or a finger's compatibility one too, since the event does not say what
  sent it, so such a press whose `mousedown` lands on the band leaves focus
  where it was (`T3-report.md`, concern 2).
- A finger's tap on the band's rows is moved by Chromium's touch adjustment
  onto the tile above (`T3-report.md`, concern 1;
  `T3-mut-04-probe3-browser.log`); that it then turns to that tile's page
  is inferred from the click landing on the tile, not seen. Nothing on the
  line answers touch (spec goal 2). A known edge.

**The drive** (`drive-chromium.txt`, `drive-firefox.txt`, screenshots in
`drive-shots/`). A release build of `54e96319`, served from a backup copy
of the prototype server's scratch database, was driven by Playwright
1.62.1, headless at 1280×800, with a real mouse, its wheel and the
keyboard, in Chromium 151.0.7922.34 and Firefox 153.0. It took the
237-page `akame-ga-kill-v01` and the library's shortest volume, of 7
pages, each in both reading directions. Each browser read 58 PASS, 2 FAIL
and 12 NOTE, with no page error. Every reading below was driven. The drive
sent no pen or touch input, so the bullets above on a pen and a finger
rest on Task 3's probe and on reading, as they say.

- The mark drew 64 px on the long volume and 160 on the short. Drag, jump,
  both ends, no glide after a release, wake and sleep, the keep zone, a
  hold, a real Escape mid-hold, presses 12 px above and below the line,
  focus and Space after a press with focus on the page, the fill's round
  end at rest and awake, and no layout shift on waking passed in both.
  Firefox has no layout-shift entries to read, so there the boxes compared
  asleep and awake hold the last alone.
- Firefox eases the wake, as the plan asked of a Firefox of at least 128:
  `--grow` read strictly between 0 and 1 on 8 or 9 frames over 116 to
  133 ms as the line woke, and on 17 or 18 frames as it slept, as in
  Chromium.
- The wheel (a `deltaY` of 240, from the rail's middle) scrolled the rail
  over the tiles and over the rail's padding 5 px above the line's top, by
  120 px in Chromium and 240 in Firefox on the long volume. Over the
  band's top 4 px (2 px above the line's top), on the line and on the band
  below it, the rail stayed where it was: M21, the first bullet above.
- After a drag's release the mark stood off where the rail's scroll puts
  it by at most 0.04 px on the long volume, but on the 7-page one by up to
  1.46 px in Chromium and 2.66 px in Firefox, the same a second later;
  there one pixel of the rail is 2.81 to 6.81 px of the line. While a hold
  was on, the mark kept within 0.02 px of the pointer's place in Chromium
  and 0.96 px in Firefox. Left as it is: the mark stays where the mouse
  let it go until the strip next scrolls.
- The FAIL, the same in both browsers and both directions, on the long
  volume only: with a tile focused, a jump far along the line (the rail
  moved 15,551 to 15,773 px) left focus on `body`, because the strip's
  window takes a tile that far out of view off the page. A wheel over the
  tiles that moved the rail 10,433 to 10,760 px dropped focus the same
  way, so it reads as the window's behaviour from before O286, not the
  line moving focus. That rests on reading: the wheel's path is one O286
  leaves alone, and the branch changes no window code in `Filmstrip.tsx`;
  it was not run on `main`. It is not fixed here, and is filed as O289.
  A press on the mark
  where it stood, and every jump on the 7-page volume, left the tile
  focused; with focus on the page, as the reader usually has it, a press
  kept it, and Space and ArrowLeft did after the press what they did
  before it.
- The test library's `library.db`, `-wal` and `-shm` had the same
  `sha256sum` and `stat` before and after (`drive-before.txt`,
  `drive-after.txt`).

## Books: sizing paged text keeps the page it began on (2026-11-15)

Reported: paged, `=` or `-` left the reader on another page, not the one
whose text it had been reading. The reader kept only the block at the top,
and a page laid out again went to the page holding that block's first line,
pages back when the page had started inside a long paragraph; each size
step crept back again.

Driven after the fix in Chromium at 1905×2053 on Harry Potter 1, Korean,
paged, on a copy of the local store: page 5 starts inside block 108
("네모난 안경을 쓴…"). `=` three times and `-` three times went 18 → 24 →
18 px, the book 121 → 163 → 121 pages, and those words were on the page
after every step, the reader ending on page 5. The wheel, four notches up
and four down, did the same.

## Books: a library of translations and originals (2026-11-15)

The test library's books, scanned whole for the first time (Literature,
Poetry and Light Novels): 612 English EPUBs and 7 Korean, and no other
language.

- **Strict XHTML refused 14 of them.** Thirteen used HTML's named
  references (`&nbsp;` in all but one) and read once those are rewritten as
  numbers; one (*Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea*, SUNY) has tags that
  do not match, and is still refused.
- **Fifteen works came in 2–5 English translations**, each in its own
  directory and none numbered. Nine were grouped by a title rule and a key
  rule apiece: the Odyssey, the Iliad, the Aeneid, Crime and Punishment,
  Anna Karenina, Don Quixote, Les Misérables, the Metamorphoses and the
  Prince. Dante waits: one translation is three files, the other one.
- **Originals added beside them**, public domain: Spanish *Don Quijote*
  (Project Gutenberg 2000), Russian *Анна Каренина* and *Преступление и
  наказание* (Wikisource, modern spelling, complete), and Japanese
  *坊っちゃん* (Wikisource, with ruby readings) against Mori's *Botchan*
  (Gutenberg 8868). Each aligns to its translations on first open.
- **Editions split their text very differently**, which the paragraph
  aligner feels: Fagles' *Aeneid* is 1,905 blocks against Fitzgerald's
  17,013 (stanzas against lines), and Bartlett's *Anna Karenina* 2,221
  against Schwartz's 8,412. Front matter differs too: Gutenberg's licence,
  a publisher's introduction, Wikisource's list of chapters.
