## Content matching PR 2: fingerprints in the server (2026-11-17)

The spec is
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-content-matching-fingerprints-design.md`
and the plan
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-17-content-matching-fingerprints.md`.
PR 2 stores a fingerprint of every page of each library with matching on,
in a background pass in `taiyaku-serve`, and matches nothing, so O338
stays open. This section holds what the plan settled that the design does
not and why, and what the owner's hand-check found.

**Where the moved code lives.** The design left the crate to the builder.
It is `taiyaku-serve`, as `pub mod fingerprint`. `taiyaku-cli` already
depended on `taiyaku-serve`, and `taiyaku-serve` already depended on
`image` 0.25.9 with its default features, so the move added no dependency
edge and no crate. A new crate would also have had to join the workspace's
members, both crate lists in `.forgejo/workflows/mutants.yml` and
`scripts/comment-budget.json`. The CLI keeps its `rayon` batch
(`partition_by_size`, `decode_all`, `fingerprint_edition`,
`describe_pages`) and calls the moved functions through
`taiyaku_serve::fingerprint`, re-exporting the names its own modules used,
so its call sites and tests compiled unchanged. A test in each crate's
`fingerprint/tests.rs` pins the moved code's output to what
`describe_pages` gave before the move, on one fixture.

**The build a row names.** A file stored partial or unreadable is due
again when the server's build changes (the design's §9). The build is
`about::build_label`'s commit, with `-dirty` when the label is marked
(`about::build_stamp`), since a marked build of a commit need not read
pages as that commit's clean build does; a build that names no commit
stamps none. The commit is the one per-build value the server has:
`CARGO_PKG_VERSION` is `0.0.0` in every crate, the Dockerfile passes
`TAIYAKU_COMMIT` to the build, and `taiyaku-serve`'s `build.rs` reads
git's HEAD otherwise. The due test compares builds with `IS NOT`
(`fingerprints`' due condition), so a row stamped with no build is
settled for a build with none, rather than read again by each such build.

**Priority, through two commands.** The coordinator and each worker lower
their own thread: `renice --priority 19 -p <tid>` and
`ionice -c 3 -p <tid>`, the thread id read from `/proc/thread-self`
(`fingerprint_pass::priority::lower`). Linux keeps niceness and I/O
priority per thread, so each thread sets its own, and the workers are
threads of the pass's own, never tokio's blocking pool, whose threads go
on to serve pages. The calls are subprocesses, as `taiyaku-cli`'s
`user.rs` runs `stty`, because the system calls need `libc` and
`unsafe`, which the workspace forbids (`unsafe_code = "forbid"` in the
root `Cargo.toml`), and no crate in the shipped graph wraps `ioprio_set`:
`rustix` is reached only through `tract-onnx`, a dev-dependency of
`taiyaku-cli`, and `cargo tree --workspace -e normal,build -i rustix`
prints nothing. `--priority` rather than `-n`, which util-linux reads as
an increment under `POSIXLY_CORRECT`. Both commands are in
`debian:bookworm-slim`, the base of the image's runtime stage
(`docker run --rm debian:bookworm-slim sh -c 'command -v renice && command -v ionice'`).
Where they are missing the pass runs at the server's own priority, and the
coordinator says so on stderr.

**A lowered thread decodes alone.** jxl-oxide renders on rayon's shared
pool by default, and that pool's threads keep the priority of the thread
that first used it. A pass's decode there would run at normal priority, and
a lowered thread that started the pool would leave every reader's decode at
its priority. So a decode on a thread below the main thread's priority
renders on that thread, and any other uses the pool (`jxl::render_pool`,
`priority::thread_is_lowered`). The measure is the main thread, not niceness
0, so a server started under `nice` still decodes in parallel, and a worker
`renice` could not lower is not below the main thread and uses the pool.

**Which rows a pass drops.** At the end of each pass the store drops every
row whose digest no claimed unit holds, in any directory, covered or not,
and no entry's held reading names (`fingerprints::drop_unclaimed`). The
design's §3 was amended to say that rows no claimed unit holds are dropped,
to match its §2; the held readings' exception is this section's own. Not "no
due unit": a library switched off, or a directory paused by a Cancel, keeps
the fingerprints it has, as the design's §8 has it for the switch. Not "no
entry": a rules edit that moves a claim, so that a directory's chapters are
claimed in place of the directory, say, leaves the directory's entry and its
digest in `scan_entry`, and a row only that entry held would stay for good.
The held readings are kept because a paused directory's frozen works are
read by them (migration 27), while the claims name each file by the digest
it has now. The claims, the held readings and the stored digests are read in
a snapshot of their own, which takes no write lock, and the digests neither
a claim nor a held reading names are worked out from it. Where there are
none, the usual case once a library has been read, no write is asked for:
the drop runs on the coordinator's lowered thread at the end of every pass,
so after every scan that ends without a Cancel, and a write lock held there
would hold every other writer behind it. Otherwise those rows are deleted by
digest in one short write, which reads the held readings again, so a pause
since the snapshot still keeps the row its works are read by. A claim made
since the snapshot costs one file read again rather than a wrong row. The
drop does not wait out a reader's quiet as each file does: its usual case
writes nothing, and a wait would keep the pass's job showing for as long as
a reader reads. A Cancel that lands while the pass waits for the job lock
before dropping ends the wait with nothing dropped; the next pass drops what
it left.

**A folder whose pages do not hash to its digest.** A folder's own size and
mtime do not move when a page in it is rewritten in place, so a scan keeps
the digest it took, and the hash the walk takes of the pages it reads cannot
match it: each pass reads such a folder whole, stores nothing, and does not
try it again that pass (`fingerprint_pass::read`'s `Read::NotItsDigest`). A
folder that cannot be listed, or whose walk ends on a read error, hashes
short of its digest the same way, where a file in that state is stored
unreadable or partial (O347). The pass says so on stderr each time, naming
the folder, with the error where one ended the read, since nothing else
shows the cost. A rewrite lasts until the folder's own mtime moves and a
scan takes its digest again.

**What makes a file partial.** A page that fails to decode keeps its place
as a record that it was not decoded, the border sample passes over it as
PR 1's `common_border` does, and the file is stored partial; a file with
no page hashed is stored unreadable. An entry that is neither a page nor a
companion makes the file partial too. A companion is a resource fork or a
dotfile, or a file of a type in `taiyaku_read`'s `COMPANION_EXTENSIONS`,
at any depth: `txt`, `nfo`, `url`, `sfv`, `md5`, `sha1`, `xml`,
`json`, `htm`, `html`, `md`, `rtf`, `ini`, `db` and `ds_store`. So
`ComicInfo.xml`, `Thumbs.db`, `desktop.ini`, a credits text or a
checksum file beside the pages leaves a file whole, and an image of a type
the reader cannot decode yet makes it partial, so that it is read again
once a build reads that type.

**Cancel and a kick.** A Cancel also forgets a kick the running pass has
not yet read (`Pass::cancel`), so that it stops what was asked of the pass
before it: files a scan found just before the Cancel wait for the next
scan, as the owner's ruling has the rest wait.

**The feed's count.** A pass's `of` is the number of units queued across
its listings, and `done` the number workers have finished with, whatever
came of each (`fingerprint_pass`'s `Counts`). A file a scan walks again
mid-pass with a new size or modification time is queued again at the next
listing, so it counts twice, and `of` can end above the number of files. A
file passed over while its directory was not covered counts once more each
time a later listing queues it again. A file whose library is
switched off after it was queued is taken and counted too, though nothing
is read: its own check finds it no longer due (`Reading::one`), and the
worker counts it all the same (`Reading::work`). So once a library is
switched off, its files still queued are counted off, and the pass's line
can run to its total before it goes. A library's own page shows the pass
only while it covers that library (`fingerprintJob` in `scanFeed.ts`), and
each file's check reads again which libraries the pass covers, so there the
line goes once the next file is checked.

**The feed's cadence while a pass runs.** The plan had an administrator's
tab ask the feed every `FEED_IDLE_MS`, five seconds, while only a pass
runs, since the pass holds no library (its Task 10). At the owner's
request during the hand-check, the feed is asked every `SCAN_POLL_MS`, a
second, while it lists the pass, as while a job holds a library, so the
count moves as files are read (`scanFeed.ts`'s `ask`). The request
replaced the plan's cadence; the plan is left as it was written. A reader
is sent no jobs, so a reader's tab still asks every `FEED_IDLE_MS` while
only a pass runs.

**The owner's hand-check.** The owner drove a server built from this
branch over a scratch copy of three series, one of cbz volumes, one of
folder volumes and one a directory of chapters alone, served from a fresh
store. Once the first scan had ended, the pass's line showed on the
Libraries list and on the library's page. Cancel took the line away, and
Scan library then started a new pass with fewer files left to read.
Unticking the library's box stopped the pass starting files, and ticking
it again started a pass at once. A server restarted while a pass ran
started a pass of its own with the rest. The owner found the step's words,
"Fingerprinting pages", and the box's label, "Match editions by page
content", fine, and the Matching section where it is.

**A Cancel during a scan.** A Cancel of the pass while a scan runs can
leave the line reading "Cancelling…" until the scan ends: a worker whose
read has ended waits for the job lock before it stores what it read,
cancel or not (`Reading::one`), and the scan holds the lock. The scan,
ending without a Cancel of its own, then starts a pass, as the design has
it: Cancel stops the current pass only, and the next scan to end without a
Cancel starts a pass that carries on from there. Dropping a read that had
ended would take the line away at once and leave that file to be read again;
at the hand-check the owner kept the behaviour as built.

## Korean dictionary: installed and measured on Harry Potter 1 (2026-11-17)

`kaikki.org-dictionary-Korean.jsonl` came down at 207,649,961 bytes, the size
the design named, and `taiyaku dictionary import ko` built `ko.db` (34 MB)
from it: 42,690 entries, 518,129 form rows, no line passed over. `es.db`,
`ru.db` and `ja.db` were left as they were.

The measure is the first 200 words of *Harry Potter 1* in Korean (the
Pottermore EPUB, through `taiyaku_read::read_book`), taken as spaced words
with the punctuation trimmed off the ends and the words with no Hangul
skipped, against the real `ko.db`. These are words found, not words found
correctly: a hit says the dictionary has an entry under the stem, not that
it is the entry the book means. About 90 of the 200 words are the
dedication and the table of contents, and 36 of the found words are the
제 and 장 of the chapter markers, so the sample says little of running prose.

First measure, before the fixes below:

- `lookup` finds 121 of 200.
- `lookup_korean` finds 164 of 200, so taking particles off is 43 words.

The 36 words `lookup_korean` then missed, by why:

- **Names**, 20 (some the same name again): 해그리드, 해그리드의, 더즐리 (five
  times), 포터 (twice), 두들리라는, 두들리처럼, 노버트, 앨리, 제시카와, 다이애건,
  플라멜, 프리벳, 그루닝스라는, 퀴디치, 핼러윈. Wiktionary has no entry for
  these transliterated names, so the particle coming off does not help.
  Some names do collide with a common noun: 해리 is in `ko.db` only as
  "nautical mile", and 론 has five entries with the name Ron fourth among
  them, so a lookup of 해리가 finds an entry and it is the wrong one, a hit
  that the counts above cannot tell from a right one.
- **A common compound**, 1: 사냥터지기 (a gamekeeper), which is not a name and
  is in no entry.
- **A conjugated verb or adjective**, 8: 있었는데, 없다고, 싶지, 자랑스럽게,
  기이하거나, 정상적이라는, 금발이었고, 것이었는데. The headwords (있다, 없다, 싶다,
  자랑스럽다, 기이하다) are in `ko.db`; the conjugated forms are in no `form`
  row, and `lookup_korean` takes off particles only. The last three are
  nouns with the copula, and the fixes below find them.
- **A numeral with a counter or particle**, 4: 9와, 4분의, 3번, 4번지에. No entry has these with their digits, and taking the particle off leaves a digit. A tap in a Korean book sends the same run, because it takes in the digits joined to the word, so these answer "Not in the dictionary"; 3번 and 4번지에 no longer open on 번 and 번지. Where the dictionary has the number and counter as one word a tap finds it: 7월, and 11월이 through 11월. A tap on a bare number looks nothing up. A drag over the letters alone sends only those letters, so 년 dragged out of 10년 is looked up as 년.
- **A contraction**, 1: 그건 for 그것은; and **누구라도**, one more particle
  than the list has.
- **An ideophone**, 1: 뒤룩뒤룩, which has no entry.

The 해리 and 론 collision, counted over all of Harry Potter 1 among the words
that taking particles off newly finds: 해리 1,465 and 론 454.

After the fixes (the copula after a vowel, 야, 이야, 라는, 이라는, 라도,
이라도, 인, 이고, 이었고, 이었는데, 만큼 and 대로 added, a word found only as a form of
something also stripped, 이고 taken after a vowel as well as a consonant, and
a stem's affix entries passed over), the same measure, and the whole of Harry
Potter 1 (Korean) read the same way, 64,750 words with repeats, in a scratch
test that is not in the tree:

| | words | `lookup` | `lookup_korean` |
|---|---|---|---|
| first 200 | 200 | 121 | 168 |
| whole book | 64,750 | 32,914 | 50,990 |

The whole book finds 78.7% with particles against 50.8% plain, so taking
particles off is 18,076 words, and the first 200 words' 84% is an
overestimate of it by about five points, for the front matter's sake.

The last two fixes changed the answer of 356 of the book's 17,463 distinct
words, 2,123 occurrences. In 348 of them (2,094) a stem's affix entries left
the list and the first headword stayed. Five (22) open on another headword:
거라는 and 거라도 on 거, 밖에는 on 밖, 하고는 on 하고 and 만큼이나 on 만큼. 마법사이고 and
사이이고, once each, are found where they were not. **갔을 (5) lost its only
answer.** Its stem 갔 has only affix entries, the suffix -갔- and a form row
leading to -겠-, and `ko.db` lists neither 갔 nor 갔을 as a form of 가다, though
it lists 갔다 and 갔어. An affix still answers for the word as written, so 거라
shows -거라, and 보는, a form of 보다, still lists the particle -보다 filed under
the same key.

The first group is a fact about the dictionary and the second a gap in the
code; they are O377 and O376 in `docs/status.md`, with the numerals O378.
The measuring program was a scratch test and is not in the tree.

## RAR through libarchive: the compress-tools spike (2026-11-17)

**The versions.** compress-tools 0.16.1, the newest 0.16.x. libarchive
3.8.11 on the dev machine, and 3.6.2 (Debian bookworm's `libarchive13`
3.6.2-1+deb12u5) in `rust:1-bookworm` and in `debian:bookworm-slim`, the
runtime image's base. RARLAB's rar and unrar 7.23 made and checked the RAR5
fixtures. rar 7.23 has no `-ma` switch and cannot write RAR4, so the two
RAR4 fixtures come from RARLAB's rar 6.24, whose `-ma4` can, fetched into a
scratch directory and never installed.

**How it was measured.** A throwaway crate read each archive through a
`Read + Seek` wrapper that counts the bytes `read` returns and the calls to
`seek`. It listed through `ArchiveIterator` with a filter that records each
entry and refuses it, and again through `list_archive_entries`; it read one
entry through `uncompress_archive_file`; and it walked a whole archive with
`ArchiveIterator`. It ran in three places: the dev machine, under its own
UTF-8 locale and under `LC_ALL=C`; `rust:1-bookworm`, under `LC_ALL=C` and
`LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`; and `debian:bookworm-slim` with `libarchive13`, under the
image's own environment, which sets no locale, and under `LC_ALL=C`. Besides
the fixtures it read copies of three kinds of real material: Zelda v01 (RAR5,
not solid, 381 entries), the library's ten RAR4 comics, and RuriDragon v02
(RAR5, 203 entries, every name holding non-ASCII bytes).

**1. Skip: fails, on the fixture's entry size.** Reading Zelda v01's last
entry read 6,160,384 bytes more than reading its first, in all six runs,
against a bound of 26,969,306.8: a tenth of the 269,693,068 packed bytes
before the last. On `rar5-stored.rar` the difference is 81,759 against
195,495.5, half of the 390,991 packed bytes between the first page and the
last. On `rar4.rar` it is 249,488 against 99,341.5, half of 198,683, where it
could be measured (the dev machine's locale and `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`): the read
of the last page returned 396,948 bytes from a 331,408-byte file, and the
read of the first, a 66,228-byte page, 147,460. Under the C locale the last
page does not read at all (criterion 3).

The cause is the size of `rar4.rar`'s entries, not RAR4. compress-tools
registers a seek callback and no skip callback, and hands libarchive at most
16 KiB per read. Without a skip callback libarchive, 3.6.2 and 3.8.11 alike,
seeks past the rest of an entry only when more than 64 KiB of it remain
after the bytes it already holds, and otherwise reads them; both RAR readers
skip an entry through that one path. `rar4.rar`'s entries are 66,227 and
66,228 bytes, so they are read through, and `rar5-stored.rar`'s, 97,747 and
97,748 bytes, are sought over. Two control archives of stored noise pages show it:
RAR5 with five pages of 66,227–66,228 bytes fails the same way, 249,760
against 99,341 with no extra seek, and RAR4 with six of 97,746–97,748 bytes
passes, 81,413 against 195,495.5 with five extra seeks. Real RAR4 material passes: on
Fantastic Four v1 247, one of the library's RAR4 comics (not solid, 24
entries, pages packed to 266,271–607,725 bytes), reading the last page read
324,019 bytes more than reading the first page, and 618,931 more than
reading the first entry, a directory, against a bound of 749,679.3, a tenth
of the 7,496,793 packed bytes before the last, with one more seek for each
page skipped, on 3.6.2 and 3.8.11. A binding that registers a skip callback
would have libarchive skip an entry of any size.

**2. Encryption: fails.** Both listings show `p02.png` exactly as their
neighbours in both encrypted-entry fixtures, in all six runs: a file, with
its size, and no error. `p03.png` is listed. Reading `p02.png` fails
everywhere, but the error names encryption only on 3.8.11 for RAR5 ("Reading
encrypted data is not currently supported"); 3.6.2 gives "Unsupported block
header size (was 3, max is 2)" for RAR5, and both versions give "Invalid
location to Huffman tree specified" for RAR4. A whole `ArchiveIterator` pass
stops at `p02.png`'s error and never reaches `p03.png`. `p03.png` reads to
its sha256 everywhere. A probe outside the criteria stored the encrypted
entry instead of compressing it (`-m0`): on 3.6.2, for RAR5 and RAR4, and on
3.8.11 for RAR4, the read succeeds with no error and returns 12,656 bytes of
ciphertext for a 12,651-byte page.

libarchive itself marks an encrypted entry while listing
(`archive_entry_is_data_encrypted`), and compress-tools binds neither that
call nor `archive_read_has_encrypted_entries`. The flag is set on `p02.png`
for RAR4 on 3.6.2 and on 3.8.11, and for RAR5 only on 3.8.11: 3.6.2's RAR5
reader skips the encryption record without marking the entry, and reports
`archive_read_has_encrypted_entries` as -2, unsupported. So on bookworm's
3.6.2 no binding of libarchive learns from it that a RAR5 entry is
encrypted, and a stored one is handed over as ciphertext; an encrypted RAR4
entry can be refused before it is read.

**3. Names under C: fails, on RAR4, through compress-tools.** Under the C
locale, RAR5 names are byte-equal to the expected names in every run: 4 of 4
in `rar5-japanese.rar`, 203 of 203 in RuriDragon v02. `rar4.rar`'s
`ページ05.png` is not: `list_archive_entries` fails with "archive entry has
unreadable filename.", its message for a pathname libarchive did not give,
and the iterator dies with SIGSEGV after the fourth entry, because in
compress-tools 0.16.1's source it hands the same pointer to `CStr::from_ptr`
without that check. libarchive's RAR4 reader converts a name to the current
locale as it reads the header. Under C that fails, with the warning
"Pathname cannot be converted from UTF-16BE to current locale", and every
form of the name is lost: `archive_entry_pathname`,
`archive_entry_pathname_utf8` and `archive_entry_pathname_w` all return NULL,
on 3.6.2 and on 3.8.11. Switching the reading thread to C.UTF-8 first
(`uselocale` with `newlocale(LC_CTYPE_MASK, "C.UTF-8", 0)`) gives all five
names under `LC_ALL=C` on both versions, and `debian:bookworm-slim` has that
locale. compress-tools' locale guard asks `newlocale` for "" instead, the
environment's own locale, which under `LC_ALL=C` is C. Under
`LC_ALL=C.UTF-8` all five names list correctly through compress-tools too.

**4. libarchive 3.6.2: fails, through criterion 3.** Under `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`
all 30 reads of a page or a `ComicInfo.xml` match their manifests; under
`LC_ALL=C`, and in the slim image's own environment, 29 of 30 do, with
`ページ05.png` failing on its name. The headers-encrypted fixture fails every
call with "Encryption is not supported", and `rar5-compressed.rar` cut to 590
of its 1,181 bytes fails the listing, the iterator and a read of `p1.png`, an
entry past the cut, with "Truncated input file", in all six runs: no panic
and no timeout. On the truncated copy the iterator reports the end of
`p2.png`, the entry the cut falls in, with no data, before the error, and on
3.8.11 a read of `p2.png` succeeds with no bytes, as it does with the
patched crate below.

**The RAR4 comics (Review Focus 5): pass.** In the slim image under
`LC_ALL=C`, all 258 names of the ten RAR4 comics equal `unrar lb`'s byte for
byte, in both listings, and so they do in every other run. Eight of the ten
were made on Windows and two on Unix; 123 names carry a `/` separator and
none a backslash. Every name is ASCII, so no legacy code page was tested.

**Also.** `rust:1-bookworm` ships `pkg-config` 1.8.1-1 but not
`libarchive-dev`. compress-tools 0.16.1 exposes no libarchive version.

**The fixtures.** Ten archives in `crates/taiyaku-read/fixtures/rar/`, each
with a manifest: its entries in archive order, with kind and size; its pages
in reading order and the other entries read by name, with sha256; or the
line saying it is refused. Sizes and sha256 come from the source files, not
from a RAR tool. Every page is generated by ImageMagick in `make.sh`, noise
or an 8×8 gradient, never a published page. RAR5: stored; compressed, with
a `ComicInfo.xml`; solid; one encrypted entry; encrypted headers; a layout of
directories, `__MACOSX` and dotfiles; Japanese names; no pages. RAR4: stored,
with one Japanese name; one encrypted entry. rar writes directory records
after the files in whatever order they are added, so `rar5-layout.rar` lists
`vol/cover.png` and `vol` last; and rar recurses a named directory in the
file system's own order, so `make.sh` names each member rather than using
`-r`. The headers-encrypted fixture's manifest holds only its format and the
refusal: unrar cannot list it without the password, and lists `p01.png` with
it. Eleven more were added on the branch, so the directory holds twenty-one:
a RAR5 file reference (`rar -oi`); a solid RAR4, whose manifest holds its
entries and the refusal, since libarchive refuses a solid RAR4 at its second
entry ("RAR solid archive support unavailable"); and, for the checksum check
below, a RAR5 that declares BLAKE2, an empty entry in each format, four
volumes of split sets, a RAR4 with a comment and a RAR4 with a recovery
record.

Four criteria fail, so the plan's hard stop applies: the owner chooses
before Task 2 is dispatched.

### The patched compress-tools (owner's fork, 2026-11-17)

The owner patched compress-tools in a fork: four commits on upstream's
master, whose source differs from 0.16.1 only in reflowed comments and a
Windows link flag. The four:

- entry names are read under a UTF-8 locale (`C.UTF-8`, else `C.utf8`),
  whatever locale the environment sets;
- the iterator returns an error for an entry libarchive gives no pathname,
  instead of passing NULL to `CStr::from_ptr`;
- a skip callback is registered, so libarchive seeks over a skipped entry of
  any size;
- the locale guard no longer leaves a thread using a freed locale when two
  iterators on it are dropped in creation order.

The same spike, with its dependency changed and the stored-encrypted probes
added to every run, ran in the same six runs over the same fixtures and
fresh copies of the same material. All 462 of its commands exited cleanly:
no crash, no panic, no timeout.

**1. Skip: passes.** On `rar4.rar`, reading the last page read 49,917 bytes
more than reading the first (197,377 against 147,460), in all six runs,
against the bound of 99,341.5; on 0.16.1 the difference was 249,488. Zelda
v01's difference, 6,160,384 against 26,969,306.8, and `rar5-stored.rar`'s,
81,759 against 195,495.5, are 0.16.1's to the byte: their entries were
already sought over. The skip callback seeks three times for each entry it
skips (the position, the end, the target), so reading Zelda's last entry
made 1,134 more seeks than reading its first, where 0.16.1 made 378 on 3.6.2
and 379 on 3.8.11, and `rar4.rar`'s last page 12 more, where 0.16.1 made
none. Listing `rar4.rar` reads 147,467 bytes, where 0.16.1 read 396,948
under a UTF-8 locale.

**2. Encryption: passes, as restated.** The owner ruled that encrypted
archives are not a concern and that no encrypted flag is added, so the
criterion asks only that a listing goes on past an encrypted entry, that
reading it is an error, and that the page after it reads. In both
encrypted-entry fixtures, in all six runs, both listings go on past
`p02.png` to `p03.png` with no error; `p02.png` lists as a 321-byte file,
like its neighbours. Reading `p02.png` fails with 0.16.1's texts: for RAR5,
"Reading encrypted data is not currently supported" on 3.8.11 and
"Unsupported block header size (was 3, max is 2)" on 3.6.2; for RAR4,
"Invalid location to Huffman tree specified" on both. `p03.png` reads to its
sha256. A whole `ArchiveIterator` pass stops at `p02.png` with the read's
error and never reaches `p03.png`. The stored-encrypted probes give what
they gave on 0.16.1, now in all six runs: on 3.6.2, reading the encrypted
page succeeds for RAR5 and RAR4 and returns 12,656 bytes of ciphertext for a
12,651-byte page, and the iterator goes on to `p03.png`; on 3.8.11 RAR4 does
the same, and RAR5 fails with "Reading encrypted data is not currently
supported".

**3. Names under C: passes.** Under `LC_ALL=C` on the dev machine and in
`rust:1-bookworm`, and in `debian:bookworm-slim` under its own environment
and under `LC_ALL=C`, every name is byte-equal to the expected one in both
listings: 4 of 4 in `rar5-japanese.rar`, 5 of 5 in `rar4.rar`, `ページ05.png`
included, and 203 of 203 in RuriDragon v02. A whole iterator pass over
`rar4.rar` reads all five pages to their sha256 in every run, where 0.16.1
died with SIGSEGV after four under C.

**4. libarchive 3.6.2: passes.** All 30 reads of a page or a `ComicInfo.xml`
match their manifests in every run, under every locale; 0.16.1 managed 29
under C. The headers-encrypted fixture fails every call with "Encryption is
not supported", and the truncated copy fails the listing, the iterator and a
read of `p1.png` with "Truncated input file", as on 0.16.1, with no panic and
no timeout.

**A truncated entry reads as empty.** The entry a cut falls in comes back as
a success with no bytes. Reading `p2.png` from the 590-byte copy returns 0
bytes and no error, and so does reading `p1.png`, the last entry, from
copies cut at 1,000 and 1,170 of the 1,181 bytes, on 3.6.2 and on 3.8.11;
0.16.1 does the same on 3.8.11. `uncompress_archive_file` takes libarchive's
end of data as the end of the entry. A whole iterator pass reports the end
of that entry with no data, then the truncation error. So a backend must
compare the bytes it receives for an entry with the entry's declared size,
on both paths, and refuse the page unless they are equal; more bytes than
declared is wrong too, as a stored encrypted page comes out at 12,656 bytes
for 12,651.

**The RAR4 comics (Review Focus 5): pass.** All 258 names equal `unrar lb`'s
byte for byte, in both listings, in the slim image under `LC_ALL=C` and in
every other run.

**The pin.** taiyaku's dependency is pinned to d823828, the code the spike
ran, tidied for upstream, until upstream compress-tools takes the fixes. The
fork still exposes no libarchive version.

## RAR through libarchive: the checksum check (2026-11-18)

The second whole-branch review of RAR PR 1 found that libarchive does not
compare a stored entry's data with the checksum in its header. A RAR made
with `-m0` whose page bytes had changed read back as good on 3.8.11 and on
3.6.2, in RAR4 and in RAR5, where a stored zip with the same damage is refused.
The owner ruled that PR 1 checks it. Every read now walks the archive's block
headers on the file it hands to libarchive and holds each entry's data to the
CRC32 its header declares.

**What the owner's 21 RARs hold.** `unrar lt` on each archive, read-only from
the NAS: 3,063 files, every one with a CRC32 and none with a BLAKE2 hash. 291
of them are stored, in seven archives, two of which are stored whole:

| Archive | Format | Files | Stored |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Donald Duck 029 | RAR4 | 36 | 36 |
| Fantastic Four v1 378 | RAR4 | 23 | 17 |
| Fantastic Four v1 413 | RAR4 | 23 | 21 |
| Gekijouban Soushuuhen Jujutsu Kaisen | RAR5 | 56 | 48 |
| My Dressup Darling, Marin cosplays | RAR5 | 9 | 2 |
| Ruri Dragon v01 | RAR5 | 166 | 166 |
| The Legend of Zelda (Legendary Edition) v02 | RAR5 | 407 | 1 |

**What the check leaves out.** An encrypted entry, an entry split across
volumes, a file reference, link or directory, an empty file, and a RAR5 entry
that declares only a BLAKE2 hash (O383).

**The 21 through the check.** Each archive's pages were read one by one and
as a whole book, read-only from the NAS, on libarchive 3.8.11 and on
bookworm's 3.6.2, the image's version. The check refused no page on either.
3,037 pages read on 3.8.11 and 3,035 on 3.6.2. Three archives hold pages that
libarchive itself cannot decode (O386), though `unrar t` passes all three:

| Archive | Fails on | Where | libarchive's error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fantastic Four v1 360 (RAR4) | 3.8.11 and 3.6.2 | all 24 pages | `Prefix found` |
| Zelda v01 (RAR5) | 3.6.2 | `index-080_1.jpg` | `Block checksum error` |
| Zelda v03 (RAR5) | 3.6.2 | `index-210_1.jpg` | `Unsupported block header size` |

The entries of Fantastic Four v1 360 declare unpack version 20, which
`unrar lt` prints as `RAR 1.5(v20)`. A failed page also fails its archive's
whole-book reads.

*On the owner's ruling of 2026-11-19 the image and CI moved to Debian
trixie's libarchive 3.7.4, which reads both Zelda pages; see "libarchive
3.7.4: the image and CI move to Debian trixie (2026-11-19)" below.*

**Archives the walk reads differently from libarchive.**

- Volumes joined with `cat` list their pages, and every read of them is
  refused: the walk ends at the first end block, where libarchive reads on.
  `unrar t` fails such a file too.
- A RAR5 block continued from the previous volume takes no position in the
  walk, since libarchive does not list one, so a set's last volume reads as it
  did before the check. libarchive does list a continued RAR4 entry, so the
  walk counts it.
- A RAR4 cut less than seven bytes into a block's header lists and counts as a
  shorter archive, and every read of it is refused (O351).

A crafted archive of tiny blocks can cost a read about 2 s on this workstation,
bounded by `MAX_BLOCKS` (2^20 blocks), where the walk stops and the file is
refused: page 0 of a 7.3 MB RAR4 of 1,040,000 comment blocks took a median of
1,916 ms over five rounds at a load of 15 to 17, against 11.5 ms before the
check, and a file over the cap was refused after 2,027 ms.

## JPEG XL pages: the decoder, the clients and a real archive (2026-11-17)

O130, closed by the JPEG XL pages PR. The evidence is in
`.superpowers/sdd/jxl-pages-evidence/`, not committed: `T1/` holds the
decoder comparison, its harness (`T1/compare/`, a standalone crate with a
counting global allocator) and the script that makes the test fixtures,
which the PR keeps as `crates/taiyaku-serve/fixtures/jxl/make.sh`; `T9/`
holds the run over a real archive. Each figure below names its file there.

**The decoder.** Task 1 decoded every page of the Bisque Doll original, a
zip of 185 `.jxl` pages, with each candidate through its own `image`
decoder, and compared each page with `djxl` 0.12.0's PNG of it, channel by
channel. `jxlinfo -v` read every page as a bare codestream, lossy and 8-bit,
173 grey and 12 RGB, with no ICC profile (`T1-report.md`, "Step 1" and
"Colour").

| | jxl-oxide 0.12.6 | jxl 0.8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Licence (its `Cargo.toml`) | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | BSD-3-Clause |
| Pages decoded (`correct.log`) | 185 of 185 | 185 of 185 |
| The worst page's largest difference from `djxl` (`correct.log`) | 1 level | 1 level |
| The smallest `max_alloc` that decodes an image (`threshold.log`) | a little below its peak heap on each Bisque page tried: the limit counts its working memory | exactly twice the image's output buffer on every image tried, whatever the decode then takes |
| `rust-version` (its `Cargo.toml`) | none declared | 1.89.0 |
| A recompressed JPEG rebuilt (`rebuild.log`) | byte for byte, ending `FF D9` | no API for it |
| All 185 pages on the NAS, default threads (`nas.log`) | 29.39 s, 8 threads | 18.57 s, one thread, through `image`; 4.93 s through its own API with a parallel runner |

Correctness came first, so jxl-oxide won: `jxl` fails the plan's
Decision 7 (a decoder counts its own working memory against `max_alloc`),
and its `rust-version` of 1.89 was above the 1.88 the workspace declared
when the comparison was made (it declares 1.91 since #265). Speed would have
chosen `jxl`. jxl-oxide is also the heavier: its peak heap was more than twice the
page's decoded size on all 185 pages and `jxl`'s on 77, and the worst page
took 26.81 and 2.34 times it (`mem.log`, its summary line). A
GPL-3.0-or-later program can take in either licence. The NAS runs ran in a
container of the deployed image with the share mounted read-only
(`T1-report.md`, "Step 5"), at a load average between 3.34 and 5.26
(`nas.log`).

**The real archive.** Task 9 copied the Bisque Doll original and four
volumes of two Bocchi the Rock! series into a scratch library and scanned
it with release builds of main and of this branch. Main's scan counted the
Bisque archive unreadable: "4 unreadable (1 whose pages could not be
counted: …/Bisque Doll de Chu ♡.cbz, 3 holding no page images)"
(`main-scan.txt`). This branch's scan of a copy of main's store read
"0 added, 0 updated, 0 gone; derived 3 series, 5 works, 5 editions, 5
members, 3 unreadable (3 holding no page images)" (`branch-scan.txt`). The
Bisque row now holds 185 pages and the original's SHA-256, and every other
row's count and digest are as main left them (`main-entries.tsv`,
`branch-entries.tsv`). Bytes
read per archive by that scan, under `strace` (`strace-bytes.tsv`):

| Archive | Size | Bytes read | Reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bisque Doll de Chu ♡ | 167,884,874 | 167,975,902 | 11 |
| Bocchi the Rock! - Anthology Comic v01 | 47,143,620 | 85,706 | 10 |
| Bocchi the Rock! - Anthology Comic v02 | 46,959,500 | 86,938 | 10 |
| Bocchi the Rock! - Gaiden v01 | 72,139,695 | 243,170 | 10 |
| Bocchi the Rock! - Gaiden v02 | 72,951,385 | 244,374 | 10 |

The Bisque archive was read whole once, to hash it, since main never hashes
an entry it could not count (`strace.txt`); nothing else was hashed again.

**A page each way.** On a release server over loopback, at a one-minute load
average of 17.38 (`step5-curl.tsv`), the first and last pages of that
work, as stored and as the JPEG made for a client that does not name
`image/jxl`:

| Page | As stored | The JPEG, made | The JPEG, from the cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `image/jxl`, 339,199 bytes, 0.0186 s | 515,496 bytes, 0.206 s | 0.0012 s |
| 184 | `image/jxl`, 474 bytes, 0.0105 s | 71,607 bytes, 0.142 s | 0.0008 s |

Both JPEGs were decoded and encoded, not rebuilt: no page of this archive
carries the data to rebuild a JPEG (`T1/rebuild.log`). Every answer
carried `Vary: Accept`, and the stored body equalled the entry's bytes.
The work's cover, asked for with each of the four curl `Accept`s below,
was a JPEG at a `-j1` address (`v=…-0-2-j1`) with no `Vary` each time; the
512 px cover's tag ends `-j1` as well, and the 160 px tile has no tag
(`step5-cover.tsv`).

**What each client sends.** The `Accept` a client sends for a page image,
whether it names `image/jxl`, and what it was sent for a JPEG XL page at
full size. The curl rows replay the three strings the plan's tests use,
copied from earlier logs, and are not this run's devices:

| Client | `Accept` | Names `image/jxl` | Sent | Where read |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| curl, with iPhone Safari's string (Version/26.6.1, from `o145-o146-o175-evidence/requests.jsonl`) | `image/webp,image/avif,image/jxl,image/heic,image/heic-sequence,video/*;q=0.8,image/png,image/svg+xml,image/*;q=0.8,*/*;q=0.5` | yes | `image/jxl`, as stored | `T9/step5-curl.tsv`, `T9/requests.jsonl` |
| curl, with Panels/950's string (from `panels-o55.jsonl`) | `image/jxl, image/heic, image/avif, image/webp, image/jpg, image/jpeg, image/jpe, image/jfif, image/jfi, image/jif, image/png, image/gif, image/bmp, image/dib, image/tiff, image/tif, image/*` | yes | `image/jxl`, as stored | `T9/step5-curl.tsv`, `T9/requests.jsonl` |
| curl, with Chrome 154's string (from `o182-o138-evidence/requests.jsonl`) | `image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,image/svg+xml,image/*,*/*;q=0.8` | no | `image/jpeg` | `T9/step5-curl.tsv`, `T9/requests.jsonl` |
| curl, with no `Accept` | none | no | `image/jpeg` | `T9/step5-curl.tsv` |
| Desktop Chrome 157, Linux | `image/jxl,image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,image/svg+xml,image/*,*/*;q=0.8` | yes | `image/jxl`, as stored | `T9/chrome-network.tsv`, `T9/requests.jsonl` |
| iPhone Safari 27.0.1 (`Version/`; the `iPhone OS 18_7` token is frozen), the owner's phone, in the reader | `image/webp,image/avif,image/jxl,image/heic,image/heic-sequence,video/*;q=0.8,image/png,image/svg+xml,image/*;q=0.8,*/*;q=0.5` | yes | `?w=3072` pages 1-5: bytes equal the stored entries', so `image/jxl` as stored | `T9/clients.md`, `T9/requests.jsonl` lines 327-332 |
| Desktop Firefox 161, Linux, the owner's, in the reader | `image/avif,image/jxl,image/webp,image/png,image/svg+xml,image/*;q=0.8,*/*;q=0.5` | yes | `?w=3072` pages 1-4: bytes equal the stored entries', so `image/jxl` as stored | `T9/clients.md`, `T9/requests.jsonl` lines 367-371 |
| Panels/979 on the owner's iPad (iPadOS 27.0.1), over OPDS | `image/jxl, image/heic, image/avif, image/webp, image/jpg, image/jpeg, image/jpe, image/jfif, image/jfi, image/jif, image/png, image/gif, image/bmp, image/dib, image/tiff, image/tif, image/*` | yes | `/raw/pages/{n}` with no width, 101 pages: all 102 byte counts equal the stored entries', so `image/jxl` as stored; the cover (46,838 bytes) was no entry's size | `T9/clients.md`, `T9/requests.jsonl` lines 383-490 |

Chrome 157 names `image/jxl` where the Chrome 154 the plan copied did not.
In the reader it asked for its pages at `?w=1024`, a long edge below
their own, so they were resized, and a resized page is always a JPEG: in
the reader Chrome was sent JPEGs, tagged as the stored variant
(`chrome-network.tsv`). The tests keep Chrome 154's string
as a client that does not name JPEG XL.

The owner judged the pages right in both, and, of Panels over OPDS, which asked for 101 pages with no width and was sent each as the stored JPEG XL, wrote "ok it seems to work" (`T9/clients.md`). The reader's widest rung, a long edge of 3072, is one the pages they read already fit, so both were sent the stored JPEG XL (byte counts equal the entries'; the log holds no content type; `T9/clients.md`), not the JPEG that Chrome's `?w=1024` got.

**The one-time cost (the plan's Decision 3).** The variant is chosen from
the request before the page is read, so a client that does not name
`image/jxl` is given JPEG-variant tags, ending `-j1`, for every page it
asks for, JPEG XL or not. After the upgrade such a client holds tags
without it, so it fetches each page it had cached once more, and every
library cover's `v=` gains `-j1` (`step5-cover.tsv`: `…-0-2-j1`), so each
cover is fetched once at its new address. A client that names `image/jxl`
keeps its tags. The owner was told of both on 2026-11-17 and raised no
objection.

**Memory after a burst (O349).** The release server above, at rest and
while a client sending Chrome 154's `Accept` read all 185 pages at full
size, four at a time (`t1d-summary.txt`, read from `/proc`):

| When | VmRSS | Load average, one minute |
|---|---|---|
| At rest | 46,356 kB | 35.75 |
| Peak, at the end of the read | 960,704 kB | 37.55 |
| 30 s after the last response | 956,560 kB | 28.94 |
| About 4.5 minutes later, Chrome's requests between | 754,880 kB | 13.15 |

The read took 26.10 s, and two decodes run at once
(`MAX_CONCURRENT_GENERATIONS`). Measured on this desktop, not on the NAS.

*O349 has since closed: see "jemalloc as the allocator: memory after a
burst (2026-11-19)" below.*

**The ICC profile (O350).** Read in the source, not measured. jxl-color
0.11.0's `read_icc` (`src/icc/decode.rs`) refuses an encoded size or a
profile size above `1 << 28`, and resizes a buffer to the encoded size
before decoding it; jxl-oxide 0.12.6's `JxlImageBuilder::read` reads its
input 4 KiB at a time and, until the header is complete, calls `try_init`,
which reads the profile, after each read. A file
that does this has to be built by hand: in the whole-branch review `cjxl`
refused a 100 MB profile from a PNG (`final-review-a.md`, M1).

**Beyond the plan.** A page cut short is never decoded in part:
jxl-oxide renders what it has of a frame not fully read, so the decoder
first checks the first frame is whole; where the server has to decode such
a page it refuses it, and a client that names `image/jxl` is sent the
stored bytes as they are. Where the server has to decode a page, metadata
boxes, `brob` boxes and a `jbrd` box's compressed stream, are capped at 16
MiB together before jxl-oxide inflates them, which it does outside
`max_alloc`; a page sent as stored at full size is not decoded, so the cap
does not reach it. And every
JPEG the server encodes from an image with transparency, of any format,
lays it on white, covers and tiles included, with no format version
moved: a rendering of a PNG page with transparency cached before the
upgrade, a resized page, a tile or a cover, keeps the ground it was cached
with until it is made again.

### The rebase and its fix round (2026-11-18)

Review after the rebase onto `be02b5ab` found the following. Each was changed
on this branch except O388, which stays open. The logs named are under
`.superpowers/sdd/jxl-pages-evidence/rebase-2026-11-18/fix-round/`.

- **A folder kept a digest no read could hash to.** A folder's digest covers
  the pages the reader of its day read, and counting `.jxl` moves no stamp,
  so a folder holding both kinds kept that digest at its new count, and a
  folder of just the hashed pages passed for it. A folder that holds a
  digest, was listed whole and is walked at another page count than it
  stored now gives the digest up as a changed folder does
  (`scan::Held::digest_outdated_by`). In `real-upgrade.log`, a scratch
  library scanned by main and then by a build with this change, `Delta v01`
  went from 2 pages under `Eta v01`'s digest to 3 pages under a digest of
  its own at the first scan, and the second scan reported 0 updated. While
  its directory is paused such a folder waits for the Scan, read by its held
  reading, which reverses call 6 of the paused-directory design's §8. A zip
  keeps its digest, so O390 stands for zips alone.
- **A directory newly nested over such a folder kept the old digest.** The
  take-over copied it onto a row the nested walk had already written at the
  new count, so no later walk saw the counts differ. `scan::carry_reading`
  now gives the digest up and holds it, as the outer directory's walk would.
- **A walk short of a directory stored its short count on a folder that kept
  its digest.** Two defects had that one cause. A 3-page volume an outer walk
  could not list whole was stored at 1 page; once it listed whole and a nested
  directory took it over, the count of 3 read as a change, and a derive with
  that directory paused wrote 1 page to the member with all 3 on disk. And a
  nested directory's first walk that could not list `c001/part` stored 1 page
  beside the digest of all 3; `part` then deleted, which moves no stamp of the
  volume's, every later walk counted the 1 it had stored and the digest stayed.
  A walk not listed whole, at a size and mtime that did not move, now changes
  no digested folder's count, whether its total is lower or higher
  (`scan::record`, `scan::carry_reading`); a folder whose size or mtime moved
  is read as changed, its digest cleared and the walk's total stored. A higher
  total stored hid the same loss: in
  `probe-raised-count-then-lost-directory.log` a throwaway test stored 6 pages
  beside a digest of 3, and the whole walk after the loss kept that digest. The
  next walk that lists the folder whole compares its total with the stored
  count and takes the digest again where they differ.
- **O388: a zip replaced at the same size and mtime with another page count is
  read by every pass.** A throwaway pass test read such a file again at each of
  three passes, with the entry's stamp set to the replacement's rather than a
  zip built to the same size. An intact copy sharing the digest was left with
  the replaced file's row when the pass read the replaced file for it; when the
  pass read the copy, the replaced file was left with the old pages' row, the
  counts agreed and neither was read again (`item3-o388-probe.log`).
- **A stored fingerprint row could number other pages than its file.** A
  re-count keeps a zip's digest, so a row read before it went on numbering
  the old pages. A whole or partial row of a zip this reader counted, whose
  page count differs from the entry's, is now read again whichever build
  stored it (`fingerprints::numbers_other_pages`).
- **A lowered decode used the shared pool.** With the defect in place, a
  decode on a lowered thread that started rayon's pool left the pool's
  threads at niceness 19 with the process at 0
  (`d3-red-against-the-defect.log`). A decode below the main thread's
  priority now renders on that thread (`jxl::render_pool`).
- **No test held `serve` to registering the decoder.**
  `serve_registers_the_jpeg_xl_decoder` now starts `serve` in a process of
  its own and decodes a JPEG XL fixture there.
- **The metadata cap was claimed too widely**, as the page cut short had
  been: a client that names `image/jxl` and asks for the page at full size
  is sent the stored bytes with nothing decoded, so the cap holds where the
  server has to decode the page.

## libarchive 3.7.4: the image and CI move to Debian trixie (2026-11-19)

On the owner's ruling of 2026-11-19, every stage of the image and every
`container:` image in the workflows move from Debian bookworm to trixie, so
the image links trixie's libarchive, `libarchive13t64` 3.7.4-4+deb13u1,
where it linked bookworm's `libarchive13` 3.6.2. 3.7.4 was measured first, in
`rust:1-trixie` with `libarchive-dev` 3.7.4-4+deb13u1, against main at
3c85ee95 (#264).

**The owner's 21 RARs.** The probe of "RAR through libarchive: the checksum
check (2026-11-18)" read every page of each, one by one and as whole books,
read-only from the NAS. 3.7.4 read 3,037 pages with 26 refusals, as 3.8.11
did; 3.6.2 read 3,035 with 32. Its output equals 3.8.11's line for line,
once the path prefix and the error text before `Prefix found` are set
aside. Against 3.6.2 it differs only on the two Zelda volumes and in the
totals:

| Archive | 3.6.2 | 3.7.4 | 3.8.11 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zelda v01 (RAR5) | `index-080_1.jpg` refused, `Block checksum error` | all 381 pages read | all 381 pages read |
| Zelda v03 (RAR5) | `index-210_1.jpg` refused, `Unsupported block header size` | all 405 pages read | all 405 pages read |
| Fantastic Four v1 360 (RAR4) | all 24 pages refused, `Prefix found` | the same | the same |

So no libarchive tried reads Fantastic Four v1 360 (O386).

**Why Fantastic Four v1 360 is refused.** `unrar lt` (UNRAR 7.23, read-only
on the NAS) lists all 24 of its files as `RAR 1.5(v20) -m3`: compressed with
the RAR 2.0 algorithm, unpack version 20. Fantastic Four v1 247, which
reads, lists its 23 files as `RAR 1.5(v29) -m3`. libarchive's RAR reader
(`archive_read_support_format_rar.c` at v3.8.11) declares an entry's unpack
version, `unp_ver`, at line 187 and reads it nowhere, so every compressed
RAR4 entry goes to its one decoder, the RAR 2.9 one; `Prefix found` is
raised at lines 2752 and 2811, in `add_value`, as that decoder builds a
Huffman code. The refusal is a decoder libarchive lacks, not damage.
Upstream libarchive's PR #3823, "RAR 2.0 decompressor", adds one; on
2026-11-19 it was open, and no maintainer had reviewed it.

**The owner's ruling, 2026-11-19:** Fantastic Four v1 360 stays refused
for now. *Superseded the same day: on the owner's word it was converted to
a stored zip of its 24 pages, and the original RAR is kept on the NAS under
`needs_processing/taiyaku-originals/`. O386 stays open for a user's RAR 2.0
archive.*

**taiyaku-read's suite on 3.7.4**, with strace installed so that its strace
tests ran: every feature, 235 passed and 0 failed; the default features,
171 passed and 0 failed.

**Encrypted, empty and reference entries.** A C program read archives
through libarchive directly, printing each entry's
`archive_entry_is_data_encrypted` and what reading its data gave, and
`archive_read_has_encrypted_entries` at the end: the fixtures' two
encrypted-entry archives, their two empty-entry archives and their RAR5 file
reference, and the spike's two archives with a stored encrypted entry. Run
on 3.6.2 and 3.8.11 as controls, it gave what the spike recorded on each. On
3.7.4 every entry's line is 3.6.2's:

- no RAR5 entry is marked encrypted, and every RAR5 archive answers -2,
  unsupported, to `archive_read_has_encrypted_entries`; the encrypted RAR4
  entries are marked;
- a stored encrypted page reads with no error as 12,656 bytes for its
  12,651, in RAR5 and in RAR4, where 3.8.11 refuses the RAR5 one with
  "Reading encrypted data is not currently supported";
- a compressed encrypted page fails, with "Unsupported block header size
  (was 3, max is 2)" in RAR5 and "Invalid location to Huffman tree
  specified." in RAR4;
- an empty entry in either format, and the RAR5 file reference, list as
  regular files of size 0 and read as no bytes with no error.

So O381 holds on 3.7.4 as written for 3.6.2.

**The other packages.** Under the t64 transition trixie's libarchive
runtime package is `libarchive13t64`, and the Dockerfile names it.
`libarchive-dev` and `strace` keep their names; trixie's strace is
6.13+ds-1, its `nodejs` 20.19.2+dfsg-1+deb13u3, and its glibc 2.41.
`rust:1-trixie` carries no node, sets `RUST_VERSION`, and ships `pkgconf`
