## JPEG XL pages: a cap on the embedded colour profile (O350, 2026-11-19)

Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-19-jxl-icc-cap-design.md`. The logs
named are under `.superpowers/sdd/jxl-icc-cap-evidence/`.

**The hand-built page.** `jxl/icc_pages.rs` builds, for the tests, a bare
codestream of 23 bytes whose header wants an ICC profile and declares its
encoded size as 2^28, the largest jxl-color's `read_icc` accepts. After the
size comes the start of the profile's stream: an entropy code, then symbols
that read as a decoded size of 2^28 and an empty command stream. They pass
each check `read_icc` makes before it fills its buffer: the encoded size is
at most 2^28, the command stream fits inside it, and the decoded size is at
most 2^28 and not far smaller than the encoded one. So jxl-oxide, with
nothing ahead of it, zero-fills a buffer of the declared size and then runs
out of bits. `the_hand_built_pages_declare_what_they_say` pins the bytes and
reads the header and the size back through jxl-oxide's own parser, and a
container made by `in_jxlc` or `in_jxlp` back through jxl-oxide's own
container reader. `every_shape` gives each page bare, whole in one `jxlc`
box, and split across `jxlp` boxes so that the header and the size each run
across a box boundary.

**The reproduction.** Written before the check, the two process tests in
`jxl/process_tests.rs`, each run in a process of its own, failed at their
memory assertion (`reproduction.log`): decoding the 2^28 page through the
hook raised the process's peak resident memory (`VmHWM`) by 275,378,176
bytes, and `jxl::rebuilt_jpeg` on the same page split across `jxlp` boxes
raised it by 273,653,760 bytes. With the check both pass. Each asserts a
rise below 128 MiB, then, as a control measured afresh, that jxl-oxide
reading the page with no check ahead of it raises the peak by at least that
much. The reproduction measures what O350 had only read in the source.

**The cap.** `jxl::icc_fits` takes the page's codestream through
`jxl::codestream` (the bare page, a `jxlc` box's payload, or the `jxlp`
payloads joined without their index), parses jxl-oxide's `ImageHeader` from
it and, where the colour encoding wants a profile, reads the encoded size
the header declares; above `ICC_CAP`, 64 KiB, the page is refused. A size of
exactly 65,536 bytes passes and one byte more is refused. The hook checks it
beside `metadata_fits`, before jxl-oxide sees the page, and refuses the page
as it refuses a metadata bomb (`ImageError::Limits`); `rebuilt_jpeg` checks
it beside `metadata_fits` too and makes no JPEG. `cover::fits_within`,
`cover::decode_limited`, `fingerprint::decode_page` and the cut-short check
reach jxl-oxide only through the hook. A page sent as stored is never
parsed, so the cap does not reach it. A page whose size goes unread passes,
since jxl-oxide fills nothing for it either: it stops where the check does
at a header that does not parse or that ends before the size, and a header
that wants no profile has none to fill.

**The shapes.** A page declaring 2^28, or one byte over the cap, is refused
in every shape by the check
(`a_colour_profile_declared_over_the_cap_is_refused_in_every_shape`) and
through the hook
(`a_page_declaring_a_colour_profile_over_the_cap_is_refused`), and the size
asked before a decode is refused too
(`the_size_of_a_page_declaring_a_colour_profile_over_the_cap_is_refused`).
At the cap the page passes in every shape and reaches jxl-oxide, which
refuses it as a broken page, `ImageError::Decoding` and not the cap's
`Limits` (`a_page_declaring_a_colour_profile_at_the_cap_reaches_jxl_oxide`).
The page cut inside its header or inside its size passes the check and is
refused through the hook as a broken page
(`a_header_that_ends_before_its_profile_size_passes`). A page that wants no
profile, followed by bits that would read as a size of 2^28, passes in every
shape (`a_page_that_wants_no_colour_profile_is_not_read_for_one`).

**A real profile.** `fixtures/jxl/icc.jxl`, made by `make.sh`, is a lossless
page carrying libjxl's own Display P3 profile, which `cjxl` kept whole from
a PNG; jxlinfo and `djxl --icc_out` each read the profile as 516 bytes
(`icc-facts.log`). `a_page_with_a_real_colour_profile_passes_the_check`
first reads through jxl-oxide that `icc.jxl` carries a profile of its own
and `lossless.jxl` none, then that the check passes it; its row in
`every_fixture_decodes_through_image_reader_as_djxl_does` decodes it through
the hook exactly as djxl does.

**What the cap leaves, and why it is 64 KiB.** A profile the cap passes is
still read whole, decoded and parsed outside every limit: jxl-oxide's
`try_init` reads it with `read_icc` and decodes it with `decode_icc`, and
building the render context parses the result with
`ColorEncodingWithProfile::with_icc`, which keeps a copy of a profile it
cannot turn into an enum encoding. These notes first said `decode_icc`
writes only what the stream carries; the whole-branch review found that
wrong, and jxl-color 0.11.0's source bears it out: a tag command writes up
to 36 bytes and most read no data, and the tag loop returns at the end of
the commands without comparing what it wrote against the decoded size the
stream declares. So the decoded profile grows with the encoded one, and the
cap was 1 MiB until the owner's ruling of 2026-11-19 lowered it to 64 KiB,
so that the worst a page's profile costs, decoded and parsed once, stays
within what its metadata boxes may inflate to; the cost is a genuine profile
that encodes above 64 KiB, refused with its page. A lossless CMYK JPEG XL
page carrying Ghostscript's `default_cmyk.icc` (187,484 bytes) declares an
encoded profile of 187,433 bytes and is refused (`cmyk-profile.log`; `cjxl`
0.12.0 would not transcode a CMYK JPEG, so the page was made from a CMYK
PAM image).

`icc_pages::expanding_profile` builds, after the review's probe, the
encoded profile that decodes to the most from a given length: the decoded
size 2^28, a tag count of three per command, every command tag code 2
(rTRC, which `decode_icc` writes with gTRC and bTRC), then 128 header
bytes that give the decoded profile's size field its real length, so the
parse reads every entry; bytes left over are data no command reads.
`the_worst_profile_the_cap_passes_is_decoded_and_parsed_within_the_metadata_cap`,
in a process of its own, decodes and parses it at `ICC_CAP` bytes and
asserts the rise in peak resident memory is below `METADATA_CAP`, 16 MiB,
after checking that the profile decoded to at least 35 times its length and
that the parse kept a copy of it. It calls jxl-color, a dev-dependency at
the version jxl-oxide resolves to, rather than decoding a page: `read_icc`
hands `decode_icc` such a stream, and a page carrying it would have to be
entropy-coded by hand. In a debug test build under the system allocator
(`worst-case.log`): at 65,536 bytes the profile decoded to 2,354,424 bytes
and the decode and parse raised the peak by 11,743,232 and 11,214,848 bytes
in two runs; at 1,048,576, the first cap, it decoded to 37,743,828 bytes and
raised the peak by 153,677,824 and 154,030,080, and the test failed.

Not measured: a page through the hook. A decode there builds two images,
jxl-oxide's decoder and then the first-frame check's while the first is
held, and each decodes and parses the profile once and keeps the decoded
profile and, on a page not stored in XYB, the parse's copy. Changed for two
runs to decode and parse the stream, keep both results and do it again, the
test read rises of 15,642,624 and 15,405,056 bytes at 65,536
(`worst-case.log`), under 16 MiB by little. A page with a frame to render
has its profile parsed again when the colour transform is built, more than
once for a page not stored in XYB (jxl-render's `cache_color_transform`
parses it in `with_icc`, then in `icc_tf` through `suggested_hdr_tf`), also
not measured. Below the cap, too, jxl-oxide still reads a declared profile
again after every 4 KiB of input until the header is whole; that cost is
bounded by the cap and was not measured. The decoded profile's declared size
is not checked: it is the first value inside the entropy-coded stream, so
reading it means entropy-decoding, and it would not bound what `decode_icc`
writes (the spec's approach 4).

**Watched failing.** Every defect below was put in by hand and the test
watched failing; `mutations.md` has the command, the failing tests and
the first message of each, with a log per mutation.

- M1, the cap as `64 + 1024`, and M2, `<=` as `<`:
  `a_colour_profile_declared_at_the_cap_passes_in_every_shape` and
  `a_page_declaring_a_colour_profile_at_the_cap_reaches_jxl_oxide`; M1
  also the worst-profile test, at its check that the profile decoded to 35
  times its length, which 1,088 bytes is too short to reach. (Before the
  cap was lowered, the same two at 1 MiB, as `1024 + 1024`.)
- M14, the cap put back to `1024 * 1024`, and M15, the cap one byte higher:
  `a_colour_profile_declared_over_the_cap_is_refused_in_every_shape` and
  `a_page_declaring_a_colour_profile_over_the_cap_is_refused`, at
  65,537 bytes; M14 also
  `the_worst_profile_the_cap_passes_is_decoded_and_parsed_within_the_metadata_cap`,
  at its memory assertion.
- M3, `icc_fits` passing every page: the over-the-cap tests, by the check
  and through the hook, the size test and the two process tests on the
  2^28 page.
- M4, the hook's check taken out:
  `a_page_declaring_a_huge_colour_profile_is_refused_before_jxl_oxide_fills_it`,
  `a_page_declaring_a_colour_profile_over_the_cap_is_refused` and the size
  test. M5, `rebuilt_jpeg`'s taken out:
  `a_page_declaring_a_huge_colour_profile_is_not_rebuilt_and_never_filled`
  alone.
- M6, a `jxlp` payload read with its index; M7, the codestream ending after
  the first box; M8, a container read as a bare page:
  `a_colour_profile_declared_over_the_cap_is_refused_in_every_shape`,
  `a_page_declaring_a_colour_profile_over_the_cap_is_refused` and
  `a_page_declaring_a_huge_colour_profile_is_not_rebuilt_and_never_filled`.
- M9, `want_icc()` inverted: the tests M3 fails and
  `a_page_that_wants_no_colour_profile_is_not_read_for_one`.
- M10, a size that cannot be read refused, and M11, a header that does not
  parse refused: `a_header_that_ends_before_its_profile_size_passes`, by its
  check assertion and, with that taken out for a run, by its decode through
  the hook, which gave `Limits`.
- M12, the cap as 16 bytes, and M13, every page that wants a profile
  refused: `a_page_with_a_real_colour_profile_passes_the_check`, the
  `icc.jxl` row of `every_fixture_decodes_through_image_reader_as_djxl_does`
  and the two at-the-cap tests; M13 also
  `a_header_that_ends_before_its_profile_size_passes`.
- `icc.jxl` swapped for a lossy encode, which `cjxl` gives an enum colour
  encoding and no profile:
  `a_page_with_a_real_colour_profile_passes_the_check`, at its fixture
  check.
- `expanding_profile` made to write tag code 4, one 12-byte entry a
  command: the worst-profile test, at its fixture check. Its check that the
  parse kept a copy was not watched failing; no profile was built that
  jxl-color parses as an enum encoding.

A cargo-mutants sweep over the branch's diff, run after the review's fixes
and the branch's first rebase onto main (`f5fa08df`), caught all 26 mutants
it made, none of them unviable (`docs/mutants-baseline.md`, 2026-11-19). The
later rebase onto main changed no code the sweep mutated. cargo-mutants
makes no mutant of the parts M6, M7, M10 and M11 put wrong by hand.

## jemalloc as the allocator: memory after a burst (2026-11-19)

O349, closed by the jemalloc PR: the `taiyaku` binary allocates through
`tikv-jemallocator` 0.7.0 with its `background_threads` feature, so
jemalloc's background threads give memory freed after a burst back to the
system on a timer, whether or not the server makes another allocator call.
It sits on `tikv-jemalloc-sys` 0.7.1, which bundles jemalloc 5.3.1 and builds
it with jemalloc's own `configure` and `make`. The design is
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-19-mimalloc-design.md`. The evidence is in
`.superpowers/sdd/mimalloc-evidence/`, not committed; each figure below
names its file there.

**The route.** Each attempt was measured by the same `fetch.sh` and
`sampler.sh` against the same three criteria: the branch's reading 30 s after
the last response within 102,400 kB (100 MiB) of its own reading at rest, its
mean peak at most 1.10 times main's, and its mean wall time at most 1.10
times main's.

- mimalloc, the design's first choice, with its defaults (`T2/verdict.md`),
  failed the first. It gives freed memory back only when a later allocator
  call finds its purge delay passed, and a server sent nothing after the
  burst may make no such call.
- mimalloc with `MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY=0` (`T2b/verdict.md`) passed the first
  two and failed the third: its mean wall time was 2.78 times main's.
- jemalloc's first run (`T2c/verdict.md`) passed the first two and failed
  the third, with main-1's fetch at a one-minute load of 4.90 to 7.66 and the
  other three's at 26.83 to 40.60, from work outside the measurement. The
  owner ruled to measure again with each run starting only under a load of 8.
- That run (`T2d/`) passed all three; the rest of this section reports it.

**The run** (`T2d/run.sh`, `T2d/verdict.md`). Two release builds on this
desktop: main, the build of fc484285, which was the branch's merge base with
main when the runs were made, and the branch, the build of this branch's
code on fc484285 (`T2d/binaries.txt`). Main's commits after fc484285, up to
44e27960, onto which the branch was then rebased, change no Rust file but
tests. The branch was later rebased onto a main that holds #274 (O350),
which checks the encoded colour-profile size a page's header declares before
jxl-oxide decodes the page; the run did not measure that check. The Bisque
Doll original was copied afresh to a scratch library (`T2d/library.txt`),
and each run started a server on it with a new database and an empty cache
and read all 185 pages at full size, four at a time, with Chrome 154's
`Accept`, through the 2026-11-17 run's `fetch.sh` and `sampler.sh`
unchanged. Resident memory was read from `/proc` at rest, through the read,
30 s after the last response and 5 minutes after it. The runs went main,
branch, branch, main.

It differs from the 2026-11-17 run in ways that are the same for both
builds. Its scratch library held the Bisque Doll original alone
(`T2d/library.txt`), where the 2026-11-17 one held four Bocchi the Rock!
volumes beside it ("The real archive" in the 2026-11-17 section above). Each
run started with an empty cache, so it made every page. Nothing reached the
server between the last response and the 5-minute reading. Content matching
was switched off on each run's scratch database before `serve`: the
2026-11-17 build predates the fingerprint pass, which would otherwise have
decoded the same pages during the readings. And no run started its server
until the one-minute load was under 8, which it reached once the machine's
other sessions had been asked, at the owner's request, to pause heavy work
(`T2d/driver.log`, `T2d/verdict.md`).

| Mean of two runs (`T2d/runs.tsv`) | Main | Branch |
|---|---|---|
| At rest | 20,166 kB | 33,306 kB |
| Peak | 979,096 kB | 623,162 kB |
| 30 s after the last response | 784,452 kB | 51,806 kB |
| 5 minutes after | 784,380 kB | 46,898 kB |
| Wall time of the read | 16.89 s | 18.075 s |

Each memory figure is VmRSS but the peak, which is the largest VmHWM read
from the start of the read to the 30 s reading. Every fetch began at a
one-minute load of 1.08 to 6.45 and ended at 4.02 to 8.36, on 32 CPUs.

- **Validity.** Each of main's runs held more than 102,400 kB above its rest
  reading at 30 s, so main still kept the memory and the run could show a
  fix.
- **1.** The branch's runs held 16,872 and 20,128 kB above their rest
  readings at 30 s, within 102,400 kB.
- **2.** The branch's mean peak was 0.636 times main's.
- **3.** The branch's mean wall time was 1.070 times main's, within 1.10: at
  a settled load the burst took longer under jemalloc than under glibc's
  malloc.

Only Rust's allocations go to jemalloc. `tikv-jemalloc-sys`'s `build.rs`
gives jemalloc's symbols the prefix `_rjem_` unless its
`unprefixed_malloc_on_supported_platforms` feature is on, and the branch
turns on only `background_threads` and the default
`background_threads_runtime_support`, so C code, the bundled SQLite and the
image's libarchive among it, still calls glibc's `malloc`. Not measured on
the NAS.

## RAR PR 2: libraries read RAR (2026-11-19)

A build with the `rar-libarchive` feature, the container image among them,
counts, derives, fingerprints, serves and downloads RAR members as it does
zips, and refuses at the count, naming the file and the cause, any RAR of a
kind libarchive could not read whole. The plan is
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-19-rar-libarchive-pr2.md`, and the design's
PR 2 notes (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-rar-libarchive-design.md`,
"Decisions") say where the work departed from the design. `docs/status.md`
records it as O391, opened and closed here; it closes O295, O381, O384 and
O385, and narrows O131, O351 and O386. The evidence named below is under
`.superpowers/sdd/rar-pr2-evidence/` in the main checkout, which is not
committed.

### The owner's rulings

Given on 2026-11-19, before the plan was written:

- **P2-R1 (O384):** `member_page` lists a RAR and reads its page through one
  open file.
- **P2-R2 (O385):** a RAR holding two entries of one name is refused at
  listing.
- **P2-R3 (O386):** an archive with an entry compressed by RAR 2.0 is refused
  at the count, from the unpack version and method its headers declare.
  Nothing is decoded at scan time.
- **P2-R4 (O381):** the proper fix, through taiyaku's own walk of the block
  headers. The owner's compress-tools fork cannot supply it: libarchive gives
  no target for a `rar -oi` file reference, and marks a RAR5 entry encrypted
  only from 3.7.7. So an empty file reads as empty, a reference or hard link
  reads its target, and an encrypted entry is refused.
- **P2-R5:** the reader signature names the libarchive version that
  `pkg-config --modversion libarchive` gives `taiyaku-read`'s build script,
  not the one loaded at run time. The fork is not changed.
- **P2-R6:** a volume of a multi-volume set, RAR4 or RAR5, is refused at the
  count.
- Standing: encrypted archives are out of scope, nothing is pushed to the
  fork, an entry that declares only a BLAKE2 hash stays unchecked (O383),
  O386 stays open, and taiyaku reads RAR for its users while the owner's own
  library aims to hold none.

### The decisions, as built

- **D1.** `Libarchive::entries` walks the block headers
  (`rar::libarchive::headers`) over the same open file libarchive lists from,
  so a listing refuses what every read of the archive would.
- **D2.** The listing refuses, each as
  `{path}: not a readable RAR archive: {cause}`, a volume of a set; a RAR4
  file whose bytes are compressed at any unpack version but 29, since
  libarchive's RAR4 reader decodes RAR 2.9's compression alone, while a
  stored file is read whatever version wrote it; an encrypted entry; a
  reference or hard link whose target is not an earlier entry of that name,
  or whose size is not its target's (added at review); two readable entries
  of one name, a rule in `pages.rs` that holds for every backend; and, added
  at the whole-branch review, a RAR5 entry libarchive lists as a regular file
  that no read gives whole: a junction or a redirection of a type libarchive
  does not read, which it gives no bytes for, and a file whose header marks
  it a directory. libarchive 3.7.4 lists such a file and the walk refuses it,
  while 3.8.11 refuses one that holds data as it lists it, with its own
  cause, "directory entries cannot have any data"
  (`pages::rar_tests::a_file_no_read_gives_whole_refuses_the_archive`).
- **D3.** An empty file reads as no bytes without asking libarchive, which
  fails on one in a solid RAR5. A reference or hard link reads its target's
  bytes.
- **D4.** `member_page` reads a RAR through `rar::Backend::read_listed`: one
  open, listed, the page picked from the listing, and read by its position.
- **D5.** The signature is `rar:libarchive-<version>:<the page extensions>`.
  The store the real-material check scanned holds
  `rar:libarchive-3.8.11:jpg,jpeg,png,webp,gif,bmp,avif,tif,tiff,jxl`
  (`real/store-1-scan_entry.tsv`).
- **D6.** A download passed through takes its type and its extension from the
  format the scan stored for the file (`scan_entry.format`), not from its
  name, and from a sniff of the file where the store has no format for it as
  it is (`download::sent_as`). Since the whole-branch review the stored
  format counts only where the file still has the size and mtime that scan
  saw, so a RAR converted to a zip in place is sent as a zip before the next
  scan. Its own extension is kept where it names that format, bytes no
  signature matches are typed by their name, and a 7-Zip or tar archive is
  sent as `application/octet-stream` under its own name. A member download
  keeps the member's file name, its extension replaced by the one sent where
  it names a format (`.cb7`, `.7z`, `.cbt` and `.tar` among them since the
  review), so a zip named `X.cb7` is sent as `X.cbz`. This closes O295, a
  download typed by its name, which the plan did not name and the
  whole-branch review found fixed
  (`download::tests::rar_members::a_misnamed_passthrough_is_typed_and_named_by_what_the_scan_read`).
- **D7.** A generated download takes a RAR page's CRC32 and size from its
  header where the header declares a CRC32.
- **D8.** The fingerprint pass's renumber rule binds the signature of every
  paged format (`fingerprints::paged_signatures`), so a RAR's row settles
  after one read, as a zip's does.
- **D9.** A count the reader refuses is written to stderr with its path,
  `taiyaku: the scan left a file uncounted: …`, for a zip as for a RAR in a
  build with the feature; a build without it hands the reader no RAR to count
  (`scan::pages_of`). It is a line on stderr, not the levelled `warn` the plan
  named. The store still keeps no cause, so O131 narrows and stays open.
- **D10.** The rollback was checked on a copy of the store a feature scan
  built from a scratch library of real archives, below; the NAS's live store
  was not used.

Decided while it was built: the licence page shows libarchive's `COPYING`
and no other notice of its files; `debian:trixie-slim`, the image's runtime
base, keeps every package's copyright file and no other doc file, and
`libarchive13t64` installed into it keeps its copyright file
(`licence-copyright-check.log`).

### What a reader of the code might not expect

- **D6 changes builds without the feature too.** `download::sent_as` asks no
  build question, so in every build a zip named `.cbr` downloads as `.cbz`
  with the zip type, and a RAR member already in the store, or in a work
  imported from its document, is still passed through as a RAR named `.cbr`,
  since passing it through reads none of it
  (`download::tests::rar_members::a_member_no_scan_holds_is_typed_by_a_sniff`
  runs in both builds).
- **D9's line is expected in test output.** It goes to stderr, so the output
  of `taiyaku-library`'s and `taiyaku-serve`'s tests carries such lines for
  the archives their fixtures refuse; they are not failures.
- **A rollback keeps counted RAR rows, not refused ones.** A scan by a build
  without the feature keeps a row a feature build counted, with its count,
  signature and digest, and sniffs the file again at each scan without
  counting it. A row a feature build refused at the count loses its
  signature, so the next feature scan tries the count again and writes its
  cause again
  (`scan::tests::a_rar_counted_by_a_build_that_reads_rar_keeps_its_row_through_any_build`,
  `scan::tests::a_rar_refused_at_the_count_is_counted_again_by_the_build_after_another`).
- **A server built without the feature drops every RAR fingerprint row.**
  Its pass keeps only the rows of what its derive claims
  (`fingerprints::drop_unclaimed`), and that derive claims no RAR, so after a
  rollback the next feature server reads each RAR once more. A scan by such
  a build keeps the rows. Found on real material (F1 in `real/report.md`) and
  accepted: scan rows, works and saved places are untouched.
- **The signature names the libarchive version `pkg-config` gave the build.**
  A store scanned by a development build (3.8.11 here) is counted again, once
  per RAR, by the image (3.7.4). The version is the one `pkg-config` gave
  when the build script last ran.
- **Serving one page of a solid RAR5 decodes the whole archive**, as it did
  before this PR: `member_page` has listed before it reads since RAR PR 1,
  and listing one decodes every entry (measured on 3.8.11, below). What this
  PR adds is a library that counts such an archive and serves its pages. O380
  holds the cost.
- **A target's bytes are kept for its references.** One pass of
  `Libarchive::visit` keeps a target's bytes from its own position to its
  last reference's, so a crafted archive can hold several pages in memory
  during it.
- **A refused page carried main's sidecar hint, until 2026-11-20.**
  `source::LocalLibrary` appended "the sidecar records N pages for this
  member; it may have been replaced" to every `member_page` error, so the log
  line for a RAR page refused by a build without the feature carried it too
  (F2 in `real/report.md`). That refusal is now handed on without the hint;
  see "RAR follow-ups: the page refusal's hint and the panel's formats
  (2026-11-20)" below.

### The owner's RARs

Checked on the branch as it stood after its licence-page commit, in
`real/report.md`. **These 21 RARs are not RAR PR 1's 21.** That census
(2026-11-17) covered every archive under `Manga/` and `Comics/`; since then
the owner converted Fantastic Four v1 360 to a zip, and the check took in
Pokemon Ep.14, a RAR4 under `Magazines/`, outside the census's scope. So
the 21 here are the census's other 20 and Pokemon Ep.14
(`real/census-pr2.txt`), while the 21 that the notes above and O380, O383
and O386 name are the census's. The scratch library held copies, made with
`cp` from the NAS, which was only read, of these 21 and of Fantastic Four
v1 360's RAR 2.0 original, kept since the conversion; every copy's sha256
was unchanged at the end (`real/copy-sha256.log`,
`real/library-sha256-at-end.txt`).

- **Read whole.** A probe built from the branch read every page of the 21,
  3,054 pages, with no refusal, on libarchive 3.8.11 and on 3.7.4 in
  `rust:1-trixie`, and the two runs agreed archive by archive, page counts
  and first and last page names included. The RAR 2.0 original was refused
  at listing with D2's cause on both (`real/t8real-3.8.11.log`,
  `real/t8real-3.7.4.log`, `real/pagenames.tsv`).
- **Counted.** A feature build's scan counted each of the 21 at the page count
  `bsdtar -tf` lists after taiyaku's filter, and left the original uncounted,
  writing its cause (`real/counts.tsv`, `real/scan-1-feature.log`).
- **Served.** A test server answered the first and last page of each with
  the bytes `unrar p` gives (`real/pages-first-last.tsv`), a cover, resized
  pages, passthrough downloads of RARs named `.cbz` and `.cbr` with the RAR
  type and a `.cbr` name, and a generated download of an edition of four RAR
  members whose pages match `unrar x` of each member and the served pages,
  in order.
- **Fingerprinted once.** The pass read each counted RAR once; a rescan and a
  restart started no further pass (D8; `real/fp-1-after-first-pass.tsv` to
  `real/fp-3-after-restart.tsv`).
- **Rolled back.** On a copy of that store, a scan and a server built without
  the feature kept every work, member, counted row and saved place, and
  refused each work's first page and thumbnail, the log saying the build
  reads no RAR; a feature scan and server afterwards gave back the same rows,
  works and first and last pages as before (`real/rollback-*`). The surprise
  was the fingerprint rows (F1, above).

The image, built from the branch before the sweep's tests were added, runs
Debian 13.7 with `libarchive13t64` 3.7.4-4+deb13u1, links
`libarchive.so.13.7.4`, starts healthy and answers `/`
(`T8b-image-checks.log`, `T8b-image-run.log`).

### The mutation sweep

Two sweeps over the branch's diff before the whole-branch review's fixes;
`docs/mutants-baseline.md`'s run log has their figures. Five survivors of the
first were real, and each is now killed by a test watched failing with the
mutant put back by hand; the other two are equivalent `|`-as-`^` entries this
branch moved, re-keyed in the baseline. Both sweeps timed out on
`scan_root_inner -> Ok(None)`, a scan with no outcome that a test waits on.
Every unviable mutant replaces a whole body with a value that does not compile
there, and the seven functions left with no viable mutant were each put wrong
by hand and failed tests (`T8b-hand-*.log`).

### What describing a solid RAR costs

`member_page_entries` takes a RAR's sizes and CRC32s from its entry headers
where the header declares a CRC32, but the listing it reads them from walks
libarchive past every entry, and in a solid RAR5 libarchive decodes each entry
it passes.

Measured on libarchive 3.8.11 with a throwaway test in `taiyaku-read`:
`rar5-solid.rar` with the data of `p2.png`, or of its last page `p4.png`, XORed
with 0x55 failed `member_page_entries` and `member_page_names` alike with
`Block checksum error`: the listing read into the damaged data.
`rar5-compressed.rar`, which is not solid, damaged the same way in `p1.png` or
`p10.png`, still listed its three pages through both. So the docs of
`PageEntry`, `rar_page_entries`, `member_page_names` and the describe step in
`download::prepare` say a solid RAR's listing decodes it whole. Reading one
entry by name (`Backend::read`) stops at it, as
`reading_a_solid_entry_decodes_nothing_after_it` pins, but `member_page` lists
through `read_listed` before it reads, so serving one page of a solid RAR5 still
decodes the whole archive.

In a library that cost multiplies. What follows was read from the code, and
has been measured since ("O380: what a solid RAR5 costs to read (2026-11-20)",
below). The fingerprint pass lists a counted RAR twice (`member_page_names`,
`member_unread_entries`), reads a sample of its pages
(`fingerprint::border_sample`) through `member_page`, which lists before each
read, and lists it once more to walk it (`fingerprint_pass/read.rs`). Where a
solid RAR5's archive order is not its reading order, that walk and a generated
download's both read each page by name (`pages::rar_for_each_page`), and each
read decodes every entry before its page, so their cost grows with the square
of the page count.

## Content matching PR 3: volume joins (2026-11-19)

The spec is
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-19-content-matching-volume-joins-design.md`
and the plan
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-19-content-matching-volume-joins.md`.
PR 3 joins the editions of a volume whose pages match at or above O340's
frozen bar of 0.87 automatically, and an admin can Split a join and Undo the
Split. It narrows O338 and O340 and opens O392 to O407 and O414.

**The server's scorer gives every O340 pair its score.** The `#[ignore]`d
test `the_server_scorer_gives_every_o340_pair_its_score` reads the 157
members of the volume test from the local test library through the server's
own fingerprint (decode, describe, encode and decode again, the blob the pass
reads), slots each right to left as O340 read every member, and scores every
pair keyed by path, as O340 keyed them, through `volume_match::score`. All
12,246 rows of O340's `scores.tsv` came back equal in every cell
(`equal: 12246 of 12246`), in 403.08 s of a release build's test time. The
control, `LONG_RUN` set to 3 in the server's copy, left 10,588 of 12,246
equal and failed the test. The server keys a pair by digest, not path, so a
pair of equal slot counts can be scored the other way round: of 298 such
pairs, the digests put the other side first for 167, and V differs for 10.
None of the 10 reaches the floor of 0.6 either way, so none crosses the bar:
the largest by path is 0.598039 (Yu Yu Hakusho v14 against v15), the largest
by digest 0.557604 (Hunter × Hunter, the official colour edition, v29
against v31). The ten rows and their digests are in the evidence's
`summary.txt`, under `.superpowers/sdd/content-volume-joins-evidence/`.

**On real material, 432 of 446 predictions held.** A release build of the
branch before the final review and its fixes ran a new store over a copy of
part of the test library (445 members) after a prediction of every file's
outcome was written. The fingerprint pass stored 444 `whole` rows and 1
`partial` (Monster v02, whose cbz holds a zip the reader does not read), so
363 files were looked up, against 364 predicted. The match pass stored 223
pairs, 179 of them at the bar, and its derive joined 58 files by content.

| | predicted | observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| join by content (files) | 62 | 58 |
| host (files) | 56 | 52 |
| together by name | 170 | 170 |
| follow | 3 | 3 |
| apart | 154 | 162 |
| no work (a chapter directory) | 1 | 1 |

Every difference is a wrong prediction, and all fourteen sit in the two
series the prediction rated low confidence. Raw Kaguya-sama v02 and v03
joined the English full-colour volumes, not the black-and-white ones,
scoring higher against colour (v02 0.977376 against 0.950450, v03 0.995238
against 0.980952), which is the design's "two possible hosts" rule (§4). Raw
Kaguya-sama v01, a folder of two-page spreads, scored 0.706422 against the
English v01, under the bar. Kobayashi-san Chi no Meidoragon v03, v05 and
v11 stayed apart from their raws: all six files were looked up and read
whole, and no pair naming any of them reached the floor among each lookup's
three leaders. The store does not say whether a partner was offered and
scored under 0.6 or not offered at all; O392 records the case. The by-hand
checks passed: ⇄ landed where the stored runs say, a raw volume's reading
position survived its join, a Split and the rescan after it, Undo brought
the position back, and the match pass's line and Cancel worked, on a
second pass over 77 files added to the copy, 54 of them due, which Cancel
stopped after four lookups: 367 in all. A restart then looked up only the
50 left due, and left those 367 lookups as they were.

**The server's memory across the match pass, on about 450 volumes.** That
build used the system allocator, before jemalloc (#276) was merged in. The
resident set's peak (`VmHWM`) was reset when the match job first showed in the
scan feed, with `VmRSS` then 97,044 kB. The pass looked up 363 files in under
four seconds. `VmHWM` read 155,096 kB at 18:13:16 UTC, a second after the job
had gone, and 155,108 kB from 18:13:30, and `VmRSS` 30 s after the pass ended
was 155,108 kB. The pass holds the slots of every file taking part (the
design's §2, "Cost"), so this reading does not speak for a library of
thousands of volumes.

**A defect in the branch's own derive that the drawn stores found.**
`drawn_stores_keep_every_rule_of_a_join`, the generator Split's fix rounds
added, was run against the derive as it stood when the derive tasks first
merged, before Split had a route, and failed its first rule (every file on
exactly one work) on two seeds of 2,000. A work whose group's files went to
two works was written by no group, and `superseded` folds a work into one
target only, so the old work kept copies of files that stood on other works.
On seed 131 Aoi's work held Chiyo's `ko` as a guest; once a pair was split,
Aoi's own editions joined Bara and Chiyo's `ko` went home, and Aoi's old
work stood with copies of both. The leave-behind rules of Split's fix rounds
made the shape common: it was most of the 129 seeds of 2,000 that failed
that rule before the fix. `move_left_behind` now
moves each edition of such a work that is bound elsewhere
(`fold::move_edition`) before `superseded` folds the rest into the hub's
target; with that step removed the generator failed the rule on 91 seeds
of 2,000.

**The drawn stores, at 2,000.** The generator draws 160 seeds and the four
that once caught a defect by default, a CI test's budget, and
`TAIYAKU_JOIN_CASES` names another count; a value that is not a count
panics. Run with 2,000 on 2026-11-20, it drew 2,000 stores and passed in
33.52 s on eight threads.

**A volume arriving where a work was placed by hand.** A row at a series'
address that another group's files hash to is that group's, since the import
finds it by their content (`derive::held_work`, `Placed::claims`), so where
derive put such a row there, a volume arriving at the address takes a work of
its own. A work an admin moved there by hand from another series
(`series_id_hand`, with or without `volume_hand`) was the address's
instead: the arriving volume was written onto it, the file the work held then
stood on two works, and the reader's place stayed with the stale copy. `main`
did this before this branch (the fix wave's review reproduced it there, on a
raw an admin moved into the English series), and the branch reached it by a
new route: a raw volume that had followed its directory, whose work an admin
then gave a hand volume or series. Now the arriving volume takes a work of its
own there too. A work placed from another series keeps its file and the
reader's place, beside the new work at the same series and volume
(`a_volume_appearing_where_a_work_was_placed_from_another_series_takes_a_work_of_its_own`,
`a_volume_appearing_where_a_work_was_placed_with_its_volume_takes_a_work_of_its_own`).
A follower given a hand volume goes back to its own series at that volume, as
one given only a hand title already did, and one given a hand series stays
beside the arriving volume on a work of its own
(`a_follower_with_a_hand_volume_goes_back_when_the_volume_it_filled_arrives`,
`a_follower_with_a_hand_title_goes_back_when_the_volume_it_filled_arrives`,
`a_follower_with_a_hand_series_stays_beside_the_volume_it_filled_when_that_arrives`).
In each, every file is on one work, the reader's place stays with its file,
and the next derive commits nothing. A hand row stays the address's where the
claiming group stands in that series, or where the row holds a file of the
arriving group, so a work placed for files yet to arrive still takes them
(`a_work_placed_at_an_address_takes_the_volume_that_appears_there`).

**What the plan settled that the design does not, and why.**

- **The scorer is a copy.** `taiyaku-serve::volume_match` copies O340's
  scorer, and its Hamming distance and informative-slot rule, rather than
  calling `match_experiment`, because editing the CLI's module would change
  the code the bar was frozen with, which `volume_test::run`'s
  `no_code_since_the_freeze` refuses. CLI tests hold the copies equal on
  fixtures, `the_server_bar_is_the_frozen_bar` holds `matches::BAR` to
  `bar.json`, and the reproduction above holds the server's scorer to every
  O340 row.
- **Only a literal `set_series` holds a file.** The rule table has no
  `set_volume` or `set_title`, so a rule's series is the only name it can
  state outright; a rule that captures from a path, seeded or written by
  hand, reads names, which content exists to overrule. No column records a
  rule's origin and nothing detects a seed, so editing a seed or importing
  rules again changes nothing about what holds a file.
- **The mark is `edition.joined_by`.** The pair that brought an edition in
  is stored on the edition because it is both the Series panel's mark and
  how a later derive finds an edition a Split or an unjoin leaves on the
  host. A mark stands only where its pair's other file is on the same work.
- **A whole-work join reuses `superseded` and `fold::absorb`.** The host's
  new edition holds the guest's digests, so `fold::edition_map` maps it and
  absorb carries reader state as for any fold. `fold::move_edition` is new
  for what absorb refuses: a work that keeps another edition, a Split, an
  unjoin.
- **An alignment's figures come from its runs.** A match row holds
  whole-page runs from `sha_a`'s pages to `sha_b`'s, the two page counts and
  the solver's floor. Derive turns them host to guest, fills the gaps and
  computes the verdict, slots, paired count and average run from them, so an
  alignment row agrees with its own runs.
- **An alignment's direction.** From the pair's edition that is the work's
  hub, else the higher kind (official, fan, raw), else the smaller key: a
  pair names already put in one work has no host and guest to go by.
- **Split splits every pair tying the file to its work.** In a triangle of
  official, fan and raw volumes pairwise at the bar, splitting one pair
  would leave another joining the file again, and Split would seem to do
  nothing. The route names the edition it splits, because where the fan and
  raw pair is the highest both files carry it as `joined_by`, and the pair
  alone cannot say which file leaves. Undo takes back the whole Split, every
  pair it set apart, with one derive (the owner's ruling of 2026-11-19, which
  replaced the plan's one pair: one Undo per pair grows unwieldy as more
  editions match together); each pair records the Split that set it apart.
- **A split pair keeps its files apart** (not always: O405). A group that
  would merge into a component holding a file one of its files is split from
  leaves that file's edition behind, as an edition whose key the component
  already holds stays behind. A Split no later derive reverses is the design's
  anti-goal, and a split pair treated only as a missing edge let a file's name
  group pull it back. Files left behind form components of their own, divided
  by the edges already applied among them and by names, with a host by the
  usual rule, and later edges treat them as any component: frozen, they would
  lose an unsplit pair at every derive. A file that a join leaves no longer
  linked to the host by applied edges is left behind too, since a missed join
  is the safer way to fail than a join to a file kept apart.
- **The pass's derive waits as a scan's does.** It takes the job lock and
  the derive lease first, because a derive beside another's, or beside a
  rules save, would write works from a store the other is rewriting. A
  Cancel during it is honoured once it ends.
- **The chain.** The fingerprint pass starts the match pass as it goes idle,
  and not when its own job was cancelled, so a Cancel there stops both.

**The first fingerprint pass hashed the copy twice.** On the run above,
the start-up scan's derive hashed all 445 files, and the fingerprint pass,
which had listed them before it, hashed them all again and stored nothing
from it before listing them afresh. It is on `main` too; O396 records it.

**A sweep that tested nothing read as clean.** One run of the sweep of the
fix for a volume arriving where a work was placed by hand, on 2026-11-19 with
no sccache server running after a reboot, built nothing. These are five of
its log's lines, in order:

```text
FAILED   Unmutated baseline in 0s build
sccache: error: path must be shorter than SUN_LEN
ERROR cargo build failed in an unmutated tree, so no mutants were tested
mutants-baseline: 0 survivor(s) this run; docs/mutants-baseline.md holds 38 accepted and 90 untriaged
mutants-baseline: no survivor outside the baseline
```

`scripts/mutants.sh` reads `cargo mutants`' exit status only where
`missed.txt` is absent ("cargo mutants failed before it could report"), and
its "Absent is not empty" check stops a run only on that same absence. This
run left a `missed.txt` with nothing in it, so the script handed
`mutants-baseline.mjs` an empty survivor list. That script prints its last
line above just before it exits 0, and as the last command of `mutants.sh`
its status is the sweep's. O414 records it.

## RAR follow-ups: the page refusal's hint and the panel's formats (2026-11-20)

Two defects that were on main when RAR PR 2 merged, neither with an
O-number.

- **A page refused for the build is not blamed on the file.**
  `source::LocalLibrary` appends "the sidecar records N pages for this
  member; it may have been replaced" to a `member_page` error. A build without
  the `rar-libarchive` feature refuses every page of a RAR that a feature
  build counted, and that refusal names the build, so the hint pointed the
  log's reader at the file. Where this build has no RAR reader and the file
  sniffs as a RAR, the refusal is handed on as it is. Every other error keeps
  the hint, a RAR's page past its end in a feature build among them
  (`source::tests::a_rar_page_error_blames_a_replaced_file_only_in_a_build_that_reads_rar`).
  The sniff is on the error path only. A zip the sidecar counted and a RAR
  has since replaced loses the hint in such a build too: the refusal names
  the build, which is the cause the operator can act on either way.
- **The proposals panel's formats follow a file converted in place.**
  `proposals::edition_formats` joined `member` to `scan_entry` by path alone,
  so a RAR repacked as a zip under its name was shown as a RAR until the next
  scan, while D6's download of the same file already said zip. The panel now
  compares the stamp `download::sent_as` compares: the stored format answers
  while the file has the size and mtime the scan saw, built by
  `fingerprints::stamp_in` as the walk writes them, for a folder as for a
  file; a file that moved is sniffed, and bytes that name no format, or cannot
  be read, contribute nothing. A file that cannot be stat'ed keeps the stored
  format, where a download asks no row of one. A member with no root still
  contributes nothing. The rule is `proposals::format_as_it_is`, in one
  place.

What a reader of the code might not expect: the panel stats each member of
the hub edition of each side's volume 1 that joins a `scan_entry` row, which
a member with no root does not, and sniffs one that moved, so its route,
`curation::detail`, reads on `Library::working()`, a connection of its own,
as `stamp::plan`'s route does. The shared connection, which every
authenticated request takes, is not held across a wait on the share
(`curation::tests::the_expanded_row_does_not_wait_on_the_shared_connections_mutex`).
On a connection of its own the panel is not kept apart from any writer,
whichever connection that writer takes (`curation::accept` the shared one,
`curation::split_match`'s derive a working one), so it reads one snapshot
(`taiyaku_library::one_snapshot`), begun before it asks whether the proposal
is there: an accept or a delete that commits while it reads leaves its answer
the state before
(`curation::tests::the_expanded_row_reads_one_snapshot_of_the_store`,
`curation::tests::the_expanded_row_reads_a_proposal_it_found_from_the_snapshot_it_found_it_in`).
The snapshot is held across the stats and the sniffs, so the WAL is not
checkpointed past it until the answer is built; no writer waits on it.
Only a regular file or a folder is sniffed, the two things a walk records: a
FIFO stats like either, and an open of one waits for a writer, so a moved
path that is anything else contributes nothing. The kind is the stat's: a
path that becomes a FIFO between that stat and the sniff's open is still
opened, as it is under a scan's walk, and the wait is then that request's,
on its own connection. And the mtime is in whole seconds, so a file rewritten
at the same length within the second it was scanned still reads as the scan
saw it, as it does to the scan's own walk.

## O380: what a solid RAR5 costs to read (2026-11-20)

What a solid RAR5 costs taiyaku to read, which "What describing a solid RAR
costs" above read from the code, measured. Nothing was built. The owner ruled
on 2026-11-20 that O380 stays open on the trigger it has, a solid RAR in a
library, that unpacking one once is not built now, and that the figures are
recorded.

Two zips of the test library, a 207-page manga volume (Dandadan v01) and a
27-page comic issue (Invincible 001), were each repacked with `rar` three
ways: as a solid RAR5 with its pages in reading order (`rar a -ma5 -s -ds`
over a list of the names in that order, since without `-ds` RAR sorts a solid
archive's files itself), as a RAR5 that is not solid (`-s-`), which is the
control, and as a solid RAR5 from the same list reversed. `unrar t` passed
each. The code was main as RAR PR 2 left it, in a release build with the
`rar-libarchive` feature on libarchive 3.8.11, on the development machine
while it carried other load, and not on the NAS, whose image links 3.7.4.
Each figure is the user CPU seconds of one process, the median of three runs,
with the archive in the page cache. The process is a throwaway example, not
committed, that makes one public `taiyaku_read` call, or one `member_page`
call per page for the read-through; for `read_unit` it is a throwaway ignored
test that drives the fingerprint pass's own `fingerprint_pass::read::read_unit`
over the one file, image decoding included.

The 207-page volume, in user CPU seconds:

| Call | Solid | Control | Unpacked directory |
|---|---|---|---|
| `member_page`, first page | 0.964 | 0.024 | 0.003 |
| `member_page`, middle page | 1.481 | 0.002 | 0.005 |
| `member_page`, last page | 2.104 | 0.004 | 0.003 |
| `member_page_names`, one listing | 1.039 | 0.004 | |
| `member_page` for every page in turn | 288.0 | 0.311 | |
| `for_each_member_page` | 2.029 | 0.114 | |
| `for_each_member_page`, archive in reverse order | 93.27 | | |
| `read_unit` | 26.95 | 5.162 | |
| `read_unit`, archive in reverse order | 119.8 | | |
| The whole archive decoded once to a directory, through `for_each_member_page` | 1.828 | | |
| The same by `bsdtar -xf` | 0.920 | | |

The control was packed in reading order only, the last two rows are the solid
archive's, and of the directory that decode writes only the page read is given
here. `rar` at its default stored nearly all of the volume's pages
uncompressed when the archive was not solid, so the volume's control is mostly
reads of stored entries; the issue's control is compressed throughout. On the
issue one `member_page` of the solid archive cost 0.123 s for the first page
and 0.273 s for the last, against 0.006 s and 0.007 s for the control.

Nothing measured contradicts "What describing a solid RAR costs". That section
counts the listing a walk begins with, but not what follows from it: the walk
in reading order decodes a solid archive twice. `pages::rar_for_each_page`
lists the archive (`rar_pages`) and then visits it (`Backend::visit`), and
each is a whole decode, so the walk costs about what one listing and
`bsdtar`'s single pass cost together, and unpacking through it costs more than
`bsdtar` does (the table's last two rows).

## O69: `member.format` dropped (2026-11-20)

The owner ruled on 2026-11-20 to drop the column rather than populate it.
Migration 031 is `ALTER TABLE member DROP COLUMN format`; no trigger, view or
index names the column, so SQLite drops it in place. The two reads left went
with it: `scan.rs`'s `MemberRow` selected it in two queries and used
nothing of it, and `derive::unchanged` required it NULL.

**Checked on real files.** Three series were copied, not linked, from
`/home/davey/temp/manga-test` into a scratch directory: `Bocchi the Rock! -
Anthology Comic` (two `.cbz`), `RuriDragon` (four `.cbz`) and one
`Kaguya-sama` colour volume held as a directory of images. Main's binary at
4b7a4f4f scanned them as two directories into a store at version 30, and the
branch's binary then opened it with `library libraries`, which migrates.

| | At 30 | At 31 |
|---|---|---|
| members, editions, works | 7, 7, 7 | 7, 7, 7 |
| `member_root` rows, series | 7, 5 | 7, 5 |
| members holding a format | 0 of 7 | no column |
| `PRAGMA integrity_check` | ok | ok |
| `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` | empty | empty |
| `structure_version.n` | 56 | 56 |

Every member's other nine values, and every `edition`, `work` and
`member_root` row, read back identical, and the open wrote a
`-before-v31` backup. The walk's own tokens stood beside them: `scan_entry`
held `zip` for the six archives and `dir` for the seven directories.

**A rescan and derive after the migration rewrote no work.** The counter
stayed at 56 and every row read back identical, as it had for a rescan with
main's binary before the migration. A derive takes the write path for a work
`derive::unchanged` does not hold, and the counter moves when it does: on a
copy of the migrated store, one member's page count raised by one moved it to
57, and the next scan rewrote that work, its page count back as the file
has it, and left the counter at 68. So every work took the `unchanged`
path that no longer reads the column.

`find /home/davey/temp/manga-test -newer` a marker stamped before the copy
printed nothing after the last scan. The copied files were deleted; the
stores and logs are kept locally under
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-20-o69-drop/evidence/real/`.

## O396: a digest taken behind the listing (2026-11-20)

`Reading::one` now asks `fingerprints::recorded_digest` for the digest a
unit's entry holds before it decides to hash a unit listed with none. The
pass and store tests were each watched failing against their own defect:

- `a_digest_the_derive_takes_while_the_pass_waits_is_not_taken_again`, on
  `main`'s code: the pass hashed all three volumes again, and with the count
  asserted first the job counted `(6, 6)`. With the fix in place and the read
  replaced by `None`, it hashed all three again.
- `a_recorded_digest_is_answered_only_while_the_entry_is_unchanged`, with
  `size = ?3` made `(size = ?3 OR 1)`: the entry whose size moved answered
  `Some("other bytes")`; with the same done to `mtime = ?4`, the entry whose
  mtime moved did. The bindings were kept, so each failure is the
  assertion's and not a parameter count's.
- The same test, with `rel_path = ?2` made `(rel_path = ?2 OR 1)`: its
  first version failed only because the entries' order put one holding no
  digest first, and with `root_id = ?1` made `(root_id = ?1 OR 1)` it
  passed, the store holding one directory. One entry is now given a stamp
  no other has, and a unit naming another path, then another directory,
  with that stamp must answer none. With each condition broken, that unit
  answered `Some("held here")`.

The control, `a_digest_the_derive_took_before_the_listing_is_not_taken_again`,
passes on `main` and with the fix. It is kept because no other pass test
asserts that a unit listed with its digest is not hashed.

## O414: a sweep with no verdict exits non-zero (2026-11-20)

`scripts/mutants.sh` read `cargo mutants`' exit status only where
`missed.txt` was absent. Each case below but the last leaves one, empty,
which the old scripts read as `mutants-baseline: no survivor outside the
baseline` and exit 0. Measured with cargo-mutants 27.1.0; each case names
what it swept, and says so where an output was made by hand:

- **An unmutated baseline that fails.** Sweeping
  `crates/taiyaku-core/src/route.rs` with `--file`, a `RUSTC_WRAPPER` that
  passes rustc's probes through and refuses every compilation fails the
  baseline's build, as O414's run with no sccache server did. `cargo
  mutants` exits 4, and its `outcomes.json` holds the baseline alone,
  `"summary": "Failure"`, with `total_mutants` 0. The script's last lines
  included, in order,

  ```text
  ERROR cargo build failed in an unmutated tree, so no mutants were tested
  mutants-baseline: 0 survivor(s) this run; docs/mutants-baseline.md holds 35 accepted and 90 untriaged
  mutants-baseline: no survivor outside the baseline
  ```

  and it exited 0. Now its last lines are

  ```text
  ERROR cargo build failed in an unmutated tree, so no mutants were tested
  error: the unmutated baseline failed, so no mutant was tested and this run has no verdict.
         cargo mutants exited 4. Its log is target/mutants.out/log/baseline.log.
  ```

  and it exits 4.
- **An unmutated baseline that fails in its tests**, which is how a flaky
  test shows itself to a sweep. A sweep of O396's fix on 2026-11-20 failed
  its baseline on
  `lease::tests::a_waiting_lease_returns_only_once_the_holder_drops_and_says_it_waits`
  and logged `ERROR cargo test failed in an unmutated tree, so no mutants were
  tested`, then `no survivor outside the baseline`, which the old script
  follows with exit 0 (`.superpowers/sdd/o396-double-hash-evidence/mutants-1.log`).
  Put in on purpose on the `route.rs` sweep with `RUST_TEST_THREADS=0`,
  which libtest refuses, the same failure reads
  `FAILED   Unmutated baseline in 4s build + 0s test`, `cargo mutants` exits
  4, and the script now prints the two lines above and
  exits 4.
- **A scope with no mutant in it**: a `--file` naming no file
  (`crates/taiyaku-core/src/no-such-file.rs`), and a shard left empty
  (`route.rs` with `--shard 29/30`), which `mutants.yml`'s matrix would
  produce only for a crate with very few mutants. `cargo mutants` prints
  `Found 0 mutants to test` and `No mutants found under the active filters`,
  writes the second to
  `mutants.out/debug.log` as a `WARN cargo_mutants::lab:` line, exits 0 and
  writes no `outcomes.json`. That is an honest answer, so by the owner's
  ruling of 2026-11-20 `mutants-baseline.mjs` reports `no mutant in scope`
  and both sweeps exit 0. It takes that from cargo-mutants' own line alone:
  handed the same output with `debug.log` removed, with that line replaced,
  or with the phrase on a line that is not that `WARN`, each made by hand,
  it exits 2.
- **A run whose every mutant fails to build** was not produced by a sweep:
  `mutants-baseline.mjs` was handed an `outcomes.json` written for it, a
  passing baseline and two mutants, both unviable. It exits 2.
- **A `--since` diff that holds no mutant**, as on a branch that changes
  only docs, web code or tests. In 27.1.0's source (`main.rs`,
  `in_diff.rs`) the `--in-diff` filter then logs `Diff changes no Rust
  source files` or `No mutants to filter` and exits 0 before it makes an
  output directory, so the old scripts read whatever an earlier run had left
  in `target/mutants.out` as this run's. A review reproduced that with the
  real binary on a scratch crate, the earlier run's output being a copy of a
  `route.rs` sweep's: `no survivor outside the baseline` and exit 0, and with
  `--baseline` a rewritten baseline file. The script now proves the
  directory is this run's, by a marker left in an earlier one, which goes
  with it when cargo-mutants moves it aside, and keeps cargo-mutants' console
  in a file of the run's own under `target/`. With one of those lines the
  run is `no mutant in scope` with exit 0, with neither it exits 2, and
  `--baseline` writes nothing. On this branch, whose diff against `main`
  changes only docs and scripts, `--since main` with the `route.rs` run of
  2026-11-20 still in `target/mutants.out` logged ` INFO Diff changes no
  Rust source files`. `main`'s scripts then printed
  `mutants-baseline: 2 survivor(s) this run` and `no survivor outside the
  baseline` and exited 0, and the new
  one prints `no mutant in scope` and exits 0. In a clone whose only Rust
  change is two lines added to `crates/taiyaku-core/src/route/tests.rs`,
  with no earlier output, cargo-mutants logged ` INFO No mutants to filter`;
  `main`'s script exited 1 on the missing `missed.txt`, and the new one
  exits 0 with `no mutant in scope`. With `--baseline`, a copy of a
  `route.rs` run's output and a baseline lacking one of that run's two
  survivors, `main`'s scripts wrote the survivor back with the placeholder
  reason and exited 1, and the new one leaves the file byte-identical and
  exits 0. With `CARGO_TERM_COLOR=always` or `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1` set,
  cargo-mutants wraps `INFO` in colour codes, so the script runs it with
  `NO_COLOR=1`; the docs-only `--since` run then still reads `no mutant in
  scope` and exits 0, in a clone of this branch. A run that makes no output
  and prints none of those lines exits 2, which was checked against a
  stand-in for `cargo` only.

The old `mutants-baseline.mjs`, handed the outputs of the failed build, the
empty scope and the hand-made unviable run, exits 0 with
`no survivor outside the baseline` each time, and its `--write` on the failed
baseline's output exits 0 having written the baseline file (a copy here).
Now `--write` exits 2 before it writes.

**A run with a verdict reads as it did.** The same file swept with a working
compiler gave 21 mutants: 12 caught, 7 unviable and 2 missed, both already in
the baseline. `cargo mutants` exited 2, and the script reported both as
known and exited 0. With one of the two taken out of a copy of the baseline,
`mutants-baseline.mjs` named it as the survivor outside the baseline and
exited 1.

The script takes 0, 2 (survivors) and 3 (timeouts) as a verdict from
cargo-mutants' documentation of its exit codes. These runs saw 0, 2 and 4
from 27.1.0, and not 3.

## O399: the serve tests' first answer in one crowded process (2026-11-21)

`scripts/mutants.sh` runs its unmutated baseline as plain `cargo test` at
niceness 19, so one process runs a crate's tests on thirty-two threads here.
Three `taiyaku-serve` tests that wait for `serve`'s first answer failed
there: nextest, which CI's test job and `check-all.sh` use, gives each test
a process of its own. The failing configuration below is
`nice -n 19 cargo test -p taiyaku-serve --lib --all-features` with no thread
count set. The logs named are kept locally under
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-o399/evidence/`.

- **The red, on `main` at `edbc19b4`** (`red-1-main-edbc19b4.log`, at a
  load of 72): 1500 passed, and `serve_binds_the_address_and_answers_on_it`,
  `serve_serves_the_web_app_it_is_given` and
  `serve_caches_covers_and_tiles_under_the_resolved_root` failed.
- **The cause.** Each of the three builds its fixture library,
  `test_support::library()`, inside the task it spawns, before that task
  calls `serve`, so the build fell inside the poll's window: 100 polls 20 ms
  apart, about two seconds. A patch that timed each step, reverted before the
  fix (`measure-instrumentation.patch`), ran four times in the failing
  configuration, at loads between 27 and 71 (`measure-failing-1.txt` to
  `measure-failing-4.txt`). The build took 2.0 to 3.1 s, of which 1.28 to
  1.84 s was spent runnable and waiting for a CPU, as
  `/proc/thread-self/schedstat` counts it, and the three answered after 89 to
  146 polls, at least one of them past 100 in each run. `serve` took at most
  2.6 ms from its entry to its bind. Run on their own and not niced, at a load
  of about 40, the same builds took 0.41 s with under 10 ms of waiting
  (`measure-idle-alone.txt`).
  `serve_marks_a_scan_cut_during_its_derive_interrupted_before_it_listens`
  polls the same way but builds its library before the spawn, and answered
  at the second poll in every run, which is why it never failed.
- **The fix**, in `crates/taiyaku-serve/src/tests.rs` alone. The four tests
  that wait for a first answer poll through one helper, `first_answer`, until
  `SERVE_ANSWERS_WITHIN`, 30 s, and still stop at the first answer. The
  helper gives up at once when `serve` has ended or answers with an error
  status, and each request is bounded by the time left.
  `serve_caches_covers_and_tiles_under_the_resolved_root` gives up before its
  cover and tile requests, which carry no deadline.
- **Green.** The failing configuration passed all 1503 tests seven times
  (`green-*.log`): six before the change that makes an error status fail at
  once, at loads from 21 to 72, and once after it, on the code as it merges,
  from a load of 17.
- **Watched failing**, each put in by hand and run alone under nextest. After
  that change (`mut-r1-*.log`): a `serve` that never binds and never
  ends, and one that binds and never answers, failed all four tests at the
  30 s deadline, each with its own message; one that ends before its bind,
  and one whose every route answers 500, failed all four within 0.1 s, the
  second with `serve answered, but not with a success: http status: 500`.
  Before it (`mut-a*.log`, `mut-b-*.log`, `mut-c-*.log`,
  `mut-m6-*.log`), each answer assertion inverted failed its test, and
  `get_thumb` caching in `cache_dir` rather than `thumbs` failed
  `serve_caches_covers_and_tiles_under_the_resolved_root` and none of the
  other three. With a `serve` that binds and never answers and the
  per-request bound taken out of
  `serve_binds_the_address_and_answers_on_it`, that test hung until nextest
  killed it at 100 s, which is what the bound is for.
- **The sweep.** `scripts/mutants.sh --since main` made no mutant, the
  branch having changed test code alone, so it ran no baseline
  (`mutants-since-main.log`). `scripts/mutants.sh --file
  crates/taiyaku-serve/src/web.rs`, the file whose code
  `serve_serves_the_web_app_it_is_given` drives, run with no
  `RUST_TEST_THREADS` set, passed its unmutated baseline, one `cargo test`
  of `taiyaku-serve` at niceness 19 on thirty-two threads: 1503 passed, at
  loads of 55 to 67 over the last minute and a half of its test run
  (`mutants-web.log`, `mutants-web-out/log/baseline.log`,
  `mutants-web-load.txt`). It caught all six mutants. In those six runs, up
  to four at once at loads up to 131, the four first-answer tests failed only
  where the mutant broke the web app: `serve_serves_the_web_app_it_is_given`
  failed on a 404 with `is_api` as `true`, and on an empty body with
  `Web::answer` as `Default::default()`.

## O416 to O428: the UI fixes (2026-11-21)

The owner's asks of 2026-11-19, the owner's rulings, the pre-flight against
closed rulings and the plan are in `.superpowers/sdd/`
(`2026-11-19-ui-fixes-followup-handoff.md` and `2026-11-20-ui-fixes/`),
which is not committed. The rows in `docs/status.md` say what each fix
does; this section holds what they point to.

**How the way back knows an entry of this app comes before.** react-router
8.3.0's `BrowserRouter` (`lib/dom/lib.js`) keeps its history with
`createBrowserHistory`, whose `getUrlBasedHistory`
(`lib/router/history.js`) writes `{ usr, key, idx }` into
`window.history.state` (`getHistoryState`). `idx` is written as 0 by a
`replaceState` when the app loads on an entry whose state holds none, as a
fresh visit's does; a push writes the current index plus one, and a replace
keeps it. The browser keeps `history.state` with its entry, through a
reload too, so `idx` above 0 says this entry was pushed by this app in this
tab, on top of one of its own, and that is what `back.ts`'s `useBack` reads
to choose a step back over a push of the last Library view. The button's
word comes from a record `back.ts` keeps in memory, the address each entry
was pushed from, so a reload loses it and the button reads "Back" while it
still steps back.

**O418: where a press on blank space landed, before the change.** On the
code as it was, in the browser project's two launches (scrollbars hidden,
and scrollbars shown), with the panel opened by a real hover and a real
click on `i`, one real mouse press each through CDP
(`web/tests/support/mouse.ts`), the element at the point read first. Both
launches gave the same outcome for every press.

| Press | Window, volumes | Element at the point | Panel after the press |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main`'s blank area below a short grid | 1440×900, 3 | `main` | kept open |
| beside the grid, right of the last tile, inside the list | 1440×900, 3 | `ul.volumes` | closed |
| `main`'s right padding beside the grid | 1440×900, 3 | `main` | kept open |
| `main`'s left padding beside the grid | 1440×900, 3 | `main` | kept open |
| the page heading | 1440×900, 3 | `h1` | closed |
| the sidebar column | 1440×900, 3 | `div.sidebar-column` | closed |
| below a one-volume grid | 390×844, 1 | `div.library` | closed |
| the window's foot, scrolled to the end | 390×844, 3 | `main` | kept open |
| `main`'s left padding | 390×844, 3 | `main` | kept open |
| the room under the last tile's panel, scrolled to the end | 390×844, 6 | `html` (the root) | kept open |
| the room under the last tile's panel, scrolled to the end | 1280×600, 18 | `main` | kept open |

With scrollbars shown, a press on the document's scrollbar at 390 px
reached the page as a `pointerdown` whose target was the root, where
`elementFromPoint` answers null, and a press on `main`'s scrollbar as a
`pointerdown` on `main`. A scrollbar and the blank space beside it share a
target, so only the point tells them apart, and the point is what
`Series.tsx`'s `onScrollbarOf` reads.

Slots count from 0 and pages from 1, so slot 4 is page 5.

**More at 0 (O424).** C3's build drew the open count even at 0, on the
