## O348: the glide-after-a-scroll case's second change, mid-glide (2026-11-21)

`reseat.browser.test.tsx`'s "starts where drawn after a scroll while the
covers glide, then the next change" failed run alone with `-t` and passed
with the rest of its file. Its premise is that the second change finds
covers still gliding. Between its two changes came `frames(2)` and then
`await userEvent.wheel(…)`. The readings below came from a temporary
`console.error`, not committed; the logs are kept locally under
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/o348/`.

- **The cause: the wheel, not the frames.** The wheel is a round trip
  through the Vitest server and Playwright, and in ten readings it took 84
  to 296 ms against the glide's 180 ms (`RESEAT_MS`) (`instr*.log`). Run
  alone it took 134 to 296 ms, and the case failed four times of four,
  finding no cover gliding; with the rest of the file it took 84 to 118 ms,
  and the case passed four times of four. In eight of the ten readings no
  frame came late.
- **The passing runs tested nothing mid-glide.** Where the case passed, its
  second change came 150 to 183 ms into the glide, with the covers 0.08 to
  1.05 px from rest in the three readings that recorded it. With a second
  change's start made to ignore the glide it interrupts (`jumped`'s `moveOf`
  given no running glide), the unfixed case still passed with the rest of
  its file, while the DRIVES block's four interruption cases failed
  (`mut-under-unfixed-file-1.log`).
- **The fix**, in `web/tests/reseat.browser.test.tsx` alone. The case calls
  `scrollerOf(host).scrollBy(0, 400)` two frames into the glide, which
  reaches the same `scroll` listener in `reseat.ts` as the wheel did. Its
  second change now comes 66.7 ms (four frames) into the glide, with the
  farthest interrupted cover still 125.19 px from the end of its glide
  (`add-N0-instr.log`). `startsOff` also returns `ahead`, what a cover's
  running glide still had to go when the new one starts, and the case's
  premise asks `underway`: some interrupted cover with more than 0.5 px to
  go. The block's other two cases still turn the wheel, through `wheeledTo`.
- **Watched failing.** `underway` failed while `interrupted` held, with the
  second change made six or seven frames later (166.6 ms in, with at most
  0.0845 px to go, and 183.3 ms in, with none) and with the old wheel put
  back, twice (`add-L6-*`, `add-L7-*`, `add-W1-*` and `add-W2-*`); the case
  before the check would have passed all four. With `jumped`'s `moveOf`
  given no running glide, cover 5 started 125.25 px from where it was drawn,
  and with the page's scroll listener removed, 400 px (`add-M1-*` and
  `add-M2-*`).
- **Green.** On the branches' first base, the case alone with `-t` passed
  three runs of three and the whole file 32 of 32 (`add-final-*.log`). On
  `main` after #288, which changed code the file imports, the whole file
  passed 32 of 32 twice and the case alone with `-t` twice, at loads from
  25 to 30; the rebase since, past #290 and #289, changed no code
  (`reseat-*.log` and `reseat-loads.txt` in
  `.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/logs/`).

## O413: book search's bounds count processor time (2026-11-21)

`bookSearch.test.ts`'s "searches a large book quickly" bounds the median of
three searches at 100 ms, and "searches a large book quickly the first time,
before any block is folded" bounds one search over blocks not yet folded at
300 ms. Both timed the search with `performance.now()`. The readings below
printed the processor time the search's thread spent
(`process.threadCpuUsage`) beside the time on the clock; the logs are kept
locally under `.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/o413/logs/`.

- **The cause: waiting counted as work.** In a run of the web tests under
  coverage, as the gate runs them, at a load of about 94, both bounds
  failed, at 108.6 ms against 100 and 373.9 ms against 300, and the cold
  search's thread had spent 207.2 ms of processor time
  (`v3-base-fullcov-0.log`). Pinned to one CPU with 0, 3 and 7 busy loops
  beside it, two runs each, the cold search took 261 to 408, 863 to 872 and
  1766 to 1825 ms on the clock, and 207 to 220 ms of processor time
  throughout (`pinned-prototype.log`).
- **The fix**, in `web/tests/bookSearch.test.ts` alone, on the owner's
  ruling of 2026-11-21. A helper, `onCpu`, returns what a call returns and
  the processor time, user and system, its thread spent on it, and the two
  tests bound that, with the same 100 ms and 300 ms. A thread's processor
  time cannot exceed the time on the clock by more than the kernel's
  accounting step, under 1 ms here (`cpuwall.log`), so outside that step of
  a bound the change can only remove failures. Two runs of the web tests
  under coverage passed 5766 of 5766, with the lock taken at loads of 25 and
  34 (`v4-proto-fullcov-*.log`).
- **What the bounds still catch**, each regression put in by hand and run
  under coverage (`pm-*-cov.log`): the cache dropped fails the warm bound at
  112.31 ms; `fold`'s ASCII path removed fails the cold at 872.076; the
  cache kept in an array searched linearly fails both, at 305.277 and
  1079.372; and `fold`'s offsets rebuilt per character fail the cold at
  472.453. Without coverage only the second and the fourth fail a bound, at
  468.067 and 312.222 (`pm-*-nocov.log`). The file's test that counts
  `normalize` calls fails on the first two in both modes. Each block's index
  found by `indexOf` passes every test with the change.
- **Not free of the machine's state.** The same cold search under coverage
  took 103.4 and 110.0 ms of processor time run alone at a load of about 9
  (`q-proto-cov-*.log`), 177.5 and 197.2 ms alone at about 87
  (`m-base-cov-*.log`), and 207 to 220 ms pinned. Pinned, the warm test's
  first search, which no bound checks, makes the same first fold and search
  of 9,000 blocks, and took up to 231.4 ms (`pinned-prototype.log`), which
  leaves the 300 ms bound 1.30 times over it. What moves processor time with
  the load was not isolated.

## O429: the waiting-lease test, starved (2026-11-21)

`lease::tests::a_waiting_lease_returns_only_once_the_holder_drops_and_says_it_waits`
failed the unmutated baseline of O396's first sweep on 2026-11-20, at its
assertion that a wait of over a second calls back at least once. The holder
dropped the lease 1.5 s after spawning the waiter, by the test thread's
clock. The readings below came from a temporary patch that timed each step
(`measure-instrumentation.patch`, not committed); the logs are kept locally
under `.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/o429/logs/`. "Starved" is
the one test pinned to one CPU at niceness 19 beside three busy loops at
niceness 0, which starves its threads without loading the rest of the
machine.

- **How `Wait::Yes` calls back.** `lease::take_file` gives the lock
  connection a busy timeout of one `SLICE`, 1000 ms, and calls back on each
  busy answer to `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`. SQLite's default busy handler,
  `sqliteDefaultBusyCallback`, gives up once the sleeps it has asked for
  add up to that timeout and reads no clock, so a thread that wakes late
  from each sleep stretches the slice.
- **The cause, measured starved.** In seven instrumented runs the waiter
  reached its first `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` 0.38 to 0.66 s after the spawn, nearly
  all of it runnable and waiting for the CPU, as
  `/proc/thread-self/schedstat` counts it. In the four runs of the old test
  the drop came 1.54 to 1.64 s after the spawn with no callback before it,
  so each would have failed at the sweep's assertion
  (`pinned-3hog-nice19.trace`). In the three of the fixed test the first
  slice took 1.16 to 1.36 s, and the first callback came 1.64 to 1.80 s
  after the spawn (`pinned-3hog-nice19-fixinstr.trace`). Uninstrumented, the
  old test failed there three runs of three, at that assertion
  (`pinned-3hog-nice19-old.log`). In the sweep's own configuration,
  `nice -n 19` and all of the package's tests in one process on thirty-two
  threads, the old test passed three runs of three at loads from 29 to 77
  (`old-loaded-*.log`), so whether the sweep's red had the same two parts is
  not measured.
- **The fix**, in `crates/taiyaku-library/src/lease/tests.rs` alone. The
  waiter's callback sends on a channel, and the holder lets go once it has
  had two callbacks, under one deadline, `CALLS_BACK_WITHIN`, 30 s: a waiter
  that never calls back fails at the deadline, and one whose thread ends
  before its second callback fails with "the waiter returned before the
  holder let go". It waits for the second callback, not the first, so that a
  waiter returning right after its first callback ends the channel rather
  than racing the drop. The waiter runs in a scoped thread and hands its
  lease back, and once the holder has let go, a third connection asking with
  `Wait::No` must be refused while that lease lives and given the lease once
  it drops. The holder keeps the time waited that each callback carries, and
  the test asks that the first be at least `SLICE` and the second at least a
  `SLICE` more. These are lower bounds only: SQLite's busy handler gives up
  only once its sleeps add up to the slice, and no sleep ends early, so a
  slow machine can only raise them.
- **Green**, on the branch's first base. Starved, three runs of three, each
  taking 21.9 to 23.3 s (`v2-pinned-3hog-nice19-restored.log`). In the
  sweep's configuration,
  `nice -n 19 cargo test -p taiyaku-library --lib --all-features`, 1765
  passed in 205.4 s (`v2-fix-cargo-2.log`). With the checks on the time
  waited, on `main` after #288 (the rebase since, past #290 and #289,
  changed no code), the test passed three runs of three alone and three
  starved (`fix2-green-[123].log` and
  `fix2-pinned-3hog-nice19.log`).
- **Watched failing**, each put into `take_file` by hand and the test run
  alone with `--exact` (`v2-mut-*.log`). A `Wait::Yes` that never calls back
  failed at the 30 s deadline. One that returns a lease holding no lock
  after its first callback, or at its first busy answer without calling
  back, failed at 1.06 s with "the waiter returned before the holder let
  go". One that does so right after its second callback returns as the
  holder lets go, which the time check cannot see, and failed at 2.06 s with
  "the lease a waiter is given holds the lock: a third asker is refused". On
  `main` after #288, a waiter's lease that never lets the lock go, its
  connection leaked with `std::mem::forget`, failed with "a third
  asker is given the lease once the waiter's drops", and passed with
  `lease.rs` restored (`mut-m3-*` in
  `.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/logs/`). With the checks on the
  time waited, on that base (`fix2-mut-*.log`), the five above still failed
  with the same messages, and a `Wait::Yes` that calls back with no time
  waited failed at 2.06 s, and one given `TRY` as its busy timeout, so that
  it calls back after each 100 ms, at 0.26 s, both at the first callback's
  check. No check bounds the time waited from above, by design, since a
  starved waiter's slices have no bound, so a `Wait::Yes` that calls back
  after slices longer than `SLICE` goes uncaught unless two of them outlast
  the 30 s deadline.
- **The sweep.** `scripts/mutants.sh --since main` makes no mutant of a
  change to test code alone, so
  `scripts/mutants.sh --file crates/taiyaku-library/src/lease.rs` was run
  with no `RUST_TEST_THREADS`, on `main` after #288. Its
  unmutated baseline, one `cargo test` of `taiyaku-library` at niceness 19
  on thirty-two threads, passed, 1767 passed and 6 ignored, from a load of
  31 when the sweep took its lock (`sweep-lease.log` and `sweep-lease.exit`
  in `.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/logs/`). The waiting-lease
  test failed only under the five mutants that break the file lease. Of the
  33 mutants, 14 were missed, none of them in the baseline;
  `mutants-baseline.md`'s row lists them, untriaged by that run. "lease.rs's
  survivors triaged (2026-11-21)" below triages them.

## O436: a lease on a lock file SQLite reads as read-only (2026-11-21)

Found while triaging the survivors of O429's sweep of `lease.rs` (the next
section). `take_file`'s busy guard forced to `true` had survived, and the
search for an error other than busy that `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` could meet once
`initialise` had read the lock file found a file it does not refuse at all.
The readings are in `triage-mutants.log` in
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/logs/`.

- **The cause, read in the `sqlite3.c` of SQLite 3.54.1**, as
  `libsqlite3-sys` 0.40.0 bundles it. `lockBtree`, which reads the header,
  marks a database read-only when the header's write version, byte 18, is
  above 2. `sqlite3_db_readonly`, which `take_file`'s `is_readonly` calls
  straight after the open, reports that mark, which is not yet set, so it
  answers writable. `initialise` then reads `user_version`, which reads the
  header and sets the mark, and `sqlite3BeginTransaction` compiles
  `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on a database marked read-only as a read transaction
  (`eTxnType = 0`), which takes a shared lock and answers OK. SQLite writes
  1 at byte 18 (`newDatabase`), or 2 for WAL (`sqlite3BtreeSetVersion`), so
  it takes a damaged file.
- **Measured** with a temporary test, not committed, at a load of 15.62.
  With byte 18 of an initialised lock file set to 3, this process was given
  the lease, another process (`another_process_is_given`) was given it while
  the first still held it, and `derive_running` from a second library read
  `false`. With the header untouched, the other process was refused and
  `derive_running` read `true`. With `user_version` 0 as well, the take
  failed at `initialise`'s write: "attempt to write a readonly database".
- **The fix.** Once `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` answers, `take_file` asks
  `Connection::transaction_state(Some(MAIN_DB))`, rusqlite 0.43's wrapper of
  `sqlite3_txn_state`, which no Cargo feature gates, and refuses with an
  error naming the file unless the answer is `Write`. Chosen over asking
  `is_readonly` again after `initialise` because it checks what the lease
  needs, a write lock, whatever led to a read transaction, where asking again
  would close only the route this one took. The check before `initialise`
  stays, because its error names the usual cause, a file this process cannot
  write, and its fix.
- **Red, green and red again.**
  `lease::tests::a_lock_file_whose_header_sqlite_reads_as_read_only_is_refused_naming_it`
  sets byte 18 to 3 in an initialised lock file and asks for the error. On
  the old `take_file` it failed, given the lease (`left: Ok(true)`), at a
  load of 21.74; with the fix it passed, at 20.39; with `lease.rs` put back
  by hand to the commit before the fix it failed again with `Ok(true)`, at
  17.93, and with the fix restored `lease::tests` gave 12 passed and 2
  ignored. The test also asks that `derive_running` read `false` after the
  refusal: with `take_file`'s `flag.store` moved above the check, it failed
  there, at a load of 25.02 (`fixw2-mut-B-*`, its load in
  `fixw2-loads.txt`).

## lease.rs's survivors triaged (2026-11-21)

The 14 mutants O429's sweep missed (`mutants-baseline.md`, its row of
2026-11-21; the list is kept as `sweep-lease-missed.txt` in
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-21-timing-tests/logs/`), triaged against
`lease.rs` with O436's fix, which moved three of them 16 lines down:
`take_file`'s busy guard from 180:23 to 196:23, `initialise`'s from 214:19
to 230:19, and `held_elsewhere`'s `|` from 229:43 to 245:43. Five new tests
in `lease/tests.rs` kill nine, and five are baselined: three equivalent, two
printed only for a person. Each test failed with its mutant put into
`lease.rs` by hand and the test run alone with `--exact`, at loads from
24.73 to 33.73, and passed with `lease.rs` restored (`triage-mutants.log`
in the same directory).

- **`take_flag`, the in-memory library's lease (six).** An in-memory library
  stands in for a file-backed one in tests across the workspace, and nothing
  tested how long its `Wait::No` tries, or its `Wait::Yes` at all.
  `an_in_memory_lease_asked_not_to_wait_is_refused_only_after_its_try` times
  a `Wait::No` against a held lease and asks for at least `TRY`: with
  `Wait::No`'s guard forced `true` it was refused in 461 ns, and with `>=`
  as `<` in 1.042 µs.
  `an_in_memory_waiting_lease_returns_only_once_the_holder_drops_and_says_it_waits`
  holds the lease until the waiter's second callback and asks that the first
  say at least `SLICE` and the second at least two. Not "a slice more", as
  the file-backed test asks: this waiter calls back on a schedule of slices
  counted from its start, so a late first callback leaves less than a slice
  before the second. With `Wait::Yes`'s guard forced `true` the first
  callback said 401 ns, and with `>=` as `<` 882 ns, both failing the first
  check; forced `false`, the waiter never called back and the test failed at
  the 30 s deadline; with `+=` as `-=` the waiter panicked in `Duration`'s
  subtraction after its second callback, and the test failed joining it.
  Its waiter fails itself if it calls back a second time after the holder
  has let go, so a flag that never clears fails the test rather than leaving
  it waiting for good: with `FlagGuard`'s drop made `()` it failed in
  4.10 s with "a waiter is given the lease once the holder lets go", and the
  four above failed as before, at loads from 33.10 to 56.41. The second
  sweep, below, ran without that guard. It also asks that the waiter return
  no earlier than the holder let go, comparing the two instants and not the
  time between them, and that a `Wait::No` be refused while the waiter's
  lease lives. With `take_flag` handing out a lease that takes no flag
  right after its second callback, which the review of this PR found the
  test passing, it failed at the first of those twice, and with that check
  taken out, at the second, each in 2.06 s at loads from 25.37 to 25.84
  (`fixw2-mut-A-*`, the loads in `fixw2-loads.txt`, from the fixer's
  transcript).
- **`take_file`'s busy guard forced `true` (196:23).**
  `a_lock_file_damaged_while_a_derive_waits_for_it_ends_the_wait_with_its_error`
  waits with `Wait::Yes` on a held lease, zeroes the lock file's first 100
  bytes at the first callback, and asks for the error the next
  `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` meets, "file is not a database". Under the mutant that
  error read as another holder's and the waiter called back a second time,
  which the callback fails on; unchecked, it would call back for good.
- **`initialise`'s guard forced `false` (230:19).**
  `a_lock_file_held_before_an_asker_could_initialise_it_refuses_the_asker`
  holds a new lock file with a plain connection's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so an
  asker reads it uninitialised and its write is answered busy, as when two
  derives open a new lock file at once. Unmutated, the asker is refused and
  then given the lease once the hold drops; in the probe the refusal took
  205 ms. Under the mutant it failed with "initialising the derive lock file
  …: database is locked".
- **`initialise`'s guard forced `true` (230:19).**
  `a_lock_file_sqlite_will_not_initialise_is_refused_with_sqlites_error`
  gives an uninitialised lock file the header O436's test gives, so
  `initialise`'s write fails with "attempt to write a readonly database".
  Under the mutant that error was passed over and the hold refused the file
  with O436's error instead. On this file O436's check leaves the mutant
  giving no lease; on a new file whose first write failed for another
  reason, the hold would begin on a file with no page, and a hold there
  writes one: the probe's plain hold on a new lock file left a journal.
- **Baselined (five).** `|` as `^` between open flags, twice in
  `take_file` and once in `held_elsewhere`, is equivalent: the flags are
  0x2, 0x4 and 0x8000 in `sqlite3.h`, and bitflags 2.13.1's `|` and `^`
  are the or and the exclusive or of the bits (`public.rs`), which agree on
  bits that do not overlap. The two `Debug` bodies print only for a person:
  with both impls deleted, `cargo check --workspace --all-targets
  --all-features` checked every target and warned only that the two types
  lack `Debug`, so nothing in the workspace formats either.
- **The second sweep** (`sweep-lease-2.log`, its lists and the log below
  in `sweep-lease-2-out/`), of the tree with the five tests but not the
  in-memory test's guard, was started at a load of 13.27, read just before
  it started (`sweep-lease-loads.txt`, from the triage's transcript). Its
  unmutated baseline passed. Of 34 mutants, one more than O429's run, the
  new one
  O436's check's `!=` as `==`, 24 were caught, 4 unviable, 4 missed and 2
  timed out, and it ended "no survivor outside the baseline", exit 0. The
  fifth entry, `142:13`'s `|` as `^`, was reported caught, which is false,
  the mutant being equivalent: under it
  `schema::tests::opens_arriving_while_another_builds_a_fresh_database_all_succeed_and_take_no_backup`
  failed: its log has the builder's open `Ok(())` and the three others
  "starting the transaction for schema version 1: database is locked", and
  the package's other tests passing, 1772 with 6 ignored. The loads read
  from eight minutes in to the sweep's end ran from 84 to 134, from another

  closed: see "O437: the fresh-build race test, starved (2026-11-21)"
  below.)* `FlagGuard`'s drop as
  `()` timed out at 918 s, where O429's run caught it, because the

- **The third sweep** (`sweep-lease-3.log`, `sweep-lease-3-out/`), of the

## O437: the fresh-build race test, starved (2026-11-21)

`schema::tests::opens_arriving_while_another_builds_a_fresh_database_all_succeed_and_take_no_backup`
failed in the second sweep of `lease.rs` by the PR that closes O348, O413
and O429, three of its four opens answering "starting the transaction for
schema version 1: database is locked" ("lease.rs's survivors triaged
(2026-11-21)" above). The test held a builder, the open path itself, by an
update hook at the second version row of a fresh build, started three opens,
slept 500 ms and let the builder go. The timings below came from a
temporary patch that timed each step (`probes.patch`, not committed); the
logs are kept locally under `.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-22-o437/logs/`.
"Starved" is the test binary pinned with `taskset` to four CPUs at
`nice -n 19`, beside busy loops at niceness 0 pinned to the same four, with
`TMPDIR` on the NVMe disk (`o437-run.sh`).

- **How an open waits.** Each open's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` waits for the write
  lock until SQLite's busy handler, `sqliteDefaultBusyCallback` in the
  SQLite 3.54.1 that `libsqlite3-sys` 0.40.0 bundles, has scheduled sleeps
  adding up to `BUSY_TIMEOUT`, five seconds. It counts the sleeps it asks
  for and reads no clock, so on a starved thread the wait runs longer on the
  clock and still gives up at the same count. Read in the source, not timed.
- **The cause, measured.** Held at its second version row, the builder had
  the rest of the build to run after the release, inside that wait. With no
  busy loops, the test neither pinned nor niced, on tmpfs and on disk, that
  rest took 48.6 to 61.4 ms in twenty runs and every open succeeded
  (`step1-*.log`). Starved, it took 6.7 to 14.2 s beside eight busy loops
  and 12.1 to 15.8 s beside sixteen; every open gave up first, after 5.21 to
  6.32 s on the clock, and the test failed seven runs of seven, each with
  the sweep's message (`step3-test-nice19-hogs8.log` and `-hogs16.log`).
  Beside four loops one batch failed four runs of four and another passed
  three of three, the builder's rest taking 5.9 to 6.3 s in the first and
  0.7 to 2.8 s in the second; beside six, one run of six lost one open,
  which gave up 4.69 s after the release, 11 ms before the builder
  committed. Across the 104 instrumented runs, every open that succeeded did
  so after the builder's commit and every one that failed gave up before it,
  each of the 34 with plain `SQLITE_BUSY`, extended code 5.
- **Niceness, not load alone.** With the test at niceness 0 beside 4 to 64
  busy loops on the same four CPUs, four runs at each, the builder's rest
  took at most 1.3 s and no open failed (`step3-nice0-hogs*.log`); at
  niceness 10, 12 and 15 to 18 beside four loops, none of 21 runs failed.
  `scripts/mutants.sh` renices itself to 19, and with no
  `RUST_TEST_THREADS`, as in that sweep, one `cargo test` process runs a
  crate's tests on thirty-two threads here; the loads read from eight
  minutes into the sweep to its end ran from 84 to 134. That its red had
  this cause is inferred from its message and from which opens failed; its
  log holds no timing of the test's steps.
- **The fix, first part: the hold**, in
  `crates/taiyaku-library/src/schema/tests.rs` alone, as is the second. The
  builder is held at the last version row of its build. `apply_one` writes
  each version row after its migration's own work, so at the last one only
  the commit is left after the release. Every `meta` write the builder's
  open makes is a version row, so the hook holds the builder at its
  `SCHEMA_VERSION`-th, and after the scope the test asserts that the open
  wrote `meta` exactly `SCHEMA_VERSION` times, which fails the test if the
  open writes `meta` other than its version rows: a migration that wrote a
  `meta` row of its own would move the hold off the last version row, and
  the test then fails on that count rather than passing. A build made
  migration by migration has committed every version but the last at that
  row, so the opens still back up a part-built store.
- **The second part: the release.** The 500 ms sleep did not make every open
  read the version before the release. In one starved run beside sixteen
  loops, the third, an open started `Library::open` 2.9 ms after the release
  (`step3-test-nice19-hogs16.log`). Held at the second row, that open still
  raced the build; with only the commit left, such an open can find the
  build finished and pass however it was committed. Each open now runs
  `Library::from_connection` through `open_telling_its_begin`, on a
  connection whose statement trace (`trace_v2`) sends `true` when it first
  starts a statement beginning `BEGIN`, and `false` if the open ends without
  one. An open issues `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` only after reading a version below
  the build's, so the test thread releases the builder once all three opens
  have sent, and past a 10 s deadline releases it anyway and fails, naming
  how many opens reached their `BEGIN`. The sleep is gone. After its checks
  of the outcomes, the test asserts that every open reached its `BEGIN`.
- **Green**, on the test as this PR leaves it. Starved beside eight busy
  loops, the test as it stood before this PR failed three runs of three with
  the sweep's message (`fix-control-hogs8.log`), and the new one passed ten
  runs of ten, and ten of ten beside sixteen (`fixw1-load-hogs8.log`,
  `fixw1-load-hogs16.log`). With no busy loops, the test neither pinned nor
  niced, it passed twenty runs of twenty (`fixw1-unmutated.log`).
- **Watched failing**, each defect put in by hand and the test run alone.
  With the fresh build made migration by migration in
  `schema::apply_pending`, its one-transaction branch never taken, the test
  failed three runs of three with two opens whose backup of the part-built
  store "could not be taken" (`fixw1-defect-i.log`), as the test before this
  PR did (`fix-mut-a-original-test.log`). With the recheck of the version
  under the write lock removed there, it failed three runs of three with all
  three opens "applying schema version 1: table series already exists"
  (`fixw1-defect-ii.log`). With one `meta` write more in the build, it
  failed three runs of three on its count of them (`fixw1-meta-write.log`).
- **The pass the release closes.** With each open delayed 700 ms and the
  build made migration by migration, the test with the hold at the last row
  and still the 500 ms sleep passed three runs of three, its opens finding
  the build finished (`wait-vacuous-old-test.log`); the new test failed
  three runs of three, with two opens whose backup "could not be taken"
  (`fixw1-vacuous-700.log`). With its release moved ahead of the wait as
  well, the new test failed three runs of three at its check that every open
  reached its `BEGIN`, "only 0 of 3 opens reached their `BEGIN`", every open
  having succeeded (`fixw1-vacuous-release-early.log`).
- **What it no longer catches.** As this PR leaves it, this test no longer
  fails when `BUSY_TIMEOUT` is cut to 50 ms, and
  `tests::every_connection_carries_the_busy_timeout` and
  `tests::several_first_opens_of_one_fresh_library_at_once_all_succeed`
  still do (`final-busy50.log`).

## O417: the Continue row's `i` (2026-11-22)

O417's row and the sentences it adds to O274, O283, O288 and O406 in
`docs/status.md` say what the PR does. The pre-flight, the plan and the
ledger are under `.superpowers/sdd/` (`2026-11-22-o417/`), which is not
committed.

**Why the panel is not inside its card.** The row's list scrolls sideways,
and `overflow-x: auto` clips it downward as well; it is masked for its fade,
and a mask paints everything inside it, a fixed-position child included. So
the panel is a child of the row's section (`.continue > .tile-panel`), laid
under the row by `tilePanel.ts`'s `layUnderRow`, and it lies after the list
in the document, outside its card, where a volume's panel lies inside its
tile's `li`. What a series page has from that nesting, the row builds by
hand:

- **The closes.** `useVolumePanel`'s close effect asks whether a press or a
  focus lands inside the open tile or its panel (`inside`), so a press in
  the row's panel is not a press outside its card. On a series page, whose
  panel is inside its tile, the second half changes nothing.
- **Tab.** Drawn after the list, the panel would follow the row's last card:
  Tab from `i` would go on to the next card, and in `button` mode focus
  arriving there closes the panel. `Library.tsx`'s `tabAcross` joins them:
  from the card's last stop into the panel, from the panel's last stop on to
  the next card with a stop, and Shift+Tab back across each, from the panel
  itself too, where a Split or an Undo leaves focus. `i` names the panel in
  `aria-controls` while it is open, since its `aria-expanded` no longer sits
  beside what it expands.
- **The pointer.** A pointer crossing between the open card and its panel
  enters neither (`crossed`, read from `relatedTarget`), as a tile and the
  panel nested in it are one element to a series page's handlers.
- **Following.** A volume's panel moves with its tile by lying inside it.
  The row's is laid again by `follow` whenever its card moves: on the row's
  `scroll`; from a `ResizeObserver` on the card, the row and the section;
  from a `MutationObserver` on the row's `style`, which `useContinueRow`
  writes frame by frame through a slide; and in the commit that draws a new
  answer (`laidFor`). Each lays from the same three boxes outside React, so
  no frame renders and a frame's reads do not grow with the cards (O304). CI
  runs no browser project, so `Library.test.tsx` also reaches that wiring
  with a stubbed `ResizeObserver`, as `Series.test.tsx` reaches the series
  page's.
- **The laying.** `panelSpan` takes its tile to lie inside the page area, so
  `layUnderRow` holds the card's box to the area first. The row's gap is the
  list's own `column-gap`. The
  panel's top is the row's foot, below the room the row keeps under its
  cards and its own scrollbar there.
- **A panel that outlives its card.** On the home page a search hides the
  row and clearing it draws the same cards again, so a panel left open would
  come back with nobody having asked; `orphaned` closes it when its card can
  no longer draw it.

**What held the panel before it moved.** Before the panel's state left
`Series` for `volumePanel.ts`, Task 1 put each defect the plan named into
the unmoved `Series.tsx` by hand, with the case the plan's reading expected
to catch it, and ran the series page's suites. Most were caught by jsdom
cases. Two were caught only by the series page's browser suites, which CI
does not run: `on-select`'s pointer guard without its arm for focus in the
open panel, for which the reading had found no case, though "reveals the
volume under the pointer again once a press outside has closed the panel"
(`Series.onSelect.browser.test.tsx`) asserts it outright; and focus sent to
`main` after an Undo empties the volume pressed on, even where the person
had moved it elsewhere ("stays where the person moved it when an Undo
empties the volume pressed on", `Series.panel.browser.test.tsx`). Four were
caught by nothing, and `Series.test.tsx` gained a case for each, watched
failing against its defect:

- "stays on the open on-select panel’s tile when the pointer comes back to
  it while a move waits on the save out";
- "asks once for a volume whose detail cannot be read, and says why at each
  open";
- "watches and lays the panel drawn again when the layout goes to the table
  and back with it open";
- "closes on focus arriving outside once the mode an open on-select panel is
  in changes to button".

From then on the plan froze `Series.test.tsx`, the four
`Series.*.browser.test.tsx` suites and `tilePanel.test.tsx`, so a red case
there would be a defect in the move, and the branch leaves them as Task 1
left them. Task 2 put those six defects and others into the moved code, and
each failed its case again.

**What the browser runs found that reading had not.**

- **The gutter moved with the row.** The pre-flight's settled point on the
  gutter kept a home page's while the row is drawn and `panel` is not `off`.
  In the browser project's launch with scrollbars hidden,
  `scrollbar-gutter: stable` still reserves a classic scrollbar's width
  though the scrollbar takes none there, and existing cases of the row's
  glides and sizes, of View and of `reseat` went red. One of them was a
  shift a person sees where scrollbars are classic and the page does not
  scroll: "moves nothing above the Continue heading" failed because the
  gutter came and went with the row, so the page area narrowed when a read
  drew the row, against the cover-size spec's constraint that nothing above
  the Continue heading moves. The gutter is keyed to the Library page's head
  instead (`div.page-head[data-panel]`), which is drawn searching or not. A
  Library page with no Continue row then keeps it as well, so cases of the
  home grid that are not about the panel, in `reseat`, `Cover` and
  `coverLayout`, draw it with Panel off, and the row's own cases whose
  fixtures it moved take a window widened by the gutter.
- **A card half past the row's end** has its `i` clipped by the row, so no
  pointer reaches it until the row is scrolled; the case that lays a panel
  from such a card opens it with a scripted click on `i`.
- **A press on a grid tile in `button` mode** moves focus to the tile's
  link, and focus arriving outside closes the panel by itself, so the case
  cannot tell that close from the press's; it holds the press's own close in
  `on-select`.
- **A Cover size step** is heard by the `ResizeObserver` and the style watch
  each, so "lies under its card and inside the page area after a Cover size
  step, in on-select mode" fails only with both removed: dropping `laidFor`,
  the defect the plan named for it, cannot fail it, and the cover size is
  not in `laidFor`.

**The try.** The owner tried the branch once the Tab bridge was built,
before the whole-branch review, served from a scratch copy of the test
library's store beside a build of main. One round: "ok all good", with
nothing asked to change.

Before the build the owner ruled the plan's two open questions, each on the
pre-flight's recommended option, and kept its six settled points. With the
row scrolled sideways under an open panel, the panel follows its card, held
to the page area, and closes after the editor's save once the card has
wholly left the row's view; the other options were a panel that follows and
never closes by a scroll, resting at the area's edge under no card, and one
that any sideways scroll closes. With `panel` set to `off` or `on-select`,
no Continue card has ↓ on its cover's corner; the other option was ↓ there
in those two modes, as on a volume's tile. The settled points: an unreadable
card has no `i`; ↓ Download in the row's panel downloads the edition the
card shows; the home page's View lists Panel; the home page keeps its
scrollbar's gutter (keyed to the head since, as above); `on-select` on the
row is the series page's, literally; and the panel's top is the row's foot.

**The whole-branch review and its rounds.** The review read the branch as
the owner had tried it: no Critical finding, one Important (I1) and three
Minor (M1 to M3), and of the task reviews' deferred minors, eleven to fix
before merge, one to a row and the rest dropped. One wave of fixes followed
and was re-reviewed, then a second round on what that re-review found,
re-reviewed in turn.

- **I1, fixed.** In `on-select`, a move to another card waiting on the
  editor's save was not dropped when focus or the pointer came back into the
  row's panel. On a series page it is: the panel lies inside its tile's
  `li`, whose `onFocusCapture` and `onMouseEnter` choose that tile again,
  which replaces the waiting move. The review ran the same steps in jsdom on
  the row and on a series page: the row's panel moved to the other card and
  focus fell to `<body>`, and the series page's stayed. `VolumePanel` now
  takes `onFocusCapture` and `onMouseEnter`, which the row passes in
  `on-select` to choose the open card, and `crossed` keeps the pointer's
  crossing between the card and its panel from choosing either, which would
  drop a move the series page keeps. The cases under "on select, a move to
  another card waiting on the save" in `Library.test.tsx` hold it.
- **Its `button`-mode twin is O438.** With a changed title, focus moved
  outside the tile and its panel asks the close, which waits on the save;
  focus brought back into the panel cancels nothing, and once the save lands
  the panel closes and focus falls to `<body>`. The review ran it on a
  series page as it was before this PR as well as on both screens on the
  branch, with that outcome on each, so it is not this PR's, and it is filed
  rather than fixed: the fix changes the series page and needs a case in
  `Series.test.tsx`, which the plan froze.
- **M1, and a loop it uncovered.** In `on-select`, with the pointer holding
  an earlier card's panel open, Shift+Tab up from the chips met the panel
  before the cards after its own, and passed them by. Fixing it found the
  forward half, which the review had not listed: with a failed save holding
  an earlier card's panel open, Tab from the row's last stop entered the
  panel again, went on to the next card and round the row, with no way out
  by Tab. While the open card does not hold the row's last stop (`away`),
  Tab from that stop now goes on to the first stop after the row, and
  Shift+Tab from there back to it. That stop, the first chip, lies outside
  the row's section, so `tabAcross` is heard on the document while a panel
  is drawn, not on the section. Browser cases with real keys hold both:
  "comes to the last card first while the pointer holds an earlier card’s
  panel open on select, then to each card before it" and "goes on from the
  row’s last stop to the first chip, not into the panel again, while a save
  that failed holds an earlier card’s panel open".
- **Which waiting closes a return drops.** As first fixed, focus or the
  pointer coming into the panel dropped any close waiting on the save, the
  close for a card that has left the row's view included, which left a panel
  open under a card out of view. The row follows the series page instead: in
  `on-select`, where focus or the pointer coming back into a series page's
  tile drops a close waiting on the save (a jsdom run on the series page
  showed it for a press outside), the row's panel drops one too, and the
  close the row alone has, for its card wholly out of view, stays waiting
  (`leave`, and `held` in `focused` and `pointed`).
- **N1, made by that round and fixed in the next.** The view's close stayed
  waiting in `on-select` when focus or the pointer came onto the card itself
  too, though focus scrolls the card into view and the pointer reaches it
  only in view: once the save landed, the panel closed under a card just
  focused or pointed at. The first re-review found it by a jsdom run.
  `follow`'s `lay` now calls `stay` as the card comes back into the row's
  view, which drops a waiting view close and nothing else; that also keeps a
  panel open on a card scrolled back with nothing focused, which closed
  before the fix wave as well. "stays open on its card in %s mode once its
  save lands, the card having left the row’s view and come back", in both
  modes, and its `on-select` cases for focus and the pointer coming onto the
  card hold it.
- **The guard.** `stay` asks for the open card again only while the view's
  close is the newest call waiting on the save (`held`); unguarded, it would
  drop whatever waited. "leaves %s waiting on the save as its card comes
  back into the row’s view, and makes it once the save lands", run for an
  Escape close and for a move to another card, fails with the guard removed.
- **O439, left open.** Read, not run: a new answer runs `follow` again with
  `inView` true, so a read that brings the card back into view while its
  close waits is not seen as the card coming back, and a run with the card
  still out asks `leave` again over an Escape close or a move waiting on the
  same save. A page read must land while a save is out; it is filed rather
  than fixed in a third round.
- **The rest** renamed the follow's `shown` to `inView`, corrected false
  comments and a test title that claimed what its case could not fail, and
  made a browser case wait for the series page to be drawn before reading
  it.

## The reader's way back and the browser's history (O431)

2026-11-22, the PR that closes O431 and with it O430 (the comic page takes
no selection) and O434 (the way back's guard reset). Their rows in
`docs/status.md` say what the PR does. The pre-flights, the plan and the
ledger are under `.superpowers/sdd/` (`2026-11-22-o431/`), which is not
committed; this section holds what the rows point to, and the owner's
rulings behind each FLAG label they cite.

**The rule.** Each reader hands its route its work's series as the library's
answer for the work lands (`App.tsx`'s and `BookReader.tsx`'s `onSeries`),
and `Routes.tsx`'s `WayOut` hands that series page, `/series/{id}`, to
`back.ts`'s `useBack`. Under "Back from reading"'s default, "Series page",
every way out, the top bar's button, `L`, `Escape` with nothing open and a
failed load's button, is then named "Series", and:

- steps back (`navigate(-1)`) where the series page is the entry under the
  reader's: the reader's entry carries the mark (`BENEATH`), or the
  in-memory record says the entry was pushed from that page, compared by
  pathname so that an `?edition=` or `?library=` on it changes nothing, or
  the hook's own rewrite has just run (`rewritten`), which covers an `L`
  whose own `keydown` made the rewrite before React drew the entry it
  pushed;
- otherwise puts the series page in the reader's place, by a replace, with
  no entry before it too. A press of the button, `L` or a failed load's
  button is itself an input, so the rewrite below runs first and the press
  steps back; only `Escape`, which is not one, meets a reader with nothing
  under it.

A work in no series, and a reader whose answer is still out or has failed,
keep O422's rule: a step back where an entry of this app comes before the
reader's, else a push of the last Library view drawn in the tab, or of `/`.
After a reload the mark is still on the entry, so the reader steps back as
it did before. An entry with neither the mark nor the record, after a reload
before the answer first landed or on an entry an older build pushed, is
taken as not opened from its series page: the way out puts the series page
in its place, or the next input puts it under, which can leave the series
page in the history twice.

**The stamp and the rewrite.** The reader puts its series page under itself
once, in one of two ways:

- *The stamp*, under either value of the setting below. A reader whose entry
  was pushed from its series page replaces its own entry with the same
  address and the mark, as the answer lands. A replace, which no browser
  skips on its Back.
- *The rewrite*, under "Series page" only. Any other reader of a work in a
  series replaces its entry with the series page, writing into that entry's
  state the address the reader was pushed from (`CAME_FROM`), and in the
  same synchronous step pushes its own address again, with its state and the
  mark. React draws only the last of the two, so the series page is not
  drawn on the way. It happens as the answer lands where the click that
  opened the reader is still the page's activation
  (`navigator.userActivation` active, the reader drawn under 5 s ago) and
  the browser is not Firefox (`rewritesAtAnswer`), and otherwise at the
  first input the HTML spec counts as an activation (`countsAsInput`: a key
  but `Escape`, a mouse's press, any other pointer's lift, a touch's end),
  heard on `window` as it is captured, so that it runs before the way out's
  handlers, which bubble, and `L`'s way out finds the page under the reader.
  A press of a way out disarms it, and so does a `popstate` while the reader
  is drawn: a push then would land over the entry the step is going to.

**Why at that moment: what each browser keeps on its Back.** Each of the
three engines skips, on its Back, some entries a page pushed by script. From
their sources, as the design read them:

- **Chromium** (Chrome, Edge, Chrome on Android).
  `navigation_controller_impl.cc`'s `SetShouldSkipOnBackForwardUIIfNeeded`
  marks the entry a script's push leaves, and every entry of the same
  document, as skipped by Back while the document has no sticky user
  activation (a click, tap or key since it loaded, which a browser-initiated
  same-document Back or Forward stops counting until the next one), and a
  later activation clears the marks (`NotifyUserActivation`; Chromium's
  `docs/history_manipulation_intervention.md` says the same). So a page that
  has had a click keeps a push it makes later with no input, and for a
  reader opened from a typed address, a bookmark, a fresh tab or a reload,
  Back skips every entry of the reader's document under a push made before
  the first input, until that input clears the marks.
- **WebKit** (Safari, and every browser on an iPhone).
  `HistoryController.cpp`'s `pushState` flags the new item as added without
  user interaction unless a gesture is being handled or the window's last
  activation is under 10 s old, and `replaceState` flags nothing. Back from
  a flagged item, by `WebBackForwardList.cpp`'s
  `itemStartingAtIndexSkippingItemsAddedByJSWithoutUserGesture`, which
  Safari's button and its swipe both take, passes the nearest unflagged item
  behind it and lands on the one before that, unless the unflagged item is
  the tab's first, so Back from a reader pushed again within 10 s of a tap
  lands on the series page, and Back from one pushed later passes it unless
  it is the tab's first entry.
- **Firefox** (desktop and Android). With
  `browser.navigation.requireUserInteraction` on (bug 1939691), Back skips
  every entry, but the first and the last, that no user activation reached
  while it was the current entry; a push starts an entry with none, and a
  replace keeps the entry's (`CanonicalBrowsingContext.cpp`). So the series
  page put under a reader survives Back only where an input reached the
  reader's entry, before the rewrite or in the moment of it, and a click on
  the page the reader was opened from does not count.

The one moment all three keep is a rewrite in the moment of an input made
while the reader is shown, or after one. Chromium and WebKit also keep one
made a few seconds after the click that opened the reader, and Firefox never
does, which is FLAG 4.1 (a)'s split. Firefox's side rests on that reading:
the browser project runs Chromium, which reaches Firefox's timing only
through a stubbed user agent, and no run of the way back in a real Firefox
is recorded.

**How the series reaches the route, and why.** The work's series is in the
library's answer for the work, which each reader asks for anyway, so the
route asks for nothing. Each reader calls `onSeries` from that answer's own
`then`, with the answer's series or `null`: never on a failure, and never
from state, since `BookReader`'s series state starts at `null`, which would
tell the route "in no series" before the answer has said anything. `WayOut`
keeps what it is told and is keyed by the slug under both reader routes
(`ReaderRoute`), so one work's series never reaches another's way out, and
neither does the hook's state for the reader on screen. The other route was
the links: a Continue card would push the series page and then the reader in
its click. Nothing would then be under a reader opened from an address,
Firefox would skip a series page that was never the current entry when the
user touched the page, and a card carries no series, so the API would
change, and so would the Continue row's link, which the O417 lane was
rewriting.

**O434: unreachable before, reachable after.** The reset clears `left` when
another entry is drawn, and it decides one case: a screen that stays mounted
while another entry is drawn, and then stands on the entry it pressed from
again with no press between. react-router keeps a screen mounted across a
change of entry only where both entries match one route, and before O431 no
two adjacent entries the app could make shared the series page's route or a
reader's: no link goes from a series page to another series page, or from a
reader to another reader, and every replace rewrites the screen's own entry.
That was read, not run. Under "Series page", a reader opened from another
series' page puts its own series page directly above that one: `/series/60`,
`/series/41`, the reader. The reader's way out steps back to 41, whose Back
steps back to 60 with the series page staying mounted; the browser's Forward
brings 41 back, still mounted, and its Back steps back again only with the
reset. A reload with neither mark nor record can make another such pair.
`back.browser.test.tsx`'s "steps back from the series page again after
Forward, round after round" walks that path with real clicks, and
`back.hook.test.tsx` holds the reset in CI.

**The O422 cases that moved.** Four browser cases O422 left in
`back.browser.test.tsx` opened the work from series 60's page while the work
is filed in series 41, which under O431 is a reader opened from another
series' page: the reader puts 41 above 60 and its way out steps back to 41.
Each now opens the work from series 41's page, with the same expectations
but the address: "goes from a book that would not open to the series page,
and from there to the grid, each a step back"; "steps back once for Escape
pressed twice in the reader", which also holds the browser's step back until
both presses are in, as the guard's other cases do; "Escape at %i px (O419)"
› "steps back from the comic reader to the series page it was opened from,
round after round"; and "steps back from a book with its bars up from a tap
to the series page it was opened from, round after round (O419)". A reader
opened from another series' page has cases of its own. The stand-in readers
report no series, so their cases still hold O422's rule.

**O430: what Chromium selects, and Firefox.** On the code before the rule, a
probe in the browser project (Chromium, 1280×800, single mode, the pages
real images, each click a real mouse event through CDP with the click count
rising per press) read the selection after each gesture:

| Gesture | Selected |
| --- | --- |
| double click, the page image's centre | nothing |
| double click, the page image's right (turn) third | nothing |
| triple click, the page image's centre | nothing |
| a press at the page area's left edge, dragged level across the image | nothing |
| the same, dragged diagonally | nothing |
| two turn clicks 100 ms apart in the right third, the second a double click's | nothing |
| double click, a gap's title sentence | a word of it |
| double click, a gap's verdict sentence | a word of it |

So `App.browser.test.tsx`'s case double-clicks a gap's sentences: it is the
gesture that selects in the browser the gate runs. Playwright's Firefox was
run against the try's builds of `main` and the branch, served side by side.
On `main`'s, a double-click on the page image selected it, and so did a
second quick page-turn click, sent as a double click's second once the
selection was cleared; the page area's computed `user-select` read `auto`.
On the branch's no step selected anything, and it read `none`.

**The FLAG labels.** The owner's rulings of 2026-11-22, each on a choice a
pre-flight put:

- **FLAG 1 (a)**, a work in no series: O422's rule, unchanged, and `L`'s
  line in Help reads "back to the series, else where you came from" (under
  "Series page", since FLAG 9.6).
- **FLAG 2 (a)**, before the work's answer lands and after it fails: O422's
  rule until the answer names a series, so the button's word may change
  once, to "Series". Nothing is under the reader in that window, so the
  browser's Back goes where the reader was opened from.
- **FLAG 3 (a)**, after a reload, when the record of where the reader was
  opened from is gone: the reader is taken as not opened from its series
  page, which then replaces it. The mark outlives a reload, so this holds
  only for an entry with neither mark nor record.
- **FLAG 4 (b)**, against the pre-flight's recommendation: the browser's
  Back and a phone's back gesture land on the series page too. It was
  designed after the ruling: the stamp, the rewrite and their timing above.
- **FLAG 4.1 (a)**, when the reader puts its series page under itself: as
  the answer lands where the click that opened the reader is fresh and the
  browser is not Firefox, else at the first input.
- **FLAG 5 (a)**, how O430's test fails against its defect: a per-element
  computed-style check in the gate, and Playwright's Firefox once, at the
  try. No Firefox in the gate.
- **FLAG 6 (a)**: the series page that takes the reader's place, or that the
  reader puts under itself, is `/series/{id}`, with no `?library=`, the
  address O427's series link uses.
- **FLAGs 9.1 to 9.6**, on the setting: below.

**The try.** The owner tried the branch over the tailnet beside a build of
`main`, both served from scratch copies of the test library. After it, the
owner asked for two things: "this should actually be a user setting —
whether to go back to the series or back to the home page when you open from
continue", and "there's sometimes flashing when you go back to the series
page from the reader when things reload. can we make a follow up task to
eliminate this?" Asked how far each went, the owner ruled the same day that
the setting goes in this PR, with the series page as its default, as O431
was ruled; that its other value covers every reader not opened from its own
series page, from the Continue row, a typed address or another series' page,
the browser's Back and the swipe included, so that those readers put nothing
under themselves; and that the flash, which `main` shows too, becomes a row
of its own once what flashes is recorded: O440. After the setting was built,
the owner looked briefly and gave the word for the PR: "ok let's do the
review and make the PR". The rounds planned for a second try, the iPhone's
swipe under each value of the setting and a change made in a second tab
among them, were not run.

**The setting.** "Back from reading" (`browseModule.ts`'s
`backFromReading`), a browse preference. The pre-flight of the setting put
six choices to the owner, ruled as follows:

- **FLAG 9.1**: the other value is O422's rule, "where you came from, else
  the last Library view", not the home page always. Where the reader was not
  opened from `/`, no move reaches `/` and keeps the browser's Back in step
  with the way out: a push leaves the reader behind `/` for Back to reopen,
  which is what O422 fixed.
- **FLAG 9.2**: its words, "Back from reading": "Series page" / "Where you
  came from". View words a control from its key and each choice from its own
  spelling (`settingsPanel.ts`'s `humanize`), so the words are the stored
  key and values, `seriesPage` and `whereYouCameFrom`, and changing them
  later is a migration of stored data.
- **FLAG 9.3**: on this device for now, through `prefs.ts`, and a follow-up
  row for account-level settings that moves a bunch of the per-device
  settings to the account: O441.
- **FLAG 9.4**: in the Library view's View panel, after Continue strip
  (`Library.tsx`'s `LIBRARY_VIEW`).
- **FLAG 9.5**: a change applies to the next reader opened.
- **FLAG 9.6**: `L`'s line in each reader's Help follows the setting, the
  pre-flight's option (b), not its recommendation: "back to the series, else
  where you came from" under "Series page", and O422's "back where you came
  from, else the library" under "Where you came from" (`keys.ts`'s
  `wayBackLabel`, handed to both readers' Help as `putsSeriesUnder`).

Why per device: every reader and browse preference is kept per device, in
`localStorage` through `prefs.ts`, whose head doc keeps position and content
on the server, because they must survive a different machine, and layout and
preference on the client; the book's compared editions sit in `localStorage`
too, outside `prefs.ts` (O441). The server stores none, and kept there this
one would have needed a migration, a store function, a route, the value in
the account's answer, a write that can fail on screen, and Rust tests.

Why read as each reader opens: the reader's routes draw no `Shell`, so the
browse preferences' context there holds only the defaults, and `WayOut`
reads storage itself (`loadBrowsePrefs`, through `putsSeriesUnder`) in a
`useState` initialiser, once per reader. Read at every press instead, a
reader's way out could change after its series page is under it, and its
button's word could change under the reader. The View panel is the Library
view's, so the tab a reader is open in cannot change the setting; another
tab can, and its change reaches the next reader opened. A reader drawn
again, by Back, Forward or a reload, reads it again and finds its entry as
it left it: an entry the default marked steps back to the series page under
either value.

The history each value leaves. H is `/`, L2 `/?library=2`, S the work's
series page, S60 another series' page, R the reader, R′ the reader pushed
again by the rewrite, X the tab's page before the app, and `*` the entry on
screen:

| Opened from | "Series page" | "Where you came from" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| its own series page | `[S, R*]`, the entry stamped; the way out and Back step back to S | the same |
| the Continue row on H | `[H, S, R′*]` as the answer lands after a fresh click, or at the first input; the way out and Back land on S, whose Back, "Library", goes to H | `[H, R*]`; the way out and Back step back to H |
| the Continue row on L2 | `[L2, S, R′*]`; S, then L2 | `[L2, R*]`; L2 |
| a typed address | `[X, S, R′*]` from the first input; Back before one goes to X | `[X, R*]`; the way out pushes H, `[X, R, H*]`; Back from R goes to X |
| another series' page | `[H, S60, S, R′*]`; S, whose Back, "Series", goes to S60 | `[H, S60, R*]`; S60 |
| a reload, with neither mark nor record, after an entry of the app | S, in R's place or, after an input, under it | a step back to the entry before, the button reading "Back" |
| a reload of a stamped or rewritten entry | a step back to S | the same |
| a work in no series, or before its answer | O422's rule | O422's rule |

**The whole-branch review's fix, and what it leaves.** Choosing an edition
on a series page the reader had put under itself dropped that page's Back
word: `Series.tsx`'s edition replace writes no navigation state, so
`CAME_FROM` went with the entry it replaced, and the Back read "Back".
`useBackTracker` now hands a replaced entry's `CAME_FROM` on, as the record
for the entry taking its place, so the Back keeps its word. That record is
in memory, so after an edition is chosen there a reload names the Back
"Back"; it still steps back to the same entry. The review also asked for a
case for the reset's `POP` half, which `back.hook.test.tsx` now has.

**Left open.** Going back to a series page can draw it with every cover
missing for a moment, on `main` too, and under "Series page" a reader opened
from a Continue card goes back to a series page the tab may not have drawn,
whose covers then come in one by one: O440. Every setting, this one
included, is kept on the device it was made on: O441.

## O314: volumes appear as a scan goes (2026-11-23)

O314's row in `docs/status.md` says what the PR builds, and its design is
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-22-first-scan-series-as-they-finish-design.md`.
The plan, the ledger and the drive's evidence are under
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-22-o314/`, which is not committed. The drive's
write-up is `evidence/drive.md` there, and each figure below names the file
beside it in that `evidence/` directory.

**The drive.** A release build of the branch, before the restart work below,
served a scratch store over copies of the test library on this machine:
Yotsuba&! from Volumes in one directory, the other 45 Volumes series in a
second, and seven Raw series in a third, every schedule Off. Matching by
content was off for the library: left on, its fingerprint pass would have
read every file during the drive, and main's one derive, the comparison, runs
no such pass. Headless Chromium tabs held a reader's Library view, loaded
once, and the admin's library page, with a feed logger and a store logger
beside them. The drive scanned the first directory alone, pressed Scan
library, cancelled at 45 % of the bytes, pressed it again, stopped the server
mid-job and started it, and pressed Scan library to finish
(`drive-steps.jsonl`, `restart-drill.json`).

- **Passes in the server's job.** The `written` marker moved 27 times across
  the three Scan library jobs (`feed-marker-moves.txt`). In the first of
  them the admin's line went from 13 to 254 volumes ready (`admin-ready-count.txt`); the
  reader's line said a scan was running, with no counts.
- **Series arrive without a reload.** The reader's view, loaded once, went
  from one card to 49 by the scan's end (`dom-R1.jsonl`), and in that first
  Scan library job it read the series and home views again once per marker
  move
  (`reader-feed-intervals.txt`).
- **Both editions at once, and nothing moves.** 85 volumes were first seen
  holding both the `en` and the `ja` edition. The store logger saw no work
  change slug, editions, series, content key or hub after it first appeared,
  across the Cancel and the restart (`store-log.jsonl`).
- **Reading during a scan.** A page read in Berserk v01, which a pass had
  written, during the job after the restart was the same page at the same
  URL after the job, and its progress row named the same work
  (`reading-during-scan.json`, `drive-steps.jsonl`).
- **Cancel.** The store held the same 269 works, with the same ids, slugs and
  editions, before the Cancel and after it, and all three directories were
  paused (`store-before-cancel.json`, `store-after-cancel.json`,
  `roots-after-cancel.json`).
- **The same library as one derive.** Main's CLI `library scan`, one derive
  over the same three copies in the same order with the same keys, made the
  same 687 works, each identical in series, volume, title, slug, hub,
  content key, editions with their members, and `member_root` count; a slug
  altered in memory made the comparison find one difference
  (`compare-branch-vs-main.json`). Neither of the two differences the
  design accepts (its call 14) arose in this material.
- **Pass time.** A pass took 114 to 793 ms over 847 `scan_entry` rows, timed
  from `strace`, which makes the write part an upper bound, and the 10 s
  floor set every gap between passes (`pass-timing.txt`). Rule 3's
  directory check sits in the part before a pass's first write, which took
  at most 25 ms, so no row is opened for a pass's cost at this size.
- **Polling.** The reader's view asked the feed a median 5.0 s apart with no
  scan and 1.0 s apart while one held the library
  (`reader-feed-intervals.txt`).
- **Not staged.** The hand-off where a pass writes a library's first works
  into an empty view; `web/tests/Library.test.tsx`'s "the line holds
  through the commit that swaps Scanning for a scan’s first works" covers it.
- **Isolation.** A listing of the test library (path, size, mtime, inode,
  link count) was byte-identical before and after, and its store's digests
  were equal (`manga-test-before.tsv`, `manga-test-after.tsv`,
  `manga-test-db-sha256-before.txt`, `-after.txt`).

What the drive found:

- **A restart did not take the job up.** A start took up only directories
  whose schedule is not Off, so for six minutes, until Scan library was
  pressed, no job ran and every directory read `interrupted`
  (`roots-after-restart.json`); main does the same. The owner answered "a"
  on 2026-11-23, and the PR builds it (below). Also seen: after the stop
  signal the job's thread hashed one more file and ran one more pass,
  writing 14 works, before the process exited (`store-log.jsonl`).
- **The grid moves (O453).** Under the Added sort every arrival moved the
  cards in view, with scroll anchoring on or off. Under the title sort
  "[Oshi no Ko]" and its Fan Translated series were hashed last and drawn
  first, so the last pass put them above all 45 series drawn
  (`arrivals-vs-title-order.txt`).
- **A stale scan line (O451).** A tab going back to the Library view after
  the scan ended drew the kept "A scan is running" for one frame
  (`dom-R2.jsonl`).
- **Scanning to the grid.** At a scan's end the view passed through "Not
  read yet" and "Nothing here" in the DOM for 2 to 6 ms, and in the one run
  sampled per frame neither was painted (`dom-R2.jsonl`). No row is opened
  for it here.

**What a restart does now** (the owner's answer "a" of 2026-11-23, and the
controller's ruling that day on migration 032; no drive ran after it). A scan
job marks its directories held (`root.scan_held_at`, migration 032) in the
write that says it waits for the job lock, and again once it holds that lock,
and clears the mark when it ends, a cancel's or an error's end included. A
stop leaves the mark, and the next start takes up every held directory
whatever its schedule, unless a cancel paused it. So a restart now scans an
Off directory again where it used to leave it reading `interrupted` until
Scan was pressed. Migration 032 marks no directory and the start marks none,
so a scan cut by a stop of an older version is not taken up by a mark, one
main was running when this version deploys included, and waits for Scan or
its schedule as before: a directory reading
`interrupted` from before says nothing of whether its scan is still wanted,
and the owner's Volumes/Raw import of 2026-11-16 was stopped on purpose,
which a backfill would have restarted at the first start after the deploy.
The cancel route clears the mark as it accepts a cancel, before the job
writes its pause, so a stop between the two leaves nothing to take up. What
is left is in the design's §7: a stop after a job starts and before its first
mark leaves none, and the clearing is best effort, one UPDATE per directory,
each able to wait out the 5 s busy timeout, so a cancel can answer slowly
and a clearing that late can wipe a newer job's mark.

**The mutation sweep** is in `docs/mutants-baseline.md`'s run log, its two
rows of 2026-11-23; the factor no test pins is O454.
*O454 has since closed.*

`sha256 IS NULL` dropped fails no test. The narrowing implies the clause: the
set of entries a pass waits on holds only entries with no digest, so the

No run put any other clause of the statement wrong, so no other clause is
watched failing.

**O450, narrowed.** By the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 a row of the stray
statement names its directory only while the pass waits on its entry.
`grouped`, in an early pass, puts each entry `hashes` accepts into `Waiting`:
the entries the queue has still to hash, a file the queue found gone among
them, since it keeps no digest. `named_directories` passes over a
stray-statement row outside that set. The SQL is as it was, and the first
statement's rows are not filtered.

Why it is safe, by a reading with one run beside it. Whether the full derive
stages an entry is decided, its digest apart, by the walk's row and the rules:
`admit`, `read_input`'s two drops and `classify`'s returns before it reads a
digest look at nothing else but the list of files the queue found gone, which
only takes entries out, and `hashes` is that test with "holds no digest"
added. One `Setup` serves the queue, every pass and the full derive. So in a
directory the job does not read frozen, an entry the full derive stages was
waited on at every pass where it held no digest, and a row a pass does not
wait on while it holds no digest is staged by no derive of the job, whoever
gives it one later: the full derive's tail (`digest_held_members`, which
hashes an entry a member names by path) or the fingerprint pass
(`fingerprints::record_digest`). Beside such an entry a pass writes what the
full derive writes. A directory the job reads frozen is the exception: paused
when the job read its `Setup` and unpaused while it runs, a row there can be
given a digest by the fingerprint pass, which asks the pause as it stands, and
where a member of the directory holds that digest `frozen_entries` then hands
on a row no pass waited on. No early write turns on it: every row
`frozen_entries` hands on with pages, a chapter apart, holds a digest a member
of the directory holds, so rule 2 (`bytes_held`) holds back every group with a
file there. The run is the tail's test, below.

The four tests. The first three stand over `beside_a_stray`, a joined raw 5
deleted:

- `a_pass_writes_a_volume_beside_a_chapter_file_of_a_gone_matched_files_page_count`:
  a chapter-only file at the stray's count beside a new raw 4, which is
  written early;
- `a_pass_writes_a_volume_beside_a_chapters_folder_of_a_gone_matched_files_page_count`:
  the same beside a chapter's folder of loose images totalling that count;
- `a_pass_leaves_a_volume_beside_a_file_of_a_strays_page_count_the_queue_found_gone`:
  raw 3 at the stray's count, deleted after the walk, and no pass writes raw 4
  beside it;
- `a_pass_writes_a_volume_beside_a_file_only_the_full_derives_tail_hashes`: a
  file a second directory, Inner, reads no series from, whose digest is a
  stray once the first directory excludes its folder. Volume 5 beside it is
  written early, the queue hashes the two volumes alone, and the entry holds
  the stray's digest after the job. Its stray is made by an exclude glob, not
  a deletion.

On the code before the narrowing the first, second and fourth failed and the
third passed. Put wrong by hand:

- the filter removed: the chapter file's, the chapter's folder's and the
  tail's tests;
- the filter inverted: all four, with the moved, folder and gone tests above;
- the set left empty, `grouped` adding no entry to it: the gone-file test,
  with the moved, folder and gone tests.

Each of the three was run by the task's implementer and again by its review.
The review's report (`task-5-review.md` in the uncommitted directory) names
four more hand mutations; its logs for them are the `task-5-review-m*.log`
files under `logs/` there, uncommitted as the rest. A file not on disk left
out of the set failed the gone-file test alone. The tail's call removed, and
the tail also run before the grouping, each with the tail's test run alone,
failed it in its second assertion. The filter comparing `rel_path` alone,
without the root, failed no test of `derive::fill`.

**What the cost runs found.** Each was a temporary test, removed after it ran,
on the code as it stood before the narrowing, which leaves the hold of an
entry the queue hashes as it was.

- A stored match that never joined (a pair stored directly at a score too low
  to join), one file then deleted: its work is marked missing, so its member

  root, holding a file still to hash at that page count, had none of its
  volumes written by a pass; at another count, it did.
- Over the gone test's stray, in the other root: a directory holding a file of

  was hashed, which wrote the directory's volumes hashed by then.
- Over the same stray, a volume-less folder at its count, which the queue

Two more of those runs no longer describe the code. A chapter-only file at the
stray's count, and a chapter's folder of loose images at it, each held a
directory to the full derive; each is now one of the four tests above, which
asserts that the volume beside it is written early.

Every cost run made its stray by deleting a matched file; none dropped one's
entry by an exclude glob.

FR2 copy row after the walk: root 3 Oshinoko/Oshinoko v05.cbz sha256=raw5's held=NULL pages=Some(3)

At the one write a pass made, raw 4's work read `series=Some("Oshinoko")

One way to close it, neither built nor run, is to read as a stray a matched
